s23g-s0101.bodyHtml:
Every comparison in epidemiology starts with counting cases and dividing by the right denominator. The exam rewards one habit above all: before you calculate, name the numerator (who counts as a case), the denominator (who could have become a case, or how much time was observed) and the time frame.

Incidence: new cases

Incidence counts new cases arising in people who were free of the disease at the start. It comes in two forms.

  • Cumulative incidence (risk, incidence proportion) = new cases during a period ÷ people at risk at the start of the period. It is a proportion between 0 and 1 and needs a stated time frame ("a 5-year risk of 3%"). It assumes everyone was followed for the whole period.
  • Incidence rate (incidence density) = new cases ÷ total person-time at risk. Its unit is "per person-year" (or per 1,000 catheter-days, per 100,000 person-years). It handles people who enter late, leave early or are lost, because each contributes only the time actually observed while at risk.

Worked example: a cohort of 500 nurses is free of asthma at baseline. 300 are followed for 4 years and 200 leave after 1 year on average. Person-time = 300 × 4 + 200 × 1 = 1,400 person-years. If 21 develop asthma, the incidence rate is 21 ÷ 1,400 = 15 per 1,000 person-years. Using 500 × 4 = 2,000 person-years as the denominator would understate the rate (10.5 per 1,000), because it credits the leavers with time nobody observed.

The attack rate is a cumulative incidence used for a short, well-defined exposure window, typically an outbreak: ill people ÷ people exposed. The secondary attack rate is new cases among susceptible contacts of an index case ÷ the number of susceptible contacts (the index cases and already-immune contacts are left out of both numerator and denominator).

Prevalence: existing cases

Prevalence = all existing cases (new and old) ÷ the population at that time. Point prevalence refers to one moment ("on 1 March, 8% had active eczema"); period prevalence counts anyone who had the condition at any time during an interval ("in the past 12 months"), so it is always at least as large as the point prevalence at the start of the interval. Cross-sectional surveys measure prevalence, not incidence.

In a steady state, and for a condition that is uncommon, prevalence ≈ incidence rate × average duration. If 3 new cases arise per 1,000 people per year and the disease lasts 6 years on average, roughly 18 per 1,000 (1.8%) have it at any moment.

ChangeIncidencePrevalence
Treatment that prolongs survival but does not cureUnchangedRises
Treatment that cures quicklyUnchangedFalls
Disease becomes more rapidly fatalUnchangedFalls
Successful primary prevention (e.g. vaccination)FallsFalls (over time)
Wider diagnostic criteria or a more sensitive testRises (recorded)Rises (recorded)
Immigration of people who already have the diseaseUnchangedRises

A rise in prevalence is not proof that a disease is becoming more common. It can mean people are living longer with it. Always ask whether incidence or duration changed. Conversely, a drop in prevalence after a new therapy can be good news (cure) or bad news (faster death).

Fatality and mortality

The case-fatality rate (really a proportion) = deaths from the disease ÷ people with the disease, over a defined course. It measures how lethal the disease is for those who get it. The cause-specific mortality rate = deaths from the disease ÷ the whole population at risk (usually per 100,000 per year); it depends on both how common and how lethal the disease is. The crude mortality rate uses deaths from all causes over the whole population. Proportionate mortality = deaths from one cause ÷ all deaths; it is not a rate and can rise simply because other causes fall.

Crude, specific and adjusted rates

A crude rate describes the whole population; specific rates describe a subgroup (age-specific, sex-specific). Because death and most chronic diseases rise steeply with age, two populations with identical age-specific rates can have very different crude rates if one is older. Standardisation removes that difference.

  • Direct standardisation: apply each population's age-specific rates to one standard population and compare the resulting "expected" totals. Needs reliable age-specific rates in each population being compared.
  • Indirect standardisation: apply standard (reference) age-specific rates to the study population's age structure to get the number of expected deaths, then compute the standardised mortality ratio (SMR) = observed ÷ expected. Useful when the study group is small (an occupational cohort) and its own age-specific rates are unstable.

An SMR of 1.0 means deaths are as expected; 1.25 means 25% more deaths than expected for the group's age structure; 0.8 means 20% fewer. Healthy working cohorts often have an SMR below 1 for all-cause mortality (the healthy worker effect), because people who are seriously ill tend not to be employed.

Rule of thumb for questions: comparing two places or two eras with different age structures needs age-adjusted rates; planning services (beds, clinics, drug budgets) needs crude counts and crude rates, because the real number of patients is what has to be served.

Prevalence drives predictive values: the same test has a higher positive predictive value where the condition is more prevalent (see the screening-test sections).

s23g-s0102.bodyHtml:
Health status measures describe how healthy a population or a patient is, rather than how often one disease occurs. They fall into four groups: mortality-based measures, morbidity measures, measures of function and patient-reported measures. Each has a fixed definition and denominator that the exam expects you to know exactly.

Mortality around birth and pregnancy

MeasureNumeratorDenominator
Infant mortality rateDeaths before age 1 year1,000 live births in the same year
Neonatal mortality rateDeaths in the first 27 days of life (under 28 days)1,000 live births
Postneonatal mortality rateDeaths from 28 days to under 1 year1,000 live births
Fetal death rateFetal deaths (stillbirths) above a stated gestational age1,000 live births plus fetal deaths
Perinatal mortality rateLate fetal deaths plus early neonatal deaths (definitions vary; one common US version uses fetal deaths at ≥28 weeks plus infant deaths under 7 days)1,000 live births plus those fetal deaths
Maternal mortality ratioDeaths during pregnancy or within 42 days of its end from causes related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management (not accidental or incidental causes)100,000 live births

Two points are tested repeatedly. First, the infant, neonatal and postneonatal rates all use live births as the denominator, not the number of infants alive; neonatal plus postneonatal equals infant mortality. Second, any measure that includes fetal deaths must add them to the denominator, because a stillborn fetus was "at risk" too. The maternal measure is called a ratio because live births are not the population at risk (women who were pregnant are).

The causes differ by period. Neonatal deaths are dominated by preterm birth and low birthweight, congenital anomalies and complications of labour, so they reflect prenatal and perinatal care. Postneonatal deaths are more often due to sudden unexpected infant death, infections and injuries, so they track the home environment and social conditions.

Life expectancy and premature death

Period life expectancy at age x is the average number of further years a person aged x would live if current age-specific death rates stayed fixed for the rest of their life. It is a summary of today's death rates, not a forecast. Life expectancy at age 65 plus 65 is always larger than life expectancy at birth, because people who reach 65 have already escaped the deaths of infancy, youth and middle age.

Years of potential life lost (YPLL) weights deaths by how early they occur. With a cut-off of 75 years, each death before 75 adds (75 − age at death); deaths at 75 or older add zero, never a negative number. Worked example: deaths at ages 2, 30 and 70 and one at 88 give 73 + 45 + 5 + 0 = 123 YPLL. Causes that kill the young (injuries, overdose, suicide, perinatal conditions) rank far higher by YPLL than by death counts.

When a stem lists a death above the cut-off age, it contributes zero YPLL. Subtracting it as a negative number, or counting the excess years, is the planted error.

Morbidity, function and self-report

Morbidity measures include incidence and prevalence of disease, hospitalisation rates, days of restricted activity and disability prevalence. Functional status describes what a person can do:

DomainExamplesWhat loss implies
Basic activities of daily living (ADLs)Bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, feedingNeeds hands-on personal care
Instrumental ADLs (IADLs)Managing money and medications, shopping, cooking, housework, using the telephone, transportNeeds help to live independently; often the first sign of cognitive decline
Mobility and performance measuresGait speed, timed up-and-go, chair standsPredict falls, disability and hospitalisation in older adults

IADLs are lost before basic ADLs in most progressive conditions, and the basic ADLs tend to be lost in a typical order, with feeding among the last. Self-rated health ("In general, would you say your health is excellent, very good, good, fair or poor?") is a single question that predicts mortality and future disability even after adjusting for diagnosed disease and examination findings, so it is a genuine measure, not a soft add-on. Health-related quality-of-life instruments and other patient-reported outcome measures capture symptoms and function from the patient's side.

Match the measure to the question: lethality → case-fatality; burden on a population → mortality rate or YPLL; independence of an older patient → ADLs and IADLs; how a treatment changes daily life → a validated patient-reported outcome measure.

Mortality and disability can be combined into single summary measures, DALYs and QALYs, covered in the next section.

s23g-s0103.bodyHtml:
Survival analysis studies the time until an event (death, relapse, hospital admission, device failure). Its special problem is that follow-up ends before the event for many participants: they are still well when the study closes, they move away or they withdraw. These participants are censored. Their data say "event-free for at least this long", which is real information, so they are kept in the analysis up to the moment they leave.

The Kaplan-Meier estimate

The Kaplan-Meier (product-limit) method recalculates survival each time an event occurs. At each event time, the conditional probability of surviving that moment is (number at risk − events) ÷ number at risk, and survival so far is the product of all these conditional probabilities. People censored before an event time are simply removed from the number at risk; they are never counted as events.

Worked example: 40 patients start. At month 2, 4 die: survival = 36/40 = 0.90. Three are censored before month 5. At month 5, 33 are at risk and 3 die: survival = 0.90 × 30/33 ≈ 0.818. Counting the three censored patients as deaths would have given (40 − 10) ÷ 40 = 0.75, an underestimate; ignoring that they left (treating them as survivors to the end) would have given (40 − 7) ÷ 40 ≈ 0.825, an overestimate that grows as censoring increases.

Reading a curve

  • The curve starts at 1.0 (everyone event-free) and only steps down, at the times events occur. Flat stretches are periods without events.
  • Small vertical tick marks on the curve show censoring. The curve does not drop at a tick.
  • Survival at time t: go up from t on the x-axis to the curve, then across to the y-axis.
  • Median survival: the earliest time at which the curve falls to 0.5 or below. Draw across from 0.5 and down from where you first meet the curve. If the curve never reaches 0.5, the median is "not reached".
  • Numbers at risk printed under the x-axis tell you how much information supports each part of the curve. Late portions with few people at risk are imprecise; one event can move a tail that rests on 8 patients by more than 10 percentage points.

Censoring is not death. A tick mark means the person was lost from view while event-free. A stem that says "patients who withdrew were counted as deaths" is describing a biased analysis that underestimates survival.

Comparing curves

The log-rank test compares two or more Kaplan-Meier curves over the whole follow-up: at every event time it compares observed with expected events in each group and sums the differences. It gives a P value, not an effect size. Comparing the proportion alive at one chosen time point (with a chi-square test) wastes information and invites cherry-picking the time point.

The hazard is the instantaneous event rate among those still at risk. The hazard ratio (HR), usually from a Cox proportional hazards model, compares hazards between groups and can be adjusted for covariates.

Hazard ratioMeaning (treatment vs control)
1.0No difference in event rate
0.70At any given time, a 30% lower event rate among those still at risk
1.5A 50% higher event rate at any given time
95% CI includes 1.0Not statistically significant at α = 0.05

An HR is not a ratio of cumulative proportions and does not say "30% fewer people die by the end". It also does not translate directly into a gain in median survival. The Cox model assumes proportional hazards: the ratio stays roughly constant over time. Curves that cross (for example, early operative deaths followed by long-term benefit) violate this, and one overall HR then hides an early harm and a later benefit.

Assumptions

  • Non-informative censoring: people censored at time t have the same future risk as those who remain. If the sickest patients drop out (too ill to attend), the remaining group looks healthier and the curve overestimates survival.
  • Survival prospects do not change with calendar time of enrolment.
  • Event times are recorded accurately.

Three facts answer most curve questions: the median is read at 0.5 on the y-axis; tick marks are censored people, not events; and separation of the curves early versus late tells you when the benefit (or harm) happens, which a single hazard ratio cannot.

Survival gains in screened groups can be an illusion created by lead time; see the section on points of intervention.

s23g-s0104.bodyHtml:
Two families of measures appear here. Composite health indicators (DALYs, QALYs) fold death and disability into one number so that very different conditions can be compared. Measures of impact (attributable risk, population attributable risk, number needed to treat or harm) translate an association into how many cases an exposure causes or a treatment prevents.

DALYs and QALYs

DALY (disability-adjusted life year)QALY (quality-adjusted life year)
MeasuresHealth lost; one DALY = one year of healthy life lostHealth gained or lived; one QALY = one year in perfect health
FormulaDALY = YLL + YLDQALY = years lived × utility (0 = dead, 1 = full health)
WeightDisability weight: 0 = full health, 1 = equivalent to deathUtility: 1 = full health, 0 = death
Typical useRanking the burden of disease in populationsCost-utility analysis of treatments
GoalFewer is better (avert DALYs)More is better (gain QALYs)
  • YLL (years of life lost) = deaths × standard life expectancy remaining at the age of death.
  • YLD (years lived with disability) = cases (prevalent, in the commonly used approach) × disability weight × duration in the period.

Worked example: a disease causes 10 deaths, each losing 40 years (400 YLL), and 500 people live with it for a year at a disability weight of 0.2 (100 YLD); the burden is 500 DALYs. Conditions that rarely kill but disable many people for years, such as depressive disorders, low back pain and hearing loss, rank much higher by DALYs than by deaths.

QALYs in cost-effectiveness

The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) = (cost of new − cost of old) ÷ (QALYs of new − QALYs of old), expressed as cost per QALY gained. A strategy that costs more and yields fewer QALYs than an alternative is dominated and is dropped without computing a ratio. A strategy that costs less and yields more QALYs dominates. Worked example: a new regimen costs $50,000 and gives 6.0 QALYs; the old one costs $20,000 and gives 5.4 QALYs. ICER = $30,000 ÷ 0.6 = $50,000 per QALY gained. Dividing total cost by total QALYs for one option (an average ratio) is the classic wrong answer.

Attributable risk

Let Ie be incidence in the exposed, Iu in the unexposed and Ip in the whole population.

MeasureFormulaQuestion it answers
Attributable risk (risk difference)Ie − IuHow much extra risk does exposure add for an exposed person?
Attributable risk percent (in the exposed)(Ie − Iu) ÷ Ie = (RR − 1) ÷ RRWhat share of an exposed person's risk is due to the exposure?
Population attributable riskIp − IuHow much of the population's incidence is due to the exposure?
Population attributable fraction (PAR%)(Ip − Iu) ÷ Ip = Pe(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + Pe(RR − 1)]What share of all cases in the population would disappear if the exposure were removed?

Worked example: incidence is 12 per 1,000 in exposed people and 3 per 1,000 in unexposed people (RR = 4). AR = 9 per 1,000; AR% = 9 ÷ 12 = 75%. If 20% of the population is exposed, PAR% = 0.2 × 3 ÷ (1 + 0.6) = 37.5%. The same RR gives a much larger PAR% when the exposure is common: at 60% exposure, PAR% = 1.8 ÷ 2.8 ≈ 64%.

A strong risk factor is not necessarily the most important one for a population. A rare exposure with RR 10 can account for fewer cases than a common exposure with RR 1.5. Questions about "how many cases in the community could be prevented" want the PAR, which depends on both the RR and how common the exposure is.

Number needed to treat and to harm

NNT = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction; NNH = 1 ÷ absolute risk increase. Both must be tied to the time frame of the study ("treat 25 people for 3 years to prevent one stroke"), and both are rounded up to the next whole person. At the population level, the number of events prevented = people treated ÷ NNT, which is why a treatment with a modest relative effect can prevent many events when the baseline risk is high.

Relative measures (RR, HR, relative risk reduction) say how strong an effect is; absolute measures (risk difference, NNT, attributable risk, PAR) say how much it matters for a patient or a population. Decisions need the absolute ones.

to the next whole person. At the population level, the number of events prevented = people treated ÷ NNT, which is why a treatment with a modest relative effect can prevent many events when the baseline risk is high.

Relative measures (RR, HR, relative risk reduction) say how strong an effect is; absolute measures (risk difference, NNT, attributable risk, PAR) say how much it matters for a patient or a population. Decisions need the absolute ones.

s23g-s0105.bodyHtml:
A population pyramid is a pair of back-to-back horizontal bar charts: age bands run up the vertical axis, males are drawn on one side and females on the other, and bar length is the number or percentage of the population in each band. Its shape is a record of past births, deaths and migration, and a forecast of the services a population will need.

The three basic shapes

ShapeAppearanceUnderlying ratesTypical service needs
ExpansiveBroad base, steep taper, true pyramidHigh birth rate; high or recently falling death rate; rapid growthMaternal and newborn care, immunisation, child nutrition, schools
ConstrictiveBase narrower than the middle; bulge in middle and older agesBirth rate below replacement for a generation; low death rate; long life expectancy; ageing and possible shrinkingChronic disease care, dementia services, long-term care, falls prevention
Stationary (near-stationary)Roughly equal bars until older ages, then a taperLow birth and death rates that have been stable for decades; little growthBalanced; steady demand across age groups

Irregular features carry their own stories. A bulge of working-age men suggests labour in-migration; a gap in young adults suggests out-migration for work or study; a notch in one cohort can follow war deaths or a birth deficit during a crisis; an excess of women at the oldest ages reflects women's longer life expectancy. A cohort bulge moves up the pyramid by one band every decade, so the "baby boom" of one era becomes the demand for joint replacements and memory clinics 60–70 years later.

Dependency ratios

The total dependency ratio = (people aged 0–14 + people aged 65 and over) ÷ people aged 15–64, usually × 100. It splits into a youth ratio (0–14 ÷ 15–64) and an old-age ratio (65+ ÷ 15–64). Worked example: 24,000 children, 56,000 working-age adults and 20,000 older adults give a total ratio of 44,000 ÷ 56,000 × 100 ≈ 79, a youth ratio of about 43 and an old-age ratio of about 36. Expansive populations have high youth ratios; constrictive ones have high and rising old-age ratios. The denominator is the working-age group, not the whole population.

The demographic transition

  1. Stage 1: high birth and high death rates; small, slowly changing population.
  2. Stage 2: death rates fall (clean water, sanitation, vaccination, food supply) while birth rates stay high; rapid growth; the base of the pyramid widens because more children survive.
  3. Stage 3: birth rates fall (urbanisation, education of women, contraception); growth slows.
  4. Stage 4: low birth and death rates; stable population; rectangular pyramid.
  5. Stage 5 (in some countries): fertility below replacement; the population ages and may shrink; constrictive pyramid.

The companion epidemiologic transition describes the shift in leading causes of death from infections, malnutrition and maternal and perinatal conditions to chronic noncommunicable diseases (cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes, dementia) as populations move through these stages.

Effects of an ageing population

  • The number of people with age-related conditions and the crude prevalence rise even when age-specific rates stay constant. Age-adjusted rates do not change unless risk itself changes.
  • Multimorbidity, polypharmacy, falls and functional dependence increase, and demand shifts toward primary care, rehabilitation, home care and long-term care.
  • The crude death rate can rise in a population whose health is improving, simply because more of its members are old.

"Cases of hip fracture doubled over 20 years" is not evidence that fracture risk rose. First check whether the age-specific (or age-adjusted) rates changed; growth and ageing of the population alone can double the count.

Read a pyramid by asking three questions: how wide is the base (recent births), how quickly does it taper (deaths), and are there bulges or notches out of keeping with their neighbours (migration, historical events)?

Comparing death rates between an expansive and a constrictive population requires age standardisation (see measures of disease frequency).

s23g-s0106.bodyHtml:
Surveillance is the ongoing, systematic collection, analysis and interpretation of health data, with timely feedback to those who need to act. Its job is to establish the usual level of a disease, detect departures from it and guide control measures.

Types of surveillance

TypeHow it worksStrengthWeakness
PassiveClinicians and laboratories report notifiable conditions on their own initiativeCheap, broad, continuousUnderreporting; completeness varies
ActiveHealth department staff regularly contact providers or laboratories, or review records, to find casesMore complete and timelyLabour-intensive; used for outbreaks and priority diseases
SentinelA selected network of sites reports detailed data on a conditionHigh-quality data and trendsNot population-wide; may be unrepresentative
SyndromicAutomated analysis of pre-diagnostic data (emergency department chief complaints, pharmacy sales, absenteeism)Early warning before diagnoses are confirmedMany false alarms; signals need verification

Notifiable diseases are conditions that clinicians and laboratories are legally required to report to the local or state health department; states share data with the CDC through the national notifiable diseases system. Some (for example, suspected measles or anthrax) must be reported immediately by telephone. The HIPAA Privacy Rule permits disclosure of protected health information to public health authorities for disease reporting without the patient's authorisation.

Patterns of occurrence

  • Endemic: the constant usual presence of a disease in an area (hyperendemic: persistently high level).
  • Epidemic (outbreak): cases clearly in excess of what is normally expected for that place and time. A single case of a disease that is normally absent (e.g. smallpox) can constitute an outbreak.
  • Pandemic: an epidemic that has spread across several countries or continents, usually affecting many people.
  • Cluster: cases grouped in place and time whose number may or may not exceed expectation.

Steps of an outbreak investigation

  1. Prepare for field work.
  2. Establish that an outbreak exists (compare with baseline; exclude artefacts such as a new test, new reporting rules or a change in population).
  3. Verify the diagnosis (records, laboratory confirmation).
  4. Construct a case definition: clinical criteria plus restrictions of person, place and time. It must not include the exposure under study. Early, a broad (sensitive) definition finds cases; later, a stricter (specific) one sharpens the analytic study.
  5. Find cases systematically and record them in a line list.
  6. Perform descriptive epidemiology: time (epidemic curve), place (spot map), person (age, sex, occupation).
  7. Develop hypotheses.
  8. Evaluate hypotheses with an analytic study: a retrospective cohort when the exposed group is well defined (all guests at a banquet), a case-control study when it is not (community cases with no list of the population at risk).
  9. Refine hypotheses and do further studies (environmental sampling, laboratory typing) as needed.
  10. Implement control and prevention measures, which should start as soon as a likely source is known, not only after the analytic study.
  11. Maintain surveillance and communicate findings.

The order is a guide; several steps run in parallel in the real world.

Epidemic curves

An epidemic curve is a histogram of cases by time of symptom onset. A point-source outbreak (one meal) produces a single tight peak whose width roughly matches the range of the incubation period; the peak minus the exposure time approximates the median incubation period. A continuous common-source outbreak (a contaminated well) rises and then plateaus until the source is removed; an intermittent source gives irregular peaks. A propagated outbreak (person-to-person spread) shows successive, increasingly broad waves separated by about one serial interval. Mixed patterns occur when a point source is followed by secondary spread.

Food-specific attack rates

For each food, compute the attack rate among those who ate it and among those who did not. The likely vehicle has a high attack rate among eaters, a low attack rate among non-eaters (a large ratio or difference) and accounts for most of the cases. A food that nearly everyone ate (bread, water) can have many ill eaters but a similar attack rate in the few non-eaters, so its ratio is near 1.

The food eaten by the largest number of sick people is not automatically the culprit. Compare attack rates between eaters and non-eaters.

Time from a shared meal to the epidemic peak points to the agent: a few hours suggests a preformed toxin (Staphylococcus aureus, emetic Bacillus cereus); about half a day to a day suggests Clostridium perfringens; one to three days suggests norovirus or Salmonella; two to five days suggests Campylobacter; weeks suggest hepatitis A or Listeria.

s23g-s0107.bodyHtml:
Infectious diseases spread when every link of a chain is intact. Control works by breaking any one link, so naming the link an intervention targets is a frequent exam task.

The chain of infection

LinkMeaningExample of breaking it
AgentThe pathogenAntimicrobial treatment, disinfection
ReservoirWhere the agent normally lives and multiplies (humans, animals, environment)Treating carriers, controlling animal reservoirs
Portal of exitHow it leaves the host (respiratory tract, stool, blood)Masking a coughing patient, covering wounds
Mode of transmissionHow it travelsHand hygiene, safe water, insect control, ventilation
Portal of entryHow it enters the new hostGloves, condoms, sterile technique
Susceptible hostA person who can be infectedVaccination, prophylaxis, treating immune deficiency

A carrier harbours and can shed the agent without symptoms. Carriers can be incubatory (shedding before illness), convalescent (shedding after recovery), chronic (shedding for a long time, for example a year or more after typhoid fever, often from the gallbladder) or asymptomatic throughout (never ill). Carriers matter because they are not recognised and keep circulating.

Modes of transmission

  • Direct contact: skin-to-skin, kissing, sexual contact.
  • Droplet: large respiratory particles travelling a short distance (traditionally within about 2 metres) onto mucous membranes. Examples: influenza, pertussis, Neisseria meningitidis, mumps.
  • Airborne: small particles that stay suspended and travel on air currents. Classic examples: measles, varicella (including disseminated zoster) and pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis.
  • Indirect contact: fomites such as bed rails and stethoscopes (Clostridioides difficile spores, MRSA).
  • Vehicle-borne: food, water, blood products, a shared medication vial; one vehicle can infect many people (common-source outbreaks).
  • Vector-borne: insects or arthropods carrying the agent mechanically or biologically (malaria, Lyme disease, dengue).
  • Vertical: mother to child during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding (HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis, cytomegalovirus).

Timing

The incubation period runs from infection to symptom onset. The latent period runs from infection to the start of infectiousness. When the latent period is shorter than the incubation period, people transmit before symptoms appear, so isolating only symptomatic people cannot stop spread. The serial interval is the time between symptom onset in a case and in the person that case infected; it sets the spacing of waves on a propagated epidemic curve. The infectious period is the time during which a person can transmit.

Reproduction numbers and herd immunity

R0 (basic reproduction number) is the average number of secondary cases produced by one case in a fully susceptible population. It depends on contact rate, probability of transmission per contact and duration of infectiousness, so it belongs to a pathogen in a particular population, not to the pathogen alone. Rt (effective reproduction number) is the average actually occurring at time t, after immunity and control measures: Rt ≈ R0 × proportion still susceptible. An epidemic grows while Rt > 1 and shrinks once Rt < 1.

The herd immunity threshold is the immune proportion at which Rt falls to 1: 1 − 1/R0. Worked example: R0 = 6 gives 1 − 1/6 ≈ 83% immune. If a vaccine protects only a fraction E of those vaccinated, the coverage needed is (1 − 1/R0) ÷ E; with E = 0.9, about 93% must be vaccinated. Highly transmissible infections such as measles therefore need very high coverage, and small pockets of low coverage allow outbreaks.

R0 does not fall as an epidemic progresses or as people are vaccinated; Rt does. And the herd immunity threshold refers to people who are immune, not people who received a dose; divide by vaccine effectiveness to get the coverage target.

Isolation, quarantine and hospital precautions

Isolation separates people who are ill or known to be infected; quarantine restricts the movement of people who were exposed but are not ill, for about the length of the incubation period. Hospitals layer transmission-based precautions on top of standard precautions:

PrecautionUsed forKey elements
StandardEvery patientHand hygiene; gloves, gown, eye protection according to expected exposure to blood and body fluids; safe injection practice; respiratory hygiene
ContactMRSA, VRE, C. difficile, scabies, many enteric infections in incontinent patientsGown and gloves on entry; dedicated equipment; single room or cohorting; for C. difficile, soap-and-water hand washing because alcohol does not kill spores
DropletInfluenza, pertussis, meningococcal disease (until 24 hours of effective therapy), mumpsSurgical mask within close range; single room or spacing; patient wears a mask when transported
AirborneTuberculosis, measles, varicella, disseminated zosterAirborne infection isolation room (negative pressure); fit-tested N95 or higher respirator for staff

Exam shortcut: name the mode, then the precaution follows. Settles on surfaces → contact; big drops, short range → droplet and a surgical mask; hangs in the air → negative-pressure room and an N95.

s23g-s0108.bodyHtml:
Every disease follows a natural history: a period of susceptibility, exposure to causes, a biologic onset that cannot yet be felt, a preclinical phase in which the disease may be detectable by testing, clinical disease and an outcome (recovery, chronic disability or death). Each level of prevention acts at a different point on this timeline.

The five levels

LevelGoalActs onExamples
PrimordialPrevent risk factors from emergingSocial, economic and environmental conditions of whole populationsSafe walking routes and parks, limits on sugar-sweetened drinks in schools, tobacco taxes that keep children from starting
PrimaryPrevent disease from starting in people who do not have itSusceptible people, with or without risk factorsVaccination, condoms, helmets, treating hypertension to prevent a first stroke, folic acid before conception, smoking cessation
SecondaryDetect and treat disease early, before symptoms or while it is still mild, to stop progressionPreclinical or early diseaseCervical, colorectal and breast cancer screening; newborn screening; blood pressure screening; contact tracing with testing
TertiaryLimit complications, disability and recurrence in established diseaseClinical diseaseCardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction, stroke rehabilitation, diabetic foot care, physiotherapy after joint replacement
QuaternaryProtect people from overmedicalisation and harm from unnecessary careAnyone, at any stage, especially the worried wellAvoiding unneeded imaging for uncomplicated back pain, deprescribing, declining screening that has more harm than benefit

Clinical language and epidemiologic language collide. Cardiologists call aspirin after a myocardial infarction "secondary prevention" (preventing a second event), but in the levels-of-prevention framework, measures in people who already have clinical disease are tertiary. Read what the stem asks: if it asks for the level of prevention, classify by stage of the natural history.

Screening as secondary prevention

Screening looks for disease in people without symptoms. It only helps when the disease has a detectable preclinical phase long enough to be found by a periodic test, and when treatment in that phase leads to better outcomes than treatment after symptoms. A good screening programme also needs an acceptable, accurate test, a disease that is an important health problem, and capacity to diagnose and treat what is found. Three biases make screening look better than it is:

  • Lead-time bias: earlier diagnosis lengthens survival measured from diagnosis even if death occurs at the same time.
  • Length-time bias: periodic screening preferentially finds slow-growing, less aggressive disease.
  • Overdiagnosis: detection of disease that would never have caused symptoms or death.

The only measure free of these biases is disease-specific mortality in the whole screened versus unscreened population, ideally from a randomised trial.

High-risk versus population strategies

A high-risk strategy identifies people at the top of a risk distribution and treats them (statins for very high cholesterol). It is efficient for those individuals and motivates both patient and physician. A population strategy shifts the whole distribution a little (lowering salt in processed food, smoke-free laws). Because most people sit in the middle of a distribution, most cases come from the large number at modest risk rather than the small number at high risk. This is the prevention paradox: a measure that brings large benefits to the community offers little to each participating individual. Worked example: if 10% of a town has severe hypertension and contributes 30% of strokes, while 90% with lower pressures contribute 70%, a programme that perfectly controlled every severe case could prevent at most 30% of strokes, whereas a small downward shift in everybody's pressure acts on the 70%.

Choosing the point of intervention

  • Before exposure: primordial and primary measures (policy, vaccination, pre-exposure prophylaxis).
  • After exposure, before disease: post-exposure prophylaxis (rabies vaccine and immune globulin, hepatitis B immune globulin for newborns of infected mothers) is still primary prevention, because it stops infection from becoming disease.
  • Preclinical disease: screening and early treatment.
  • Clinical disease: rehabilitation and complication prevention.

To classify any intervention, ask one question: does the person already have the disease, and if so, can they feel it? No disease → primary (or primordial if it targets the conditions that create risk factors); disease without symptoms → secondary; symptomatic disease → tertiary; harm from care itself → quaternary.

s23g-s0201.bodyHtml:
Every study design question on the exam can be answered by asking three things in order: did the investigator assign the exposure, is there a comparison group, and how were participants selected and in which direction does the study look in time. Descriptive studies sit at the first fork on the observational side: they describe people with a condition, but they do not compare them with anyone.

Case reports and case series

A case report describes one patient in detail: the presentation, investigations, treatment and outcome, usually because something about the case is new or unexpected. A case series describes a group of patients who share a diagnosis, an exposure or a treatment, often collected at one centre or reported to one registry. There is no formal minimum number, but a series typically means several patients described with the same framework.

Their strengths are speed, low cost and closeness to clinical practice. Their value is that they notice things first:

  • a new disease or a new syndrome (an unusual infection appearing in previously healthy people);
  • a new or rare adverse effect of a drug or device after it reaches the market;
  • an unusual presentation or a rare complication of a known disease;
  • a clustering of a rare disease in people who share an occupation, place or behaviour.

In each case the report generates a hypothesis. An analytical study (case-control, cohort or trial) is then needed to test it.

What you can and cannot calculate

A case series has a numerator (the cases) but no denominator (the population at risk) and no comparison group. Within the series you can describe proportions: if 21 of 30 patients in a series had fever, 70% of the cases had fever. You cannot calculate incidence, prevalence in a population, a relative risk, an odds ratio or an attributable risk, because each of these needs either the number of people at risk or a comparison of people with and without the exposure or disease.

FeatureCase report / case seriesAnalytical study
Comparison groupNonePresent (unexposed, controls or placebo)
MeasuresCounts and proportions among casesIncidence, prevalence, RR, OR, risk difference
Main useSignal, hypothesis generation, clinical descriptionHypothesis testing
Causal inferenceNot possiblePossible, strongest in randomized trials

Spontaneous reporting and pharmacovigilance

Post-marketing drug safety depends heavily on case reports. Clinicians and patients report suspected adverse reactions to the manufacturer or the regulator; clusters of similar reports form a signal. Such systems detect rare and unexpected events that premarketing trials were too small or too short to see, but they suffer from under-reporting, stimulated reporting after publicity, incomplete details and, above all, the lack of a denominator: the number of people taking the drug and for how long is not in the reports themselves. Estimating the risk needs prescription or claims data, or an analytical study.

Trap: a case series that reports "22 of 35 patients recovered within a month" gives a proportion among cases. It is not an incidence, a response rate in the population treated, or evidence that the drug caused the problem. If the authors chose which cases to include because of how those cases turned out, even the proportions are biased.

Contrasting cross-sectional and ecological studies

Two other designs are sometimes loosely called descriptive. A cross-sectional survey measures exposure and outcome in individuals at one time and gives prevalence; when it compares exposed and unexposed people it becomes analytical (prevalence ratio or prevalence odds ratio). An ecological study uses groups as the unit of analysis: average alcohol sales by state and state rates of liver cirrhosis, or the share of a city's households with a park nearby and the city's childhood asthma rate. Ecological data can describe population patterns and suggest hypotheses, but an association between group averages need not hold for the individuals within them (the ecological fallacy).

DesignUnitTypical outputKey limit
Case report / seriesIndividual cases onlyDescription, proportions among casesNo denominator, no comparison
Cross-sectionalIndividuals, one time pointPrevalence, prevalence (odds) ratioCannot show which came first
EcologicalGroupsCorrelation of group ratesEcological fallacy

Pearl: on the exam, the words "describes," "a series of patients" or "reports a patient" with no mention of a comparison group point to a descriptive study. The correct use is almost always "generating a hypothesis"; the correct limitation is almost always "no comparison (control) group."

Ethics of case reports

A case report is about one identifiable person, so the patient's written consent for publication is expected, identifying details should be kept to the minimum needed, and photographs need particular care. These obligations apply even though a single case report is not usually a prospective research study.

Bridge: once a case series raises a hypothesis, the choice of the next study depends on what is rare: a rare outcome points to a case-control study, a rare exposure to a cohort study (next section).

s23g-s0202.bodyHtml:
Analytical observational studies compare groups to test a hypothesis about an exposure and an outcome, but the investigator only observes; nobody assigns the exposure. The design is named by how participants were selected and when exposure and outcome were measured. The independent variable is the exposure or predictor; the dependent variable is the outcome.

Cross-sectional studies

Exposure and outcome are measured in each person at the same time, usually by survey or examination of a sample. The output is prevalence, and the comparison of exposed and unexposed people is expressed as a prevalence ratio or prevalence odds ratio. Cross-sectional studies are quick and good for describing burden and planning services, but they cannot establish temporal sequence (did the exposure precede the disease?) and they over-represent long-lasting disease, because short illnesses are less likely to be present on the survey day.

Ecological studies

The units are groups, and exposure and outcome are group summaries. They are cheap and use routine data, and they are the natural design for exposures that act at a population level (laws, prices, water supplies). Their classic error is the ecological fallacy: assuming that an association between group averages applies to individuals.

Case-control studies

Participants are selected by outcome: people with the disease (cases) and people without it (controls) from the same source population. Investigators then look back at past exposure. Because the investigator fixes the numbers of cases and controls, risks cannot be calculated; the measure is the odds ratio, which approximates the relative risk when the disease is rare.

Worked example. 100 cases, of whom 40 were exposed; 200 controls, of whom 40 were exposed. OR = (a × d)/(b × c) = (40 × 160)/(60 × 40) = 6,400/2,400 ≈ 2.7.

Strengths: efficient for rare diseases, diseases with long latency, and for examining many exposures at once. Weaknesses: recall bias (cases remember exposures differently), difficulty choosing controls, and poor suitability for rare exposures.

Cohort studies

Participants are selected by exposure and followed for the outcome, so incidence can be measured in each group and compared as a relative risk (or rate ratio) and a risk difference.

  • Prospective cohort: exposure is measured now, outcomes occur in the future.
  • Retrospective (historical) cohort: exposure and outcomes are reconstructed from existing records; the logic still runs from exposure to outcome.

Worked example. 30 events among 1,000 exposed people (3%) and 20 among 2,000 unexposed (1%). RR = 3%/1% = 3.0; risk difference = 2 percentage points.

Strengths: clear temporal sequence, several outcomes from one exposure, good for rare exposures. Weaknesses: large and slow for rare outcomes, loss to follow-up, and confounding.

Hybrid designs

A nested case-control study selects cases and controls from within a cohort that stored baseline data or samples, combining the cohort's prospectively measured exposure with the case-control study's efficiency. A case-crossover study uses only cases, comparing each person's exposure just before the event with his or her exposure at earlier times; it suits brief, intermittent exposures with immediate effects (acute triggers).

Cross-sectionalNeither (a sample at one time)Prevalence, prevalence (odds) ratioBurden, planningTemporality unknown

Case-controlOutcomeOdds ratioRare outcome, many exposuresRecall and selection bias
CohortExposureRelative risk, incidenceRare exposure, many outcomesLoss to follow-up, slow
Nested case-controlOutcome, within a cohortOdds ratioExpensive assays on stored samplesNeeds an existing cohort
Case-crossoverOutcome; self as controlOdds ratioAcute triggersUnsuitable for chronic exposures

Trap: a study that starts in 2024 and uses records from the 1970s is not automatically a case-control study. If people were selected by exposure and followed forward through the records to see who developed the outcome, it is a retrospective cohort. Ask "selected by what?", not "when was it done?".

Trap: in a case-control table, computing a/(a + b) ÷ c/(c + d) gives a number that looks like a relative risk but has no meaning, because the ratio of cases to controls was set by the investigator.

Bridge: confounding is the main threat to all observational designs. Randomization, covered next, is the only method that balances unknown confounders.

s23g-s0203.bodyHtml:
In an interventional (experimental) study the investigator assigns the exposure. When assignment is random, the randomized controlled trial (RCT) balances known and unknown prognostic factors between groups on average, so a difference in outcome can be attributed to the intervention. That is why RCTs are the strongest single design for questions about the effect of a treatment.

Trial layouts

DesignHow it worksWhen to use itWatch out for
Parallel groupEach participant receives one treatment for the whole trialMost trialsNeeds larger samples than crossover
CrossoverEach participant receives all treatments in random order, separated by a washoutStable chronic conditions, quick reversible effectsCarryover; impossible for cures or deaths
FactorialTwo or more interventions randomized at once (2 × 2 = 4 groups)Answering two questions in one trialInteraction between interventions
ClusterGroups (schools, clinics, villages) are randomizedGroup-level interventions; preventing contaminationLower power (design effect), clustered analysis
Community trialWhole communities receive or do not receive a public-health interventionPopulation programs, mass media, environmental changesFew units, so chance imbalance

A washout period in a crossover trial lets the first treatment's effect disappear so it does not carry over. In a cluster trial, people in the same cluster resemble each other, so the required sample size rises by the design effect, 1 + (m − 1) × ICC, where m is the average cluster size and ICC the intracluster correlation.

Explanatory versus pragmatic

Explanatory trials test efficacy under ideal conditions: strict eligibility, expert centres, close monitoring. Pragmatic trials test effectiveness in usual care: broad eligibility, ordinary clinicians, flexible delivery and patient-important outcomes. Most trials lie on a spectrum between the two.

Superiority, non-inferiority and equivalence

A superiority trial asks whether the new treatment is better; it succeeds when the confidence interval for the difference excludes no effect on the favourable side. A non-inferiority trial asks whether the new treatment is not unacceptably worse than an active comparator by more than a prespecified margin; it succeeds when the whole interval lies on the acceptable side of that margin. An equivalence trial asks whether the difference lies within a margin in both directions.

Worked example. Margin for the difference in cure (new minus standard) = −8 percentage points. Observed difference −0.6 points (95% CI −3.1 to +1.9). The lower limit −3.1 is above −8 → non-inferior; the interval includes 0 → not superior.

Non-inferiority trials are chosen when the new treatment offers another advantage (oral rather than intravenous, cheaper, safer, fewer doses). The margin must be justified clinically and from the comparator's known effect, and the comparator must be given well; otherwise a poor trial can make both treatments look alike.

Controls and blinding

A placebo control is appropriate when no proven treatment exists or when withholding it briefly carries only minor, reversible risk. When effective treatment exists and withholding it risks serious harm, an active control (the current standard) is used. Blinding prevents knowledge of the assignment from influencing care, reporting and measurement. Labels vary, so state who is blinded: participants (single-blind), participants and investigators (double-blind), and also outcome assessors or analysts (often called triple-blind). When participants and clinicians cannot be blinded (surgery versus physiotherapy), blinded outcome assessment still protects against measurement bias.

Phases of drug development (as designs)

PhaseTypical designQuestion
1Small, often healthy volunteers, dose escalation, often unblindedSafety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, dose
2Patients with the disease; may be randomized, often several dosesPreliminary efficacy, dose selection, short-term safety
3Large randomized trials against placebo or standard therapyConfirm efficacy and safety for approval
4Post-marketing surveillance and studiesRare and long-term harms, new populations

Trap: in a non-inferiority trial, "no statistically significant difference" does not mean non-inferior. Only the position of the lower confidence limit relative to the margin answers the question. A wide interval that crosses the margin is inconclusive.

Trap: randomization and blinding are not the same. Randomization controls who gets what; blinding controls who knows. A trial can be randomized and open-label.

Pearl: match the design to the clue: "each participant receives both" = crossover; "four groups, two interventions" = factorial; "schools/clinics/villages were randomized" = cluster; "not unacceptably worse" or "margin" = non-inferiority; "first in humans, dose escalation" = phase 1.

s23g-s0204.bodyHtml:
A systematic review answers a focused question by finding, appraising and summarising all relevant studies using an explicit, reproducible method. A meta-analysis is the statistical pooling of the results of those studies into a single estimate. Every meta-analysis should come from a systematic review, but not every systematic review includes a meta-analysis: if studies are too different, a narrative synthesis is safer.

Systematic versus narrative review

FeatureSystematic reviewNarrative review
QuestionFocused (population, intervention, comparator, outcome)Often broad
ProtocolWritten and often registered in advanceUsually none
SearchComprehensive: several databases, trial registries, unpublished dataAt the author's discretion
Selection and extractionExplicit criteria; two reviewers independentlyUnstated
AppraisalFormal risk-of-bias rating of each studyInformal
SynthesisStructured, often with meta-analysisQualitative summary

Reading a forest plot

Each row is a study. The square marks its point estimate and its area is proportional to the study's weight; the horizontal line is its 95% confidence interval. The vertical line is no effect: 1 for ratios (risk ratio, odds ratio, hazard ratio), 0 for differences. The diamond at the bottom is the pooled estimate: its centre is the summary effect and its width the pooled confidence interval. If the diamond does not touch the line of no effect, the pooled result is statistically significant at the chosen level. Ratios are plotted on a log scale so that 0.5 and 2 are the same distance from 1.

In inverse-variance pooling each study is weighted by 1/variance: larger studies with more events have narrower intervals and bigger squares. A dramatic estimate from a small study contributes little.

Worked example. If a pooled risk ratio of 0.81 is applied to a population with a baseline risk of 10%, the absolute risk reduction is 0.10 × (1 − 0.81) = 0.019, so the number needed to treat is 1/0.019 ≈ 53.

Heterogeneity and models

Heterogeneity is variation between study results beyond chance. Look first at the plot (do the intervals overlap?), then at the statistics: Cochran's Q tests whether heterogeneity is present, and I² estimates the percentage of total variation due to real between-study differences. Rough guide: about 25% low, 50% moderate, 75% or more high. High heterogeneity calls for an explanation (different doses, populations, outcome definitions, risk of bias) through subgroup analysis or meta-regression, and for caution in reporting one pooled number.

ModelAssumptionEffect on result when heterogeneity is present
Fixed effectOne true effect; differences are chanceNarrower interval; large studies dominate
Random effectsTrue effects vary around an averageWider interval; weights more even, so small studies gain influence

Publication bias and the funnel plot

Studies with striking, positive results are more likely to be published, published quickly and published in English, so a review built only on published papers can overestimate benefit. A funnel plot graphs each study's effect against its precision. Without bias it is a symmetric inverted funnel; a missing corner, usually small studies with null or unfavourable results, suggests publication bias or other small-study effects. Searching registries and unpublished data is the main defence.

Limits of pooling

A meta-analysis is only as good as the studies it contains ("garbage in, garbage out"). Pooling observational studies increases precision but not validity: confounding in each study remains in the pooled estimate. Sensitivity analyses restricted to studies at low risk of bias show whether the result depends on weaker studies.

Hierarchy of evidence (for therapy)

Systematic reviews of RCTs → individual RCTs → cohort studies → case-control studies → case series and reports → expert opinion. The hierarchy is a default: a large, rigorous trial can outweigh a meta-analysis of small, biased ones, and questions about rare harms or prognosis are often best answered by observational designs.

Trap: when every individual study's interval crosses 1 but the diamond does not, the correct reading is that the pooled evidence shows an effect. Do not "count votes" of significant and nonsignificant studies.

Trap: a low I² means results are consistent, not that they are correct. Several small trials sharing the same bias can agree perfectly.

Pearl: weight = precision. On any forest-plot question, the study with the biggest square and narrowest line carries the most weight, whatever its point estimate.

s23g-s0205.bodyHtml:
Two questions decide whether a study's comparison is fair and whether its results apply beyond the study: who was sampled, and how comparison groups were formed. Sampling governs external validity (generalizability); control selection and randomization govern internal validity.

From target population to sample

The target population is the group the results are meant to describe. The sampling frame is the list or mechanism from which the sample is actually drawn (a register, a list of households, a clinic roster). If the frame misses part of the target population, those people cannot be selected (undercoverage), and no amount of randomness inside the frame repairs it. Inclusion and exclusion criteria then define who among the sampled is eligible; strict criteria improve safety and homogeneity but narrow the population to which results apply.

MethodHow it worksStrengthWeakness
Simple randomEvery member of the frame has an equal chanceUnbiased, simple analysisNeeds a complete list; may under-sample small groups
Stratified randomDivide into strata, sample randomly within every stratumGuarantees subgroup representation; more preciseNeeds stratum information for everyone
ClusterRandomly select some groups, then study people within themNeeds only a list of groups; cheap fieldworkLess precise (design effect)
SystematicEvery kth person after a random startEasy in practiceBias if the list has a repeating pattern
ConvenienceWhoever is available or volunteersFast and cheapSelection bias; not representative

Worked example (design effect). A survey needs 400 people under simple random sampling. With clusters of 20 people and an intracluster correlation of 0.05, the design effect is 1 + (20 − 1) × 0.05 = 1.95, so about 400 × 1.95 = 780 people are needed.

Choosing controls in case-control studies

Controls should come from the same source population as the cases: people who, had they developed the disease, would have been identified as cases in this study. Common sources and their problems:

  • Population controls (random-digit dialling, registers): best match to the source population, but more expensive and lower participation.
  • Hospital controls: convenient and similarly motivated to recall, but their own illnesses may be related to the exposure, which distorts the exposure frequency (a form of selection bias sometimes called Berkson bias).
  • Friends or relatives: similar in many ways, which can make them too similar in exposure.

Matching makes cases and controls alike on chosen factors (age, sex) to control confounding. The matched factor can no longer be studied, and matched designs need matched analysis. Overmatching (matching on a factor linked to the exposure or lying on the causal path) makes cases and controls similar in exposure and biases the odds ratio toward 1.

Why a control group at all?

Without a concurrent comparison group, a before-after change can come from regression to the mean (people enrolled because of an extreme value drift back toward their usual level), the natural course of illness, other treatments, or the attention of being studied. Historical controls are better than none but differ in era, care and selection.

Randomization methods

MethodWhat it doesLimitation
SimpleCoin-toss equivalent for each participantImbalance in small trials
BlockEqual allocation within each block (for example 2:2 in blocks of 4)Predictable if the block size is fixed and known
StratifiedSeparate randomization (usually blocked) within strata of a key prognostic factorOnly a few strata are practical
ClusterRandomizes groups rather than individualsLower power; clustered analysis

Allocation concealment versus blinding

Allocation concealment hides the upcoming assignment from those enrolling participants until enrolment is irreversible (central web or telephone randomization, or opaque, sequentially numbered, sealed envelopes). It prevents selection bias and is always possible. Blinding hides the assigned treatment after allocation and prevents performance and measurement bias; it is not always possible. Alternation, date of birth, record number and day of the week are not random and cannot be concealed.

Trap: "sealed envelopes" are not enough if they are translucent, unnumbered or opened out of order. If recruiters can foresee the next assignment, concealment has failed, even though the sequence was random.

Trap: a bigger convenience sample is a more precise estimate of the wrong thing. Size reduces random error, not selection bias.

Pearl: "some whole groups chosen" = cluster; "every subgroup sampled" = stratified; "next assignment could be guessed" = failed allocation concealment; "controls admitted for a disease related to the exposure" = poor control selection biasing the OR toward 1.

s23g-s0206.bodyHtml:
Randomization creates comparable groups only at the moment of assignment. After that, participants stop treatment, switch arms, take extra treatments or disappear. How the analysis handles these events decides whether the trial's comparison stays fair.

Three analysis populations

AnalysisWho is included, and in which groupQuestion answeredMain risk
Intention-to-treat (ITT)Everyone randomized, in the assigned groupWhat happens when the treatment is offered?Dilution toward no difference
Per-protocolOnly those who followed the protocolWhat happens in those who take it as directed?Confounding by adherence
As-treatedEveryone, regrouped by treatment actually receivedWhat happens in those who took it?Breaks randomization; confounded

ITT is the primary analysis of superiority trials because it preserves randomization: adherence is a post-randomization behaviour linked to prognosis (sicker, less motivated or intolerant people stop), so removing or regrouping people by adherence recreates confounding. Its weakness is dilution: non-adherence and crossover make the groups more alike, so ITT estimates of the effect of actually taking a drug are conservative.

Worked example. Drug arm (200): 160 adherent with 8 events, 40 non-adherent with 6 events. Placebo arm (200, all adherent): 20 events. ITT: drug 14/200 = 7.0% versus placebo 10.0%, risk difference 3.0 percentage points. Per-protocol: drug 8/160 = 5.0% versus 10.0%, difference 5.0 points. The per-protocol estimate is larger, partly because adherent people have better prognoses.

Crossover, contamination and the healthy adherer

Crossover (participants switching to the other arm) and contamination (control participants receiving part of the intervention, common in behavioural and educational trials) both bias ITT toward the null. Cluster randomization reduces contamination. The healthy-adherer effect is the observation that people who take any pill faithfully, including placebo, tend to have better outcomes; it is why adherent-versus-non-adherent comparisons are not evidence of drug effect.

Loss to follow-up and attrition bias

Missing outcomes are dangerous when the losses differ between groups, or when the reasons for leaving are related to the outcome (adverse effects in one arm, lack of benefit in the other). This is attrition bias. Look at the trial flow diagram: how many left each arm, and why. Protection comes from design (minimising burden, collecting outcomes even after treatment stops) more than from analysis.

Handling missing data

  • Complete-case analysis: drops people with missing outcomes; unbiased only if missingness is unrelated to outcome.
  • Last observation carried forward (LOCF): assumes nothing changes after dropout; biased whenever outcomes change over time (in a progressive disease it flatters the arm with earlier dropouts), and its intervals are too narrow.
  • Multiple imputation: fills each missing value several times from a model of the observed data and combines the analyses, carrying the extra uncertainty; reduces bias when missingness depends on recorded characteristics.
  • Sensitivity analyses: repeat the analysis under different assumptions (for example, missing = failure) to see whether conclusions hold.

Run-in periods

A run-in before randomization (placebo or active drug for a few weeks) screens out non-adherent or intolerant participants. It increases adherence and power without harming internal validity, because exclusions happen before randomization, but it reduces generalizability: results apply to the adherent, tolerant subset.

Non-inferiority trials are different

In a superiority trial, ITT's bias toward no difference is conservative. In a non-inferiority trial, the same bias makes the treatments look alike and so favours a false claim of non-inferiority. Non-inferiority trials therefore report both ITT and per-protocol analyses and are most convincing when both meet the margin.

Trap: "analysed only participants who completed the study" is not intention-to-treat, even if it is labelled so. True ITT needs outcomes (observed or principled imputation) for everyone randomized.

Pearl: ITT = "once randomized, always analysed in that group." It answers the policy question (prescribe or not) and is conservative in superiority trials but not in non-inferiority trials.

s23g-s0207.bodyHtml:
Qualitative research studies meanings, experiences, beliefs and processes through words, observations and documents rather than numbers. It answers why and how questions (why patients stop a medication, how teams make handoff decisions) and is the natural first step when the important variables are not yet known. Quantitative research answers how many and how much and tests hypotheses.

FeatureQualitativeQuantitative
QuestionWhy? How? What is it like?How many? How much? Does X cause Y?
DataTranscripts, field notes, documentsMeasurements, counts
SamplingPurposive, snowball; until saturationProbability sampling; size from a power calculation
AnalysisCoding and themes, iterativeStatistical tests and estimates
GeneralizationTransferability to similar contextsStatistical inference to a population

Data collection methods

  • In-depth (semi-structured) interviews: one participant at a time, an interview guide with open questions and follow-up probes; best for personal experiences and sensitive topics.
  • Focus groups: a moderated discussion among roughly 6 to 10 people; the interaction is itself data, useful for shared norms and language; poor for sensitive topics and liable to domination by a few voices.
  • Participant (ethnographic) observation: the researcher watches or joins activities in their natural setting, revealing what people do rather than what they say they do.
  • Document analysis: records, policies, notes, online posts.

Sampling

Purposive sampling deliberately selects information-rich participants; maximum-variation sampling seeks a wide range of characteristics; snowball (chain-referral) sampling asks participants to recruit others and reaches hidden populations with no sampling frame. Sample size is set by saturation: data collection continues, with analysis running alongside, until new data no longer add new themes. Typical interview studies include tens of participants, not hundreds.

Analysis

In thematic analysis, researchers read transcripts closely, attach codes to meaningful segments, group codes into categories and develop themes that capture patterns across participants, revisiting the data as the analysis matures. Grounded theory goes further, building an explanatory theory from the data. Researchers look for negative (deviant) cases that contradict emerging themes and refine the themes to account for them.

Rigour (trustworthiness)

CriterionMeaningStrategies
CredibilityFindings truly represent participants' experiencesTriangulation, member checking, prolonged engagement, negative case analysis
TransferabilityReaders can judge applicability to other settingsThick description of setting and participants
DependabilityProcess is consistent and documentedAudit trail, clear methods
ConfirmabilityFindings come from the data, not the researcher's preferencesReflexivity, audit trail, multiple coders

Triangulation compares several data sources, methods or researchers. Member checking returns findings to participants to check that they recognise them. Reflexivity is the researcher's explicit examination of how his or her own background and assumptions shape the study.

When is a qualitative design the right choice?

Choose qualitative methods when the aim is to explore experiences, perceptions, decision-making or the workings of a system; when existing measures do not capture the phenomenon; when a survey or trial needs to be designed around patients' real concerns; or when a quantitative result needs explaining (why did a program fail in some clinics?). Choose quantitative methods to estimate frequency, measure change or test a causal hypothesis. Qualitative research still needs ethical review, informed consent and careful protection of confidentiality, because quotations and detailed descriptions can identify participants in small communities.

Mixed methods

Mixed-methods studies integrate quantitative and qualitative components: a survey followed by interviews to explain its findings, interviews first to build a questionnaire, or both run together and compared. They are common in health-services research and program evaluation.

Trap: counting how many participants mentioned a theme ("11 of 15") does not estimate how common that view is in any population. Qualitative samples are small and purposive by design.

Trap: power calculations, P values and randomization are not markers of qualitative rigour; saturation, triangulation, member checking and reflexivity are.

Pearl: learn the one-line definitions: saturation = no new themes emerging; snowball = participants recruit participants; triangulation = several sources, methods or researchers cross-checked; member checking = participants confirm interpretations; reflexivity = researchers examine their own influence; transferability = thick description lets readers judge fit.

s23g-s0301.bodyHtml:
Most association questions start from the same four-cell table. Rows hold the exposure (or treatment, or test result); columns hold the outcome (or true disease status). Learn one layout and use it every time: cell a is exposed with the outcome, b exposed without, c unexposed with, d unexposed without. If a question presents the table the other way round, redraw it before calculating.

Risk and relative risk

Risk (cumulative incidence) is the proportion of people at risk who develop the outcome over a stated period. It needs a group followed forward in time, so it comes from cohort studies and randomized trials. Risk in the exposed = a ÷ (a + b); risk in the unexposed = c ÷ (c + d).

The relative risk (risk ratio) is the ratio of the two: RR = [a ÷ (a + b)] ÷ [c ÷ (c + d)]. It answers "how many times as likely?" and measures the strength of an association, which is one of the considerations when judging causation.

RRMeaningExample wording
> 1Exposure associated with higher riskRR 1.5: 50% higher risk
= 1No associationSame risk in both groups
< 1Exposure associated with lower risk (protective)RR 0.8: 20% lower risk

Absolute measures: risk difference, ARR and ARI

The risk difference is risk exposed − risk unexposed. In a treatment trial where the drug lowers risk it is called the absolute risk reduction (ARR = control risk − treated risk); when an exposure or drug raises risk it is the absolute risk increase (ARI). The relative risk reduction is RRR = ARR ÷ control risk = 1 − RR.

The number needed to treat is NNT = 1 ÷ ARR, and the number needed to harm is NNH = 1 ÷ ARI. Both carry the trial's time frame ("over 3 years") and are rounded up to the next whole person.

Worked example

A trial of a fictional drug to prevent migraine-related emergency visits follows 500 patients per arm for 1 year. Visits occur in 60 of 500 on placebo (12%) and 45 of 500 on the drug (9%).

  • RR = 0.09 ÷ 0.12 = 0.75
  • RRR = 1 − 0.75 = 25%
  • ARR = 12% − 9% = 3 percentage points = 0.03
  • NNT = 1 ÷ 0.03 = 33.3 → 34 patients treated for 1 year to prevent one visit

The same 25% RRR in a population whose control risk is 40% would give an ARR of 10 points and an NNT of 10. Relative effects often stay similar across risk groups; absolute benefit grows with baseline risk.

Exam traps: (1) dividing by the column total or the grand total instead of the row total; (2) reporting RRR when the question asks for ARR or NNT; (3) forgetting to convert percentages to proportions before taking 1 ÷ ARR (1 ÷ 3 is not the NNT for a 3% ARR; 1 ÷ 0.03 is); (4) reading "reduces risk by 25%" as an absolute change.

Confidence intervals for ratios

A 95% confidence interval for an RR that includes 1 means the association is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level. The interval also shows precision: RR 0.80 (0.70–0.91) is precise and significant; RR 0.80 (0.55–1.16) is compatible with a large benefit or a modest harm. For a risk difference, the null value is 0.

High-yield pairing: relative measures (RR, RRR) describe strength of association and travel well between populations; absolute measures (ARR, NNT) describe how much difference treatment makes for a patient with a given baseline risk. Advertisements and headlines prefer the relative figure because it looks bigger.

When the outcome is uncommon, the odds ratio from a case-control study is close to the RR, which is why the two are often discussed together (next section).

s23g-s0302.bodyHtml:
Not every study can measure risk directly. The odds ratio and the hazard ratio are the association measures that come from case-control designs, logistic regression and survival analysis.

Odds and the odds ratio

Odds = probability of an event ÷ probability of no event = p ÷ (1 − p). A probability of 0.20 is odds of 0.25 (1 to 4). The odds ratio compares odds in two groups: OR = (a ÷ b) ÷ (c ÷ d) = ad ÷ bc, the cross-product of the 2×2 table.

In a case-control study, investigators choose people by outcome (cases and controls) and look back at exposure. Because they set the number of cases, the proportion with the outcome is artificial and risk cannot be calculated. The odds of exposure, however, can be compared, and the exposure odds ratio equals the disease odds ratio. That symmetry is why the OR is the measure for case-control data.

Worked example

A fictional case-control study enrols 200 adults with a rare liver injury and 400 controls. Use of a herbal supplement: 50 of 200 cases, 40 of 400 controls.

  • Cases: 50 exposed, 150 unexposed. Controls: 40 exposed, 360 unexposed.
  • OR = (50 × 360) ÷ (150 × 40) = 18,000 ÷ 6,000 = 3.0
  • Not 25% ÷ 10% = 2.5: that is a ratio of exposure proportions, not of odds.

When does the OR approximate the RR?

When the outcome is rare (a common rule of thumb is under about 10% in every group), b ≈ a + b and d ≈ c + d, so ad ÷ bc ≈ RR. For a common outcome the OR is always farther from 1 than the RR: an OR above 1 overstates the RR, and an OR below 1 understates it (looks more protective).

Baseline riskOR 2.0 corresponds to RR of about
1%1.98
10%1.82
30%1.54
50%1.33

Values computed as RR = OR ÷ (1 − p0 + p0 × OR), where p0 is the baseline risk.

Adjusted odds ratios from logistic regression

Logistic regression models the log odds of a binary outcome as a linear function of several predictors. Each exponentiated coefficient is an adjusted odds ratio: the OR for that predictor with the other variables held constant. A change from crude to adjusted OR shows how much measured confounders explained.

Hazard ratio

The hazard is the instantaneous event rate among people still at risk. A hazard ratio compares hazards between groups and comes from time-to-event (survival) analysis, usually a Cox proportional hazards model. It uses each person's follow-up time and handles censoring (people who leave or finish the study without the event).

  • HR 0.65: at any time, the event rate in the treated group is about 35% lower.
  • HR 1.4: a 40% higher event rate.
  • The proportional hazards assumption means the ratio is roughly constant over follow-up; Kaplan-Meier curves that cross suggest it fails.

How it appears on the exam

  • A case-control table with the outcome in the columns: calculate ad ÷ bc, and watch for the distractor that divides exposure percentages.
  • A logistic model in a cohort with a common outcome: recognise that the OR overstates the RR.
  • A Kaplan-Meier figure or Cox model: interpret the HR as a ratio of rates and check whether its interval includes 1.
  • A matched case-control design: the analysis uses the discordant pairs, but the result is still an odds ratio.

Exam traps: an HR of 0.65 does not mean 35% fewer people died, that survival was 35% longer, or a 35-point absolute reduction. It is a ratio of rates over time. Likewise, an OR of 3 for a common outcome is not "three times as likely".

Match the measure to the design: cohort or RCT with fixed follow-up → RR; case-control → OR; binary outcome with covariates → adjusted OR; time to event with censoring → HR. For every ratio, a 95% CI containing 1 means not significant.
