s23g-s0303.bodyHtml:
Beyond RR and OR, several measures answer different questions: how much disease is due to an exposure, how fast events occur when follow-up varies, and how often a finding occurs in the diseased compared with the healthy. Choosing the right one for the design is itself an exam skill.

Attributable risk and attributable risk percent

Attributable risk (AR, risk difference, excess risk) = risk exposed − risk unexposed. It is the extra risk carried by exposed people, assuming causation.

Attributable risk percent (attributable fraction among the exposed) = (risk exposed − risk unexposed) ÷ risk exposed = (RR − 1) ÷ RR. It is the share of cases among the exposed that would not occur without the exposure.

Population attributable risk

The population attributable risk (PAR) = risk in the whole population − risk in the unexposed. The population attributable fraction (PAF) is the share of all cases in the population due to the exposure:

PAF = p(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + p(RR − 1)], where p is the proportion of the population exposed.

Worked example (fictional numbers): an exposure is present in 30% of adults and doubles the risk (RR = 2). PAF = 0.30 × 1 ÷ (1 + 0.30) = 0.30 ÷ 1.30 ≈ 23%. Among exposed people, the attributable fraction is (2 − 1) ÷ 2 = 50%.

Rates and person-time

When people are followed for different lengths of time, count events per unit of person-time. Incidence rate = events ÷ person-time at risk (e.g. per 1,000 person-years, per 1,000 catheter-days). Compare groups with the rate ratio (incidence density ratio) and the rate difference.

Worked example: 18 infections in 3,000 person-days (6.0 per 1,000) versus 8 in 4,000 person-days (2.0 per 1,000). Rate ratio = 3.0; rate difference = 4.0 per 1,000 person-days. Comparing the raw counts (18 vs 8) would misstate the difference.

Prevalence ratio

A cross-sectional survey measures existing cases at one time, so it yields prevalence. The prevalence ratio = prevalence in exposed ÷ prevalence in unexposed. A prevalence odds ratio can also be reported, but it overstates the prevalence ratio when the condition is common.

Likelihood ratios as association measures

A likelihood ratio compares how often a test result occurs in people with the disease versus without it: LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity. It is a measure of association between a result and disease status that does not depend on prevalence, and it links directly to Bayesian updating of probability.

Which measure for which design?

Design or dataNatural measureCannot give directly
RCT or cohort, fixed follow-upRR, risk difference, NNT/NNH(all available)
Cohort with variable follow-upRate ratio, rate difference; HRSimple cumulative risk without survival methods
Case-controlOdds ratioIncidence, RR, attributable risk (without outside data)
Cross-sectionalPrevalence ratio, prevalence ORIncidence; temporal order
Two continuous variablesCorrelation, regression slopeRisk measures
Test result vs diseaseSensitivity, specificity, LRsPredictive values outside the study prevalence

How it appears on the exam

Expect a cohort table with a request for "the proportion of cases among exposed people due to the exposure" (attributable risk percent), a population question that gives exposure prevalence (PAF), or a study with different follow-up times in which only a rate per person-time gives the right comparison. A strong signal for a rate question is a denominator in person-years, patient-days or device-days.

Exam traps: using the exposed-only attributable fraction when the question asks about all cases in a population; comparing counts instead of rates when follow-up differs; and calculating an incidence or attributable risk from a case-control table.

Strength versus impact: RR tells you how strongly an exposure is linked to disease; attributable risk and PAF tell you how much disease it causes. A rare, strong risk factor can matter less to a population than a common, modest one.

s23g-s0304.bodyHtml:
Before any test is chosen, the data must be described: what kind of variable it is, where its centre is, how spread out it is and what shape it has.

Scales of measurement

ScalePropertiesExampleTypical summary and test
NominalNamed categories, no orderBlood group, sexCounts, proportions; chi-square
OrdinalOrdered, unequal stepsTumour grade, Likert ratingMedian, IQR; rank tests (Mann-Whitney, Spearman)
IntervalEqual steps, arbitrary zeroTemperature in °CMean, SD; t-test, ANOVA
RatioEqual steps, true zeroWeight, serum sodiumMean, SD; t-test, ANOVA, regression

Measures of central tendency

  • Mean: the arithmetic average; uses every value; pulled by outliers.
  • Median: the middle value of the ordered data (the 50th percentile); resistant to outliers.
  • Mode: the most frequent value; the peak of a histogram.

Skew

In a positively (right) skewed distribution the tail runs to the right (hospital costs, length of stay, many laboratory values bounded at zero): mode < median < mean. In a negatively (left) skewed distribution the tail runs to the left (age at death in a high-income country, scores on an easy test): mean < median < mode. The mean is always dragged toward the tail; the median sits between mean and mode.

Measures of spread

  • Range: maximum − minimum; set entirely by the extremes.
  • Interquartile range: 75th − 25th percentile; the middle half; pairs with the median.
  • Variance: the average squared deviation from the mean; standard deviation (SD) is its square root, in the original units.
  • Standard error of the mean (SEM) = SD ÷ √n: the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean. It shrinks as n grows; the SD does not.

Worked example: 25 patients have a mean hemoglobin of 13.0 g/dL with SD 1.5 g/dL. SEM = 1.5 ÷ 5 = 0.3 g/dL. A 95% CI for the mean ≈ 13.0 ± 1.96 × 0.3 = 12.4 to 13.6 g/dL. About 95% of individual patients lie within 13.0 ± 2 × 1.5 = 10.0 to 16.0 g/dL.

The normal distribution and z-scores

A normal (Gaussian) distribution is symmetric and bell shaped, with mean = median = mode. About 68% of values lie within ±1 SD, 95% within ±2 SD (more exactly ±1.96) and 99.7% within ±3 SD. A z-score = (value − mean) ÷ SD says how many SDs a value is from the mean. z = +1 is about the 84th percentile, z = +2 about the 98th, z = −2 about the 2nd.

Laboratory reference intervals are often set as the central 95% of healthy values, so 5% of healthy people fall outside them by definition.

Outliers and regression to the mean

An outlier is a value far from the rest; check for error before excluding it, and prefer medians when outliers are genuine. Regression to the mean: when people are selected because a measurement is extreme, a repeat measurement tends to be closer to the average, because part of the first value was chance. Uncontrolled before-and-after studies of "high" patients therefore overstate the effect of any intervention.

How it appears on the exam

Questions show a histogram and ask where the mean lies, give a mean and SD and ask what share of values lies above a cut-off, or give n and SD and ask for the SEM or a confidence interval. Ordinal outcomes appear in choice-of-test questions, where the right answer is a rank-based method.

Exam traps: confusing SD (spread of individuals) with SEM (precision of the mean); assuming ±2 SD covers 99%; reading a mean as "typical" in skewed data; and forgetting that ordinal data should not be averaged as if the steps were equal.

Fast skew rule: the mean follows the tail. If a question gives mean > median, the data are right skewed; if mean < median, left skewed.

s23g-s0305.bodyHtml:
Correlation describes how closely two variables move together; regression describes how an outcome changes with one or more predictors. Both are association, not causation.

Pearson correlation

The Pearson coefficient r measures the strength and direction of a linear relation between two continuous variables. It runs from −1 (perfect inverse line) through 0 (no linear relation) to +1 (perfect positive line). Strength is the absolute value: r = −0.7 is stronger than r = +0.5. r has no units and is not the slope.

The square, r² (coefficient of determination), is the proportion of variance in one variable explained by its linear relation with the other. r = 0.5 → r² = 0.25 → 25% explained.

Spearman rank correlation

Spearman's ρ correlates the ranks rather than the raw values. It measures a monotonic relation (consistently rising or falling, not necessarily straight), suits ordinal data and resists outliers and skew.

Linear regression

Simple linear regression fits y = a + b x. The intercept a is the predicted y when x = 0; the slope b is the change in y for each one-unit increase in x, in the units of y per unit of x. Worked example (fictional): eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²) = 125 − 0.9 × age. At age 60, predicted eGFR = 125 − 54 = 71.

Multiple linear regression adds predictors: each coefficient is the change in y per unit of that predictor with the others held constant. That is how regression adjusts for measured confounders. A coefficient that changes a lot when a variable is added suggests that variable confounds the association.

Regression models by outcome type

OutcomeModelEffect measure
Continuous (blood pressure, weight)Linear regressionSlope (difference in mean outcome per unit)
Binary (yes/no)Logistic regressionAdjusted odds ratio
Time to event with censoringCox proportional hazardsAdjusted hazard ratio
Counts per person-timePoisson regressionRate ratio

Choosing a hypothesis test

QuestionTest
Mean of a continuous outcome, 2 independent groupsTwo-sample t-test (Mann-Whitney U if skewed or ordinal)
Same people measured twicePaired t-test (Wilcoxon signed-rank if not normal)
Means of 3 or more groupsANOVA (Kruskal-Wallis if not normal)
Two categorical variablesChi-square (Fisher's exact if expected counts are small)
Two continuous variablesPearson correlation or linear regression (Spearman if not linear-normal)

Correlation is not causation

A correlation can arise from a confounder that drives both variables, from reverse causation, from chance in small samples, or from selection of the people studied. Two further pitfalls are restriction of range (a correlation looks weaker when the sample covers only a narrow range of x) and influential outliers, which can create or hide an apparent relation on their own.

How it appears on the exam

  • Two coefficients to compare: choose the larger absolute value as the stronger association.
  • A correlation coefficient given: square it for variance explained.
  • A scatter plot: estimate r, or recognise a curved pattern that r misses.
  • A study description: choose the test from the outcome type, the number of groups and whether measurements are paired.

Worked example for r²: a study reports r = −0.7 between weekly exercise minutes and resting heart rate. The association is fairly strong and inverse, and r² = 0.49, so about half the variation in resting heart rate is accounted for by its linear relation with exercise. The other half reflects age, fitness, medicines and measurement error.

Exam traps: (1) r near 0 does not mean no relation, only no linear one; a U-shaped pattern can give r ≈ 0. (2) A high r does not show agreement between two measurement methods, only that they rise together. (3) Group-level (ecological) correlations cannot be applied to individuals. (4) A steep slope is not a strong correlation, and vice versa.

Pick the test from the variables: what type is the outcome, how many groups, are the measurements paired? That decision tree answers most "which test" questions in a few seconds.

s23g-s0306.bodyHtml:
Screening means testing people without symptoms to find disease early. Because almost everyone screened is healthy, a screening programme must do more good than harm across a whole population, not just for the few who have the disease.

Conditions for a worthwhile programme

FeatureWhy it matters
Important burden (common or serious)Enough benefit to justify testing many people
Detectable preclinical phase of adequate lengthA window in which the test can find it before symptoms
Earlier treatment improves outcomeOtherwise screening only moves the diagnosis date
Acceptable, safe, affordable testHealthy people must be willing, and harms must be small
Adequate accuracy and a plan for positivesFalse positives and follow-up tests are a cost borne by healthy people
Benefit shown in outcomes (ideally mortality)Survival from diagnosis is distorted by screening biases

Reliability versus validity

Reliability (precision, reproducibility) is whether repeated measurements agree with each other; it is reduced by random error. Validity (accuracy) is whether measurements agree with the truth; it is reduced by systematic error (bias). A miscalibrated device can be precise but inaccurate. An unreliable test cannot be consistently valid.

Inter-rater reliability for categorical judgements is summarised by kappa, which corrects raw agreement for the agreement expected by chance: κ = (observed − expected) ÷ (1 − expected). Worked example: observed agreement 85%, chance agreement 50% → κ = 0.35 ÷ 0.50 = 0.70. κ = 0 is chance-level, 1 is perfect.

Combining tests: serial and parallel

StrategyRuleSensitivitySpecificityUse
Serial (series)Positive only if both positiveFalls (Se1 × Se2)Rises: 1 − (1 − Sp1)(1 − Sp2)Confirm; screening followed by a confirmatory test
ParallelPositive if either positiveRises: 1 − (1 − Se1)(1 − Se2)Falls (Sp1 × Sp2)Rule out when missing disease is dangerous

Formulas assume the tests' errors are independent given disease status. Worked example: two tests with sensitivity 85% and specificity 90% each. Serial: sensitivity 0.85² ≈ 72%, specificity 1 − 0.10² = 99%. Parallel: sensitivity 1 − 0.15² ≈ 98%, specificity 0.90² = 81%.

Screening pitfalls in brief

  • Lead-time bias: earlier diagnosis lengthens survival from diagnosis without delaying death.
  • Length-time bias: periodic screening preferentially finds slow-growing disease, which has a better prognosis anyway.
  • Overdiagnosis: screening finds disease that would never have caused symptoms; the sign is rising early-stage incidence without falling late-stage incidence or mortality.
  • False positives cause anxiety, further tests and procedures in healthy people.

These biases are covered in more depth with study interpretation; for screening, the point is that only randomized comparisons of mortality show true benefit.

How it appears on the exam

  • A list of candidate diseases or features: pick the one with a long detectable preclinical phase and effective early treatment.
  • A miscalibrated instrument: precise but not accurate.
  • Observed and expected agreement given: calculate kappa.
  • Two tests combined with "both" or "either": serial or parallel formulas.
  • Rising incidence with flat mortality after screening is introduced: overdiagnosis.

Screening recommendations for specific diseases change over time and are set by bodies such as the USPSTF; the exam tests the principles behind them.

Who pays for a screening error? A false negative falls on a person with disease who is wrongly reassured; a false positive falls on a healthy person who goes on to further testing. Because healthy people vastly outnumber the diseased in a screened population, even a small false-positive rate produces many more false positives than true positives when prevalence is low.

Exam traps: equating a high-sensitivity test with a good screening programme (a test is only one part of it); treating precise as accurate; and assuming that better 5-year survival in screen-detected cases proves screening works.

The usual screening pathway is serial: a sensitive, cheap, acceptable first test, then a specific confirmatory test for those who screen positive.

s23g-s0307.bodyHtml:
Diagnostic accuracy is measured against a reference standard in a 2×2 table: rows are the test result, columns are true disease status. Four cells: true positives (a), false positives (b), false negatives (c), true negatives (d).

Properties of the test: read down the columns

  • Sensitivity = a ÷ (a + c): of people with the disease, the proportion who test positive.
  • Specificity = d ÷ (b + d): of people without the disease, the proportion who test negative.

These do not depend on prevalence (for a similar spectrum of patients). A very sensitive test rarely misses disease, so a negative result is strong evidence against it: high sensitivity is what makes a test good for ruling out. A very specific test rarely calls healthy people positive, so a positive result is strong evidence for disease: high specificity is what makes a test good for ruling in.

Meaning for the patient: read across the rows

  • Positive predictive value = a ÷ (a + b): of people who test positive, the proportion who have the disease.
  • Negative predictive value = d ÷ (c + d): of people who test negative, the proportion free of disease.

Predictive values depend strongly on prevalence (pre-test probability). As prevalence rises, PPV rises and NPV falls; as it falls, PPV falls and NPV rises.

Worked example

A test with sensitivity 80% and specificity 95% is used in 2,000 people.

PrevalenceTPFPFNTNPPVNPV
20% (400 diseased)32080801,52080%95%
2% (40 diseased)329881,86225%99.6%

Same test, same sensitivity and specificity: at 2% prevalence, three of every four positives are false.

Moving the cut-off

For a continuous test, the distributions of values in diseased and healthy people overlap. Lowering the threshold for "positive" (moving it toward the healthy distribution) catches more cases: sensitivity rises, false negatives fall, but false positives rise and specificity falls. Raising the threshold does the opposite. NPV rises with sensitivity; PPV rises with specificity.

Likelihood ratios

LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity. In the example above, LR+ = 0.80 ÷ 0.05 = 16 and LR− = 0.20 ÷ 0.95 ≈ 0.21. LRs do not depend on prevalence and convert pre-test odds to post-test odds.

LREffect on probability
> 10 or < 0.1Large, often decisive change
5–10 or 0.1–0.2Moderate change
2–5 or 0.2–0.5Small change
About 1Little or no change

False positives and false negatives in practice

A false negative delays treatment and gives false reassurance, which is most harmful when the disease is serious and treatable. A false positive causes anxiety, more testing and sometimes unnecessary treatment, which is most harmful when the confirmatory work-up or treatment is invasive. The relative harm of each error decides whether a test should be tuned toward sensitivity or specificity.

How it appears on the exam

  • A 2×2 table: calculate any of the four measures, reading columns for sensitivity and specificity and rows for predictive values.
  • The same test moved to a population with a different prevalence: predict the direction of change in PPV and NPV.
  • A change in the cut-off: predict the change in sensitivity, specificity and each error type.

Remember that a likelihood ratio is not changed by prevalence, while a predictive value is. When a question moves a test into a new population, sensitivity, specificity and LRs stay; PPV and NPV must be recalculated from the new prevalence.

Exam traps: computing sensitivity across a row (that gives PPV); quoting a predictive value from a study population for a patient with a very different pre-test probability; and thinking a change in prevalence changes sensitivity or specificity.

Columns describe the test (sensitivity, specificity, LRs); rows describe the patient's result (PPV, NPV) and move with prevalence.

LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity. In the example above, LR+ = 0.80 ÷ 0.05 = 16 and LR− = 0.20 ÷ 0.95 ≈ 0.21. LRs do not depend on prevalence and convert pre-test odds to post-test odds.
False positives and false negatives in practice

A false negative delays treatment and gives false reassurance, which is most harmful when the disease is serious and treatable. A false positive causes anxiety, more testing and sometimes unnecessary treatment, which is most harmful when the confirmatory work-up or treatment is invasive. The relative harm of each error decides whether a test should be tuned toward sensitivity or specificity.
How it appears on the exam
A 2×2 table: calculate any of the four measures, reading columns for sensitivity and specificity and rows for predictive values.
The same test moved to a population with a different prevalence: predict the direction of change in PPV and NPV.
A change in the cut-off: predict the change in sensitivity, specificity and each error type.

Remember that a likelihood ratio is not changed by prevalence, while a predictive value is. When a question moves a test into a new population, sensitivity, specificity and LRs stay; PPV and NPV must be recalculated from the new prevalence.

Exam traps: computing sensitivity across a row (that gives PPV); quoting a predictive value from a study population for a patient with a very different pre-test probability; and thinking a change in prevalence changes sensitivity or specificity.
Columns describe the test (sensitivity, specificity, LRs); rows describe the patient's result (PPV, NPV) and move with prevalence.

s23g-s0308.bodyHtml:
A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve shows the whole trade-off between sensitivity and specificity for a continuous test, one point per possible cut-off.

How the curve is built

For each threshold, calculate sensitivity (true-positive rate) and 1 − specificity (false-positive rate). Plot sensitivity on the y-axis against 1 − specificity on the x-axis. A very strict cut-off (few positives) sits near (0, 0); a very loose one (almost everyone positive) sits near (1, 1). Loosening the cut-off moves the operating point up and to the right.

Landmarks

  • Upper-left corner (0, 1): a perfect test, with sensitivity 100% and no false positives.
  • Diagonal from (0, 0) to (1, 1): a test no better than chance, AUC 0.5.
  • Below the diagonal: the test discriminates but in reverse; flipping the positivity rule gives AUC = 1 − original AUC.

Area under the curve (AUC, c-statistic)

The AUC summarises discrimination over all cut-offs. It is the probability that a randomly chosen person with the disease has a more abnormal value than a randomly chosen person without it.

AUCUsual description
0.5No discrimination (chance)
0.6–0.7Poor
0.7–0.8Acceptable
0.8–0.9Good
> 0.9Excellent
1.0Perfect

These bands are conventions, not rules; the clinical value of a test depends on the cut-off used and its consequences. An AUC whose 95% CI includes 0.5 has not been shown to beat chance.

Comparing tests

Tests measured in the same patients can be compared on one plot: the curve closer to the upper-left corner, with the larger AUC, discriminates better overall. If curves cross, each test is better over a different range of false-positive rates, and the choice depends on which region the clinical use requires.

Choosing the cut-off

  • Equal costs of false positives and false negatives: choose the point farthest from the diagonal, i.e. the maximum Youden index J = sensitivity + specificity − 1 (often near the upper-left corner).
  • Missing disease is dangerous and a false positive is cheap (screening donated blood, ruling out a treatable emergency): choose a point on the high-sensitivity part of the curve.
  • False positives lead to harmful treatment: choose a high-specificity point.

Worked example: three cut-offs give (sensitivity, specificity) of (95%, 60%), (85%, 85%) and (60%, 97%). Youden J = 0.55, 0.70 and 0.57, so with equal error costs the middle cut-off is best.

Prevalence and spectrum

Because sensitivity and specificity are each calculated within one disease group, the ROC curve does not change with prevalence. It does change with spectrum: studies comparing advanced cases with healthy volunteers make tests look better than they will be in patients whose diagnosis is genuinely uncertain.

How it appears on the exam

  • A labelled ROC plot: name the axes, find the best balanced point or the point for a stated purpose.
  • Two curves on one plot: say which test discriminates better and whether the answer depends on the region used.
  • An AUC value: interpret it as a probability, and know that 0.5 is chance.
  • A change in prevalence or in cut-off: say whether the curve itself changes (it does not) or the operating point moves along it (it does, for a new cut-off).

Worked example for a reversed curve: a marker that falls in disease is analysed with "high values positive" and gives an AUC of 0.25. Reversing the rule (low values positive) gives an AUC of 0.75. The information was always there; only the direction of the rule was wrong.

Exam traps: putting specificity rather than 1 − specificity on the x-axis; reading the AUC as accuracy, PPV or the sensitivity at a cut-off; expecting prevalence to move the curve; and assuming the larger AUC always wins when curves cross.

Moving along the curve = changing the cut-off (trade-off). Moving the whole curve toward the upper left = a better test.

s23g-s0309.bodyHtml:
A few probability rules underlie predictive values, screening errors and genetic risk. Write the event in words first ("both", "either", "at least one", "given that"), and the rule follows.

Core rules

SituationRuleExample
Both of two independent eventsP(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)0.2 × 0.3 = 0.06
Either of two mutually exclusive eventsP(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)0.2 + 0.3 = 0.5
Either of two events that can overlapP(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)0.2 + 0.3 − 0.06 = 0.44 (if independent)
ComplementP(not A) = 1 − P(A)1 − 0.2 = 0.8
At least one of n independent events, each p1 − (1 − p)np = 0.1, n = 3: 1 − 0.729 = 0.271

Conditional probability

P(A | B), the probability of A given B, restricts attention to the people in whom B is true: P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B). Order matters. Sensitivity is P(positive | disease); PPV is P(disease | positive). Confusing them is the most common probability error in medicine.

Bayes' theorem

Bayes' theorem turns P(result | disease) into P(disease | result) using the pre-test probability. The bedside version uses odds and likelihood ratios:

  1. Pre-test odds = p ÷ (1 − p).
  2. Post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR.
  3. Post-test probability = odds ÷ (1 + odds).

Worked example: pre-test probability 30%, LR+ 5. Odds = 0.3 ÷ 0.7 ≈ 0.43; × 5 ≈ 2.14; probability ≈ 2.14 ÷ 3.14 ≈ 68%. If the result had been negative with LR− 0.2: 0.43 × 0.2 ≈ 0.086 → about 8%.

The Fagan nomogram does the same thing graphically: a straight line from the pre-test probability through the LR to the post-test probability. Results from several independent tests can be chained by multiplying their LRs, though real tests are often correlated.

Testing and treatment thresholds

Below a testing threshold the disease is unlikely enough to neither test nor treat; above a treatment threshold it is likely enough to treat without testing. A test is worthwhile only when its result could move the probability across one of these thresholds.

Simple binomial reasoning

For n independent trials, each with probability p, P(exactly k) = C(n, k) pk(1 − p)n − k, where C(n, k) counts the orders. Worked example: three unrelated patients each have a 0.3 probability of responding to a drug; the probability that exactly 1 of the 3 responds is 3 × 0.3 × 0.7² = 0.441. The expected number is n × p = 0.9.

Independence and its limits

Independence means one event does not change the probability of another. Genetic risk for each child of the same parents is independent; results of two tests that measure the same biology in the same patient often are not, so chaining their likelihood ratios overstates certainty. When a question says "assume independence", use multiplication; otherwise, consider whether the events are linked.

How it appears on the exam

Expect a pair of drug adverse-effect risks (both or either), repeated screening tests (at least one false positive), a contingency table (conditional probability) and a pre-test probability with an LR (post-test probability). Write the formula, then plug in.

Bayes' theorem in full: P(disease | positive) = [sensitivity × prevalence] ÷ [sensitivity × prevalence + (1 − specificity) × (1 − prevalence)]. This is exactly the PPV, written as probabilities instead of 2×2 cells.

Exam traps: multiplying a probability (not the odds) by an LR, which can exceed 100%; adding probabilities of events that are not mutually exclusive; and forgetting that independent events have no memory (a previous outcome does not change the next one).

"At least one" problems are almost always fastest by the complement: 1 − P(none).

s23g-s0401.bodyHtml:
An association means that two things occur together more (or less) often than chance would predict. Causation means that changing the exposure would change the risk of the outcome. Every observational association has four candidate explanations, and a causal claim is only reasonable once the other three have been considered:

  1. Chance: random variation in a sample (judged with P values and confidence intervals).
  2. Bias: a systematic error in who was studied or how exposure and outcome were measured.
  3. Confounding: a third factor linked to the exposure that independently affects the outcome.
  4. Reverse causation: the outcome, or its early phase, produced the exposure.

Only after these are addressed does the question become whether the association is causal.

Considerations for judging causation

In 1965 Austin Bradford Hill described a set of viewpoints for weighing whether an association is causal. They are not a checklist to be scored; they are questions to be weighed together.

ConsiderationQuestion it asksHow strong a requirement?
TemporalityDid the exposure come before the outcome?Required: the only logically necessary one
StrengthHow large is the relative risk or odds ratio?Supportive; large effects are harder to explain by confounding
ConsistencyIs the finding repeated in different populations, designs and investigators?Supportive
Biological gradientDoes risk rise with dose or duration?Supportive; thresholds and confounders can mislead
PlausibilityIs there a believable mechanism?Weak; limited by current knowledge
CoherenceDoes it fit with the natural history and laboratory evidence?Supportive
ExperimentDoes removing or reducing the exposure lower the outcome?Strong when available
SpecificityDoes the exposure lead to one particular outcome?Weakest; most causes have many effects
AnalogyDoes a similar agent cause a similar effect?Weak

To remember which one is indispensable, think of time's arrow: a cause has to be fired before it lands. Every other consideration can be missing in a real causal relationship; temporality cannot.

Reverse causation

Reverse causation is the most common reason an attractive association is wrong. It is likely when the disease, or symptoms that precede the diagnosis, could change the behaviour being studied. People with early heart failure may cut back on exercise; people who feel unwell may stop drinking, smoking or eating certain foods; people with early, undiagnosed disease may start a remedy for their symptoms. When the remedy then 'causes' the disease, the error is called protopathic bias. Cross-sectional studies, which measure exposure and outcome at the same moment, are especially vulnerable because they cannot show which came first.

Confounding as an alternative explanation

A confounder is associated with the exposure, is a cause (or marker of a cause) of the outcome and is not on the causal pathway between them. Older people take more medicines and have more falls; smokers drink more coffee and get more lung cancer. When the confounder is accounted for (by randomization, restriction, matching, stratification or adjustment), the association shrinks or disappears. Confounding is covered in detail in the bias section.

How study designs differ in causal strength

DesignWhat it can establishMain limitation for causation
Randomized controlled trialEffect of an assigned exposureNot possible for harmful exposures; may be small or short
Prospective cohortTemporality; incidence in exposed and unexposedConfounding; loss to follow-up
Case-controlAssociation with rare outcomesRecall and selection bias; confounding
Cross-sectionalPrevalence and associations at one timeCannot establish temporality
EcologicalAssociations between group averagesEcological fallacy; heavy confounding
Case report or seriesSignals and hypothesesNo comparison group

Randomization is the strongest tool because it balances measured and unmeasured characteristics between groups. When randomization is unethical (no one can be assigned to smoke or to a suspected toxin), causal conclusions rest on consistent observational evidence that satisfies several considerations at once, as with smoking and lung cancer.

Exam traps: (1) Choosing 'strength of association' or 'biological plausibility' as the required criterion; only temporality is required. (2) Calling a dose-response relationship 'proof'; a confounder that rises with the exposure can produce one too. (3) Accepting a cross-sectional association as causal without asking which came first.

Causation links directly to study design (which designs establish temporality) and to bias: every alternative explanation for an association is a threat to a study's internal validity.

s23g-s0402.bodyHtml:
Every study measures a sample, not the whole population, so its result differs from the truth partly by chance. Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals quantify that random error. They say nothing about bias or confounding.

Hypotheses and the P value

The null hypothesis (H0) states that there is no difference or no association; the alternative hypothesis (H1) states that there is one. A test asks how surprising the observed data would be if H0 were true. The P value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming H0 is true. If P is below the prespecified alpha (usually 0.05), H0 is rejected.

What the P value is not: it is not the probability that H0 is true, not the probability that the result is 'due to chance', not 1 minus the probability that the treatment works, and not a measure of the size or importance of an effect.

Two kinds of error

H0 true (no real effect)H0 false (real effect)
Reject H0Type I error (false positive); probability = alphaCorrect; probability = power (1 − beta)
Do not reject H0Correct; probability = 1 − alphaType II error (false negative); probability = beta

Studies usually set alpha at 0.05 and aim for power of 80% to 90% (beta 0.10 to 0.20). Power rises with a larger sample size, a larger true effect, less variability in the outcome and a higher alpha. A one-tailed test has more power than a two-tailed test for an effect in the predicted direction, but it cannot detect an effect in the opposite direction, so two-tailed tests are the default.

Think of a smoke detector. A type I error is the alarm sounding with no fire; a type II error is a fire with no alarm. Small studies are detectors with weak batteries (prone to type II errors); studies that run many tests are over-sensitive detectors (prone to type I errors).

Confidence intervals

A 95% confidence interval (CI) is the range of values for the true effect that are reasonably compatible with the data; formally, intervals built this way contain the true value in 95% of studies. For a mean difference, the 95% CI is roughly the estimate ± 1.96 standard errors.

Worked example. A trial finds systolic pressure 5 mm Hg lower with a drug, with a standard error of 2 mm Hg. The 95% CI is 5 ± 1.96 × 2 = 1.1 to 8.9 mm Hg. The interval excludes 0, so P < 0.05 (here z = 5 / 2 = 2.5, P ≈ 0.012).

MeasureNull value95% CI excludes the null value95% CI includes it
Difference (means, proportions, ARR)0P < 0.05P > 0.05
Ratio (RR, OR, HR)1P < 0.05P > 0.05

A CI also shows precision (its width) and whether clinically important effects remain possible, which a P value alone does not. A narrow interval near the null suggests no important effect; a wide interval spanning the null and important benefit means the study is inconclusive.

Multiple comparisons

Each test at alpha 0.05 carries a 5% chance of a false positive when H0 is true. With k independent tests, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.95k: for 20 tests, 1 − 0.9520 ≈ 64%. The Bonferroni correction divides alpha by the number of tests (0.05 / 20 = 0.0025). Subgroup analyses, many secondary outcomes and repeated interim looks all raise this problem.

Choosing a statistical test

OutcomeComparisonTest
ContinuousTwo independent groupsTwo-sample (independent) t-test
ContinuousSame people measured twice, or matched pairsPaired t-test
ContinuousThree or more groupsAnalysis of variance (ANOVA)
Categorical (proportions)Two or more independent groupsChi-square test
Categorical, small expected counts (under about 5 per cell)Two groupsFisher exact test
Two continuous variablesRelationshipCorrelation or linear regression

Exam traps: (1) Reading P = .03 as 'a 3% chance the result is due to chance'. (2) Treating a non-significant result as proof of no effect; check the interval and the power. (3) Using 0 as the null value for a ratio, or 1 for a difference. (4) Choosing a two-sample t-test for before-and-after measurements in the same people. (5) Thinking that lowering alpha raises power; it lowers it.

s23g-s0403.bodyHtml:
Exam questions often present results as a table, a graph or a short abstract and ask what the data show. The skill is to read the display accurately, convert it to the measure that answers the question and notice when the presentation or the authors' conclusion goes beyond the data.

Tables of results

Start with the denominators (how many in each group), the time frame and the outcome definition. Then compute what is asked.

Worked example. Over 4 years, an outcome occurs in 6% of a control group and 4% of a treated group. Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = 6% − 4% = 2 percentage points; relative risk = 4 / 6 = 0.67; relative risk reduction (RRR) = 1 − 0.67 = 33%; number needed to treat (NNT) = 1 / 0.02 = 50 over 4 years.

MeasureFormulaWhat it tells you
ARRControl risk − treated riskAbsolute benefit for a typical participant
RRRARR / control riskProportional benefit; looks large when risk is low
NNT1 / ARRPatients treated for the trial's duration to prevent one event
NNH1 / absolute risk increasePatients treated to cause one extra harm

Common graphs

  • Bar graphs compare a summary (mean, proportion) between categories. Check where the y-axis starts: a truncated axis exaggerates differences.
  • Error bars may show the standard deviation (spread of individual values), the standard error of the mean (SEM = SD / √n, precision of the mean) or a 95% CI. SEM bars are much narrower than SD bars.
  • Box plots show the median (line), the interquartile range (box, the middle 50%), whiskers (often to the furthest point within 1.5 × IQR) and outliers. A long upper whisker or high outliers indicate right skew; the mean then exceeds the median.
  • Histograms show the distribution of one continuous variable; scatter plots show the relationship between two.
  • Kaplan-Meier curves show the proportion free of an event over time. Each step down is an event; tick marks are censored participants. The median survival is where the curve first reaches 0.50. Numbers at risk below the axis show how much information supports the later part of the curve.
  • Forest plots show each study's (or subgroup's) estimate as a square, sized by its weight, with a horizontal line for its 95% CI, a vertical line at the null value and a diamond for the pooled estimate. A ratio axis is usually logarithmic, so 0.5 and 2 sit the same distance from 1.

In a forest plot, the pooled diamond can exclude the null even when most individual studies cross it; that is the point of pooling. Conversely, when the subgroup lines in a trial's forest plot all overlap the overall estimate, the trial shows no credible subgroup difference, even if some subgroup intervals cross 1.

Relative versus absolute presentation

The same result can be described as '33% fewer events' or '2 fewer events per 100 people over 4 years'. Both are accurate, but relative figures sound larger, especially when the baseline risk is low. Patients and clinicians judge benefit more accurately when given absolute numbers in natural frequencies.

Subgroup analyses

Subgroup results are credible only when they are few, prespecified with a predicted direction, supported by a formal test of interaction, biologically plausible and replicated. Many unplanned subgroups make a chance 'difference' likely. A subgroup interval that crosses 1 does not show that the subgroup failed to benefit; it may simply have fewer events.

Reading the text: is the conclusion supported?

Compare the abstract's conclusion with its design and numbers:

  • Does the conclusion rest on the primary end point, or on a secondary or subgroup finding?
  • Is a claim about a clinical outcome made from a surrogate?
  • Does an observational study use causal language ('reduces', 'prevents')?
  • Does a non-significant superiority trial claim the treatments are 'equivalent'? Equivalence needs a prespecified margin and a CI within it.
  • Does a before-after comparison ignore a trend that was already under way?

Exam traps: (1) Reading the line in a box plot as the mean. (2) Judging a difference from bar heights without checking the axis. (3) Reading a Kaplan-Meier median from the wrong curve. (4) Taking SEM error bars as the spread of individual patients. (5) Accepting the authors' conclusion without checking it against the primary result.

s23g-s0404.bodyHtml:
Bias is a systematic error that pushes a study's estimate away from the truth. Unlike random error, it does not shrink as the sample grows. Biases are grouped by where they arise: in choosing or keeping participants (selection bias), in measuring exposure or outcome (information bias), or from a third variable (confounding).

Selection bias

TypeHow it arisesTypical setting
Berkson biasExposure and disease both raise the chance of hospital admission, so inpatients show a spurious associationHospital-based case-control studies
Healthy worker effectEmployed people are healthier than the general population, which includes those too ill to workOccupational cohorts compared with population rates
Non-response / volunteer biasPeople who agree to take part differ from those who do notSurveys, screening studies
Attrition biasLoss to follow-up that differs between groups and relates to the outcomeCohorts and trials analysed per protocol

Information (measurement) bias

  • Recall bias: cases remember past exposures differently from controls (case-control studies).
  • Interviewer or observer bias: knowledge of a participant's group influences how exposure or outcome is recorded; blinding prevents it.
  • Observer-expectancy (Pygmalion) effect: an investigator's expectations influence participants' outcomes.
  • Hawthorne effect: participants change their behaviour because they know they are being observed.
  • Misclassification: putting people in the wrong exposure or outcome category. If the error is the same in all groups (non-differential), a binary exposure's estimate is usually biased toward the null. If it differs between groups (differential, as in recall bias), the bias can go either way.
  • Procedure or channelling bias: patients are steered to one treatment by their prognosis (for example, sicker patients receive the newer drug), so outcomes reflect who got the treatment rather than its effect.

Screening biases

Lead-time bias: earlier diagnosis lengthens the measured time from diagnosis to death even when death is not delayed. Length-time bias: periodic screening preferentially finds slow-growing disease, which has a long detectable preclinical phase and a better prognosis. Overdiagnosis is its extreme: detecting disease that would never have caused harm. All three make survival after diagnosis look better; none changes population mortality. Screening is therefore judged by disease-specific mortality in a randomized comparison.

Confounding and effect modification

A confounder is associated with the exposure, independently affects the outcome and is not on the causal pathway. It distorts the crude association. When the analysis is stratified by the confounder, the stratum-specific estimates are similar to each other but differ from the crude estimate.

Effect modification is not a bias. It means the effect itself differs across levels of a third variable (for example, a drug's harm is much greater in carriers of a genetic variant). Stratum estimates differ from each other, and they should be reported separately rather than pooled.

Method to address confoundingStageNote
RandomizationDesignBalances known and unknown confounders
RestrictionDesignEnrol only one level of the confounder; limits generalizability
MatchingDesignControls for matched factors only; common in case-control studies
StratificationAnalysisEstimate within levels of the confounder
Multivariable adjustmentAnalysisHandles several measured confounders; cannot fix unmeasured ones

Publication bias

Studies with positive or striking results are more likely to be published, published quickly and cited. Meta-analyses of published studies can therefore overestimate effects. Trial registration and funnel plots help detect it.

To tell confounding from effect modification at a glance, compare the strata with each other first. Strata that agree with each other (but not with the crude estimate) mean confounding: adjust. Strata that disagree with each other mean effect modification: report each.

Exam traps: (1) Calling longer survival in screen-detected patients proof that screening works. (2) Assuming all misclassification inflates effects; non-differential error usually hides them. (3) Treating an effect modifier as a nuisance to be adjusted away. (4) Thinking that statistical adjustment removes confounders that were never measured.

s23g-s0405.bodyHtml:
Two different questions are asked of every study. Internal validity: is the result correct for the people who were studied, or could bias, confounding or chance explain it? External validity (generalizability): does the result apply to other people, settings and times, and in particular to the patient in front of me? Internal validity comes first; an internally invalid result is not worth generalizing.

What protects internal validity

  • Random allocation with allocation concealment (no one can predict or change the next assignment).
  • Blinding of participants, clinicians and outcome assessors, especially for subjective outcomes.
  • Complete follow-up and intention-to-treat analysis (analysing everyone in the group to which they were randomized).
  • Valid, reliable outcome measures applied in the same way to all groups.

Threats include selection bias, differential loss to follow-up, unblinded assessment, contamination (control participants receiving the intervention) and confounding in observational designs.

What limits external validity

  • Eligibility criteria: trials often exclude older adults, pregnant women, people with kidney or liver disease, multiple comorbidities or many medications.
  • Run-in periods that remove non-adherent people, placebo responders or those with early side effects.
  • Setting and expertise: academic centres, specialist staff and high-volume operators.
  • Intensity of follow-up: frequent visits and pill counts that improve adherence beyond usual care.
  • Time and place: different background treatment, health systems or populations.

Efficacy and effectiveness

Explanatory trial (efficacy)Pragmatic trial (effectiveness)
QuestionCan it work under ideal conditions?Does it work in usual practice?
ParticipantsHighly selected, adherentBroad, typical patients
SettingSpecialist centres, close monitoringOrdinary clinics and staff
StrengthHigh internal validityHigh external validity
Usual effect sizeLargerSmaller

A pragmatic randomized trial keeps randomization (internal validity) while enrolling broadly in usual settings (external validity).

Random sampling versus random allocation

These two uses of 'random' protect different things. Random sampling selects participants from a population so that the sample represents it, which supports external validity (for example, a prevalence survey). Random allocation assigns enrolled participants to groups, which supports internal validity. A trial can randomly allocate a highly unrepresentative sample.

Applying a trial to a patient

Ask three questions: Would my patient have been eligible? If not, is there a plausible reason the effect would differ (age, kidney function, comorbidity, interacting drugs)? Are the harms likely to be greater (older patients are usually more susceptible to adverse effects)? If the answers raise doubt, the trial's numbers are a starting point, not a forecast.

A quick internal-validity check for a trial

Work through the trial in order. Was allocation random and concealed? Were the groups similar at baseline (the first table of most trials)? Who was blinded, and were the outcomes objective (death) or subjective (pain, symptom scores, which are more vulnerable to unblinded assessment)? How many participants were lost, and was loss similar between groups? Was the analysis by intention to treat? Did the trial stop early for benefit, which tends to overestimate effects? A 'no' to any of these weakens confidence in the result before generalizability is even considered.

A useful habit when reading any abstract is to scan the Participants paragraph twice: once for who was included and once for who was left out. Exclusions describe the patients the trial cannot speak for.

Exam traps: (1) Saying a randomized trial 'lacks internal validity' because its participants differ from your patient; that is external validity. (2) Equating random sampling with randomization. (3) Assuming that a larger sample improves generalizability; a large unrepresentative sample is still unrepresentative.

External validity is the bridge between a trial's result and an individual decision: the next sections convert a valid, applicable result into an absolute benefit for a specific patient.

s23g-s0406.bodyHtml:
A result is statistically significant when chance is an unlikely explanation (P below alpha, or a CI that excludes the null). It is clinically significant when the effect is large enough to matter to patients. The two are independent: a huge trial can make a trivial effect significant, and a small trial can fail to confirm an important one.

The minimal clinically important difference

The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) is the smallest change in an outcome that patients perceive as beneficial and that would justify a change in management. It is used to plan sample size (the target difference) and to judge results.

Effect and 95% CI compared with the MCIDInterpretation
Whole CI above the MCIDSignificant and clinically important
CI excludes 0 but lies wholly below the MCIDSignificant but clinically trivial
CI excludes 0 and straddles the MCIDSignificant; clinical importance uncertain
CI includes 0 and extends above the MCIDInconclusive; an important effect is still possible
CI includes 0 and lies wholly below the MCIDNo important effect likely

Worked example. A trial of 30,000 people finds that a supplement lowers LDL cholesterol by 1.5 mg/dL (95% CI, 0.9 to 2.1; P < .001). The effect is statistically significant but far smaller than the changes that alter cardiovascular risk meaningfully, so it is not clinically important.

Surrogate and patient-important end points

A surrogate end point is a biomarker or physiological measure (blood pressure, LDL, HbA1c, bone density, viral load, tumour shrinkage, arrhythmia counts) used in place of an outcome patients experience. Patient-important outcomes are how people feel, function or survive: death, stroke, fracture, hospitalization, symptoms and quality of life.

Surrogates make trials smaller and faster, but drugs have repeatedly improved a surrogate while failing to improve, or while worsening, the clinical outcome. Recurring patterns include drugs that suppress an arrhythmia on monitoring yet increase deaths, agents that raise a 'good' lipid fraction without preventing heart attacks, and intensive lowering of a laboratory value that adds harm. A surrogate is trustworthy only when changes in it have been shown to predict changes in the clinical outcome across treatments.

Composite end points

A composite end point counts a participant as having the outcome if any of several events occurs (for example, cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke or revascularization). It increases the event rate and power. The cautions: components may differ greatly in importance; the treatment may affect them differently; and a softer, more frequent component (a procedure, a hospital visit) can drive the whole result. Always read the components.

Primary, secondary and post hoc end points

The primary end point is prespecified, drives the sample-size calculation and is the basis of the main conclusion. Secondary end points support or explore it; when many are tested, some will be significant by chance. Post hoc analyses chosen after seeing the data are hypothesis-generating. Changing the primary outcome after the fact (outcome switching) invalidates the main test, which is why trials are registered in advance.

Individual versus population importance

Clinical significance is judged for the decision at hand. A blood-pressure fall of 2 mm Hg is trivial for one patient's symptoms but, applied across a whole population through salt reduction, can prevent many strokes. Conversely, a large relative reduction in a very rare outcome may matter little to an individual. State whose perspective the judgement takes: the patient, the clinician choosing a drug or the health system deciding a policy.

Before reading a P value, ask 'How big?' and 'In what outcome?' A large effect on a surrogate, a small effect on a clinical outcome and a large effect on the least serious part of a composite all need different answers to 'Does this help my patient?'

Exam traps: (1) Treating P < .001 as proof of a large effect. (2) Treating a non-significant result from a small trial as proof of no effect when the point estimate exceeds the MCID. (3) Accepting a surrogate result as evidence of clinical benefit. (4) Reporting a composite as if every component were reduced.

s23g-s0407.bodyHtml:
Trials report average effects in groups. Applying them to one patient means asking three questions: Is the result valid? Does it apply to this patient? And how large are the benefit and harm for this patient, given their own baseline risk and values?

From relative to absolute benefit

Relative risk reductions are often similar across groups with different baseline risks. Absolute benefit is not: it is proportional to baseline risk.

Patient ARR = patient's baseline risk × RRR, and patient NNT = 1 / patient ARR.

Worked example. A treatment has an RRR of 20% over 5 years. For a patient with a 5% baseline risk, ARR = 0.05 × 0.20 = 1% (NNT 100). For a patient with a 30% baseline risk, ARR = 0.30 × 0.20 = 6% (NNT 1 / 0.06 = 16.7, so 17). The same drug, with the same relative effect, is six times more worthwhile in absolute terms for the higher-risk patient.

Baseline 5-year riskRRRARRNNT (rounded up)
5%20%1%100
15%20%3%34
30%20%6%17

Harms usually do not scale with baseline risk of the disease being prevented; a bleeding risk from an anticoagulant, for instance, depends on the patient's bleeding risk. So low-risk patients can face a similar absolute harm for a much smaller absolute benefit.

Weighing benefit against harm

Compare the NNT with the number needed to harm (NNH = 1 / absolute risk increase), keeping the time frame the same and considering how serious each outcome is. Expressing both per 1,000 patients makes the comparison concrete: with an ARR of 1% and an absolute risk increase of 0.5%, 1,000 treated patients have 10 events prevented and 5 harms caused.

Communicating risk

  • Use absolute numbers and natural frequencies ('out of 100 people like you, about 6 would have a stroke in 5 years without treatment and about 5 with it').
  • Use the same denominator and time frame for benefits and harms.
  • Avoid relative risks on their own and avoid mixing formats ('1 in 50' versus '3%').
  • Icon arrays and decision aids improve understanding, especially for people with limited numeracy.
  • Check understanding with teach-back.

Values, preferences and guidelines

Evidence does not make the decision; it informs it. Two patients with the same numbers may reasonably choose differently because they value outcomes (a stroke versus a bleed, a daily pill versus an infection) differently. Shared decision-making combines the best evidence, the clinician's expertise and the patient's values. Guidelines summarize evidence for typical patients; departing from them can be appropriate for a patient who differs from the trial populations or who has different priorities, provided the reasoning is explained and documented.

When no trial matches the patient

Many patients (the very old, the pregnant, those with several chronic diseases) were excluded from the trials that support a treatment. Options are to look for subgroup data or observational studies in similar patients, to reason from biology about whether the relative effect should hold, to weigh the patient's competing risks and life expectancy (a benefit that takes 10 years to appear may never be realized), and to start cautiously with monitoring when the balance is uncertain. Saying honestly that the evidence is limited is part of shared decision-making.

The quickest way to individualize a trial is to keep its relative effect and swap in your patient's baseline risk. Risk calculators supply the baseline; the trial supplies the RRR.

Exam traps: (1) Using the trial's NNT for a patient whose baseline risk differs. (2) Computing NNT as 1 / RRR. (3) Comparing an NNT over 5 years with an NNH over 1 year. (4) Presenting only the relative risk reduction to a patient.

s23g-s0501.bodyHtml:
Consent for research is stricter than consent for treatment because the purpose is different. Clinical care aims at the good of the individual patient; research aims at generalizable knowledge, and the participant accepts risk partly for the benefit of others. The federal rules for most US research (the Common Rule, 45 CFR 46, for federally funded work, and the FDA rules, 21 CFR 50, for studies of drugs, biologics and devices) therefore spell out what a participant must be told, how the decision must be made and when the usual process can be changed.

Three ingredients of valid consent

  • Disclosure: the information a reasonable person would want before deciding.
  • Comprehension: the person actually understands it. Since the 2018 revision of the Common Rule, a consent document must open with a short, focused summary of the key information (why the study is being done, what joining involves, the main risks and benefits and the alternatives) before the details.
  • Voluntariness: the choice is free of coercion and undue influence, and the person can stop at any time.

What the participant must be told

ElementWhat it means in practice
This is researchPurpose, expected duration, procedures, and which procedures are experimental
Risks and discomfortsReasonably foreseeable ones, including the inconvenience of extra visits
BenefitsTo the participant or to others; payment is not counted as a benefit
AlternativesOther procedures or treatments that might help the person, including standard care outside the study
ConfidentialityHow far records will be kept confidential and who may see them (for FDA studies, that the FDA may inspect)
InjuryFor more than minimal risk: whether any compensation or medical treatment is available if injury occurs, and where to learn more
ContactsWhom to ask about the study, about participant rights and about a research-related injury
VoluntarinessJoining is voluntary; refusing or withdrawing brings no penalty or loss of benefits the person is otherwise entitled to
Future useWhether identifiers might be removed and the data or specimens used in future research, or that they will not be

Additional elements are added when they apply: risks to an embryo or fetus, circumstances in which the investigator may end participation, extra costs, consequences of withdrawal, the promise to share significant new findings, the approximate number of participants, commercial profit from specimens, whether clinically relevant results will be returned, and whether whole-genome sequencing will be done.

The rule requires the form to say whether compensation or treatment for research injury is available. It does not require the sponsor to provide compensation. A form that says "no compensation is offered" can be compliant; a form that is silent is not.

Coercion, undue influence and payment

Coercion is an overt or implied threat of harm or loss to make someone join (for example, a supervisor hinting that employees who decline will lose shifts). Undue influence is an excessive or inappropriate reward or offer that distorts judgment about risk. Payment for time, travel and inconvenience is acceptable; the IRB judges whether the amount and schedule are reasonable. Payment is usually prorated across visits so that a person who leaves early is not penalized, and any bonus for finishing should be small. Students, employees and patients of the investigator are at risk of subtle pressure, so recruitment is often done by someone outside the relationship.

Therapeutic misconception

A participant has a therapeutic misconception when they believe that research decisions (randomization, fixed doses, placebo, extra tests) are being made for their personal benefit, as in ordinary care. It undermines comprehension, so the person obtaining consent should explain randomization and blinding plainly and check understanding, for example by asking the person to explain in their own words how their treatment will be chosen.

People who cannot consent for themselves

  • Children: parents give permission and the child gives assent, an affirmative agreement appropriate to age and maturity. Simply not objecting is not assent. When research offers the child no prospect of direct benefit, a child's refusal should normally be respected.
  • Adults who lack capacity: a legally authorized representative (LAR), defined by the applicable state law, gives consent based on the person's known wishes or best interests. The participant's objection or distress should be respected, and if capacity returns the person should be asked for their own consent to continue.
  • Emergency research: the FDA exception (21 CFR 50.24) allows enrolment without prospective consent in narrowly defined trials of life-threatening conditions where current treatments are unproven or unsatisfactory, consent is not feasible within the therapeutic window, the intervention offers a prospect of direct benefit and the study could not otherwise be done. It requires IRB approval, community consultation and public disclosure before the study starts, an independent data monitoring committee, and attempts to contact a family member or LAR as soon as feasible, who may then end participation.

Consent is a process, not a signature. It continues through the study: participants are told about significant new findings that might change their willingness to continue, and they can withdraw at any time for any reason.

Waivers and alterations

An IRB may waive or alter consent, or waive the signed document, only when specific criteria are met. For a waiver of consent under the Common Rule the research must involve no more than minimal risk, be impracticable without the waiver (and, if identifiable information is used, impracticable without the identifiers), and the waiver must not adversely affect participants' rights and welfare; participants are given pertinent information afterwards when appropriate. Signed documentation can be waived when the signature would be the only record linking the person to the study and the main risk is a breach of confidentiality, when the study is minimal risk with no procedure that normally needs written consent, or when signing forms is not the norm in the participant's community. Investigators never decide on their own that consent can be skipped.

Clinical consent covers the same elements (nature, risks, benefits, alternatives) but has emergency and therapeutic-privilege exceptions that do not carry over to research.

s23g-s0502.bodyHtml:
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) sets national rules for how health information is used and disclosed. Its Privacy Rule governs protected health information in any form; its Security Rule adds safeguards for electronic information; its Breach Notification Rule says what to do when unsecured information is exposed. State laws that protect privacy more strictly still apply alongside it.

Who and what is covered

Covered entities are health plans, health care clearinghouses and health care providers who conduct standard electronic transactions such as billing. Business associates (a billing company, a cloud host, a transcription service) handle information on their behalf under a written business associate agreement and are directly liable for complying. HIPAA does not reach everyone who holds health data: a consumer fitness app the patient chose, an employer's personnel file or a school's education records are outside it, although other laws may apply.

Protected health information (PHI) is individually identifiable information about a person's health, care or payment for care, held or sent by a covered entity or business associate, whether on paper, spoken or electronic.

Uses and disclosures

CategoryPatient authorization needed?Examples
Treatment, payment, health care operationsNoSending a referral letter, billing an insurer, internal quality review
To the patientNoPatient requests a copy of their record
Family or friends involved in careNo, if the patient agrees or does not object when given the chance; professional judgment if the patient is incapacitatedTelling a spouse at the bedside about discharge plans
Public interest purposesNo (within the conditions of each category)Reportable diseases to public health, suspected child abuse, FDA adverse-event reports, health oversight, court orders, limited law-enforcement requests, coroners, organ procurement, serious and imminent threats
ResearchYes, unless an IRB or privacy board waives it, or the data are de-identified or a limited data setChart review for a study
Marketing, sale of PHI, most psychotherapy notesYesGiving patient lists to a drug company

The minimum necessary standard requires covered entities to limit uses, disclosures and requests to the least information needed for the purpose. It does not apply to disclosures to another provider for treatment, to the patient, to disclosures under the patient's authorization, to HHS for enforcement, or to disclosures required by law.

Treatment disclosures between clinicians do not need the patient's signature. A consultant can receive the full relevant record over the phone or through the EHR. Refusing to share for treatment "because of HIPAA" is a common real-world and exam error.

Patient rights

  • Access: to inspect and get a copy of their records, in the form requested if readily producible, within a deadline set by the rule, for at most a reasonable cost-based fee. Access cannot be refused because the patient owes money.
  • Amendment: to request a correction. The entity may deny it if the record is accurate and complete, and the patient may then file a statement of disagreement that travels with the record.
  • Accounting of disclosures: a list of certain disclosures made for purposes other than treatment, payment and operations.
  • Restrictions: to ask for limits; the provider must agree not to send information to a health plan about care the patient paid for in full out of pocket.
  • Confidential communications: to be contacted at an alternative address or number.

De-identification and limited data sets

De-identified data are not PHI and are no longer regulated by HIPAA. There are two methods. Safe harbor removes 18 types of identifiers of the person and relatives, employers or household members, and the entity must have no actual knowledge that what remains could identify someone. Expert determination has a qualified statistician document that the risk of re-identification is very small.

Safe harbor removes (selected)May remain
Names; street address, city and full ZIP code; all elements of dates except year (birth, admission, discharge, death); ages over 89Year of an event; age 89 or younger; state; first three ZIP digits when that area holds more than 20,000 people
Phone, fax, email, Social Security, medical record, health plan, account, license, vehicle and device numbers; URLs and IP addresses; biometrics; full-face photographs; any other unique codeDiagnoses, laboratory values, medications, sex

A limited data set strips direct identifiers (names, street addresses, contact numbers, record numbers, photos) but may keep dates, city, state, ZIP code and age. It can be used for research, public health or operations without authorization, but only under a data use agreement in which the recipient promises not to re-identify or contact individuals.

Ladder of data for research: identifiable PHI needs authorization or an IRB/privacy board waiver; a limited data set needs a data use agreement; de-identified data need neither.

Research under HIPAA

A research authorization is a specific signed permission that names the information, the recipients and the purpose; it may be combined with the research consent form and can be revoked in writing. An IRB or privacy board can waive authorization when the use poses minimal risk to privacy (with a plan to protect and destroy identifiers), the research could not practicably be done without the waiver and could not practicably be done without the PHI. Investigators may review records preparatory to research (to design a protocol or count eligible patients) if they do not remove PHI from the covered entity.

Security and breaches

The Security Rule requires administrative safeguards (risk analysis, workforce training), physical safeguards (locked areas, device controls) and technical safeguards (access controls, audit logs, encryption where reasonable) for electronic PHI. A breach of unsecured PHI is presumed reportable unless a documented risk assessment shows a low probability that the information was compromised. Affected individuals must be told without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery; HHS must be notified, and large breaches (more than 500 residents of a state) also require notice to the media. Information encrypted to the HHS standard is "secured", and its loss is not a reportable breach.

s23g-s0503.bodyHtml:
An institutional review board (IRB) is a committee that reviews research with human participants before it starts and while it runs, to protect participants' rights and welfare. Federally funded research falls under the Common Rule (45 CFR 46, subpart A), adopted by many federal agencies and revised with effect from 2019. FDA-regulated studies of drugs, biologics and devices fall under the FDA's parallel rules (21 CFR 50 and 56). Many institutions apply the same standards to all their research regardless of funding.

Who sits on an IRB

  • At least five members with varied backgrounds, sufficient to judge the research and community attitudes.
  • At least one member whose main concerns are scientific and at least one whose main concerns are nonscientific (for example, a lawyer, ethicist or member of clergy).
  • At least one member not otherwise affiliated with the institution and not in the immediate family of someone who is.
  • Members with a conflicting interest in a study may give information but do not take part in the review or vote.
  • When prisoners are involved, at least one member must be a prisoner or a prisoner representative.

What the IRB looks at

Before approving, the IRB must find that risks are minimized and reasonable in relation to expected benefits and the importance of the knowledge; that selection of participants is equitable; that informed consent will be sought and documented appropriately; that there is adequate monitoring of data for safety when appropriate; that privacy and confidentiality are protected; and that extra safeguards exist for people vulnerable to coercion or undue influence. Approval comes before any participant is enrolled. Changes to an approved protocol also need IRB approval before they are implemented, except a change needed to eliminate an apparent immediate hazard to participants, which is reported promptly afterwards. Unanticipated problems involving risks to participants or others must be reported promptly. The IRB can suspend or terminate approval.

Levels of review

LevelApplies toWho reviews
ExemptLow-risk categories such as research on normal educational practices; anonymous surveys, interviews or observation of public behaviour; benign behavioural interventions with adults; certain secondary research with existing information; taste and food quality studiesAn institutional determination, usually by the IRB office rather than the investigator; some categories need a limited IRB review of privacy protections
ExpeditedNo more than minimal risk and fits a published category (for example, modest blood draws by venipuncture or finger stick, noninvasive specimen collection, routine noninvasive clinical measurements, existing records, surveys or recordings), or minor changes to approved researchThe chair or one or more experienced members; they can approve or require changes but cannot disapprove
Full boardGreater than minimal risk, or anything not fitting the other categoriesA convened meeting with a majority of members present, including a nonscientist; approval by majority vote

Minimal risk means the probability and magnitude of harm are not greater than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during routine physical or psychological examinations.

"Exempt" does not mean exempt from ethics or from the institution: an exempt study still needs an institutional determination, honest information for participants and protection of their data. An investigator who self-declares a study exempt and starts recruiting has skipped a required step.

Continuing review and multisite research

Under the revised Common Rule, studies approved by the full board are reviewed at least annually. Continuing review is generally no longer required for studies eligible for expedited review or for studies that have moved to data analysis or collecting follow-up data from routine care, unless the IRB documents why it wants it. FDA-regulated studies remain subject to annual continuing review under FDA rules. For federally funded cooperative (multisite) research at US institutions, the Common Rule requires a single IRB of record, which avoids each site re-reviewing and changing the protocol.

Extra protections: subparts B, C and D

SubpartPopulationKey protections
BPregnant women, fetuses, neonatesAppropriate preclinical and nonpregnant data first; risk to the fetus is minimal unless the research may directly benefit the woman or fetus; the woman's consent suffices unless the benefit is solely to the fetus, when the father's consent is also sought (unless he is unavailable, incompetent or temporarily incapacitated, or the pregnancy resulted from rape or incest); no inducement to end a pregnancy; investigators take no part in decisions about ending a pregnancy or about neonatal viability
CPrisonersResearch limited to specific categories (the causes and effects of incarceration, prisons as institutions, conditions affecting prisoners as a class, practices likely to benefit the participant); advantages of joining must not be so large that they impair judgment; risks acceptable to non-prisoner volunteers; parole boards may not take participation into account; selection fair and free of interference from prison authorities
DChildrenFour approvable risk categories: minimal risk; greater than minimal risk with prospect of direct benefit; a minor increase over minimal risk without direct benefit but likely to yield vital knowledge about the child's condition (both parents' permission, where reasonably available); otherwise only after federal review. Parental permission plus child assent

The IRB's three core questions mirror the Belmont Report: are risks justified by benefits (beneficence), is consent adequate (respect for persons), and are participants chosen fairly (justice)?

Data and safety monitoring boards watch accumulating outcome data during a trial; IRBs oversee protection of participants. A large trial usually has both, and the IRB receives the monitoring board's summary reports.
