s23g-s0504.bodyHtml:
An interim analysis is a look at the accumulating outcome data of a trial before its planned end. Interim looks protect participants: if one arm is clearly better or clearly harmful, continuing to randomize people to the worse option is no longer ethical, and if the trial cannot possibly answer its question, continuing wastes participants' time and risk. But every look is also a chance to be fooled by random variation, so interim analyses are planned in advance, done by an independent group and judged against stricter thresholds than the final analysis.

Who looks: the data and safety monitoring board

A data and safety monitoring board (DSMB), also called a data monitoring committee, is a small group of clinicians, a biostatistician and often an ethicist who are independent of the sponsor and the investigators. Only the DSMB (and an independent statistician who prepares its reports) sees comparative results by arm. Investigators, participants and the sponsor stay blinded. After each review the DSMB recommends continuing unchanged, modifying the trial (for example, changing eligibility or adding monitoring) or stopping; the sponsor and steering committee act on the recommendation. DSMBs are expected for large trials, trials with mortality or major morbidity end points, trials in vulnerable populations and trials that use the emergency consent exception.

Three reasons to stop early

ReasonWhat the DSMB seesTypical evidence threshold
Efficacy (benefit)Difference favouring the new treatment crosses a prespecified, very strict boundaryOverwhelming: a much smaller P value than 0.05 at early looks
HarmExcess deaths or serious adverse events in one armOften less strict than for benefit, and may rest on clinical judgment as well as a statistical rule
FutilityEven if the rest of the trial went as hoped, a meaningful benefit is very unlikely (low conditional power)Prespecified futility rule; stopping does not prove the treatments are equivalent

Why each look needs a stricter threshold

If a test at P < 0.05 is repeated at several looks, each look gives chance another opportunity to produce a "significant" result, so the overall probability of a false-positive conclusion (the type I error) rises above 5%. Because the looks reuse accumulating data, they are correlated, so the inflation is smaller than for independent tests, but it is still substantial: with five equally spaced looks each tested at 0.05, the overall false-positive rate is roughly 14%.

Group sequential designs fix this by spending the overall alpha of 0.05 across the looks. A simple and conservative approach divides it equally: with five planned analyses each is tested at 0.05 ÷ 5 = 0.01. Most trials instead use boundaries that are extremely strict early (when few events have accrued) and relax towards the end, so the final analysis can still be tested at a level close to 0.05. An alpha-spending function lets the looks happen at flexible times, defined by the information fraction (the proportion of planned events observed so far), while keeping the total at 0.05.

An interim P value of 0.01 sounds significant, but if the boundary at that look is P < 0.001 the correct decision is to continue the trial. The prespecified boundary, not 0.05, decides.

What early stopping does to the evidence

  • Effect size is overestimated. Trials tend to cross an efficacy boundary early when random variation happens to exaggerate the benefit. If the true relative risk is 0.80, a trial halted at an early look will often report something like 0.55. Pooled analyses show that truncated trials report larger effects than completed trials of the same question.
  • Precision is lower: fewer events give wider confidence intervals.
  • Safety and secondary outcomes are underexplored: rare or delayed harms may not yet have appeared.
  • Subgroups are unreliable.

Interim results must stay confidential. If investigators learn that one arm is ahead, they may change whom they enroll, how they assess outcomes or how they treat participants, and the trial's integrity is lost. A sponsor that asks to see unblinded interim data for business planning is asking for something the trial design forbids. Participants asking "is it working?" are told honestly that the investigators do not know, that an independent board is watching the results and that they will be told of any finding that matters to them.

  • "Prespecified stopping boundary", "independent committee", "information fraction", "conditional power" signal interim analysis.
  • Questions ask who should see interim data (the DSMB), why the threshold is stricter (type I error inflation from multiple looks), what an early stop implies (overestimated effect) or what a futility stop means (unlikely to show benefit, not proof of equivalence).

But every look is also a chance to be fooled by random variation, so interim analyses are planned in advance, done by an independent group and judged against stricter thresholds than the final analysis.

s23g-s0505.bodyHtml:
In the United States the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) decides whether a drug, biologic or medical device may be studied in people and marketed. Its rules give a sequence every new drug follows, and exam questions usually ask what a given step is for or who takes part in it.

Before people: preclinical work and the IND

Laboratory and animal studies characterize pharmacology, toxicity and a safe starting dose. Before the drug is given to any person in a US clinical investigation, the sponsor submits an Investigational New Drug (IND) application describing the preclinical data, manufacturing and the clinical protocol. The trial may begin 30 days after the FDA receives the IND unless the agency places it on clinical hold. Each site also needs IRB approval.

Clinical phases

PhaseMain questionTypical participants
0 (exploratory)Does the drug reach its target and how is it handled? Microdoses, no therapeutic intentA handful of people
ISafety, tolerability, dose range, pharmacokineticsTens of healthy volunteers; patients when the drug is too toxic for healthy people (for example, many cancer drugs)
IIDoes it work? Dose finding and short-term safetyUp to a few hundred patients with the condition
IIIConfirm efficacy against placebo or standard care, detect less common adverse effectsHundreds to thousands of patients, usually randomized and blinded
IV (post-marketing)Long-term and rare harms, use in broader populations, required confirmatory studiesPatients in routine practice

Approval

A sponsor seeks approval with a New Drug Application (NDA) for small-molecule drugs or a Biologics License Application (BLA) for biologics such as antibodies and vaccines. The FDA judges whether substantial evidence shows effectiveness and whether benefits outweigh risks for the labeled use, and it approves the label, including any boxed warning. Since 2015, drug labels describe risks in pregnancy and lactation in narrative sections rather than the old letter categories.

Faster routes for serious conditions

  • Fast track: more frequent meetings and rolling submission of the application.
  • Breakthrough therapy: preliminary evidence of substantial improvement over existing therapy; intensive FDA guidance.
  • Priority review: a shorter review goal.
  • Accelerated approval: approval based on a surrogate end point (a laboratory value, image or other marker) reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit, for a serious condition with unmet need. The sponsor must complete confirmatory trials of real clinical benefit; the FDA can require these to be under way at approval and can withdraw the approval through an expedited process if they fail or are not done.

A surrogate end point is not the outcome patients care about. A drug can improve a marker and still fail to improve survival or symptoms, which is why accelerated approval carries a confirmatory-trial obligation.

After approval

Premarketing trials are too small and too short to detect adverse effects that occur in, say, 1 in 10,000 users or after years of use. Post-marketing surveillance fills the gap. Clinicians and patients report suspected serious reactions voluntarily through MedWatch; manufacturers must report the adverse events they learn of. Reports go into the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), a passive system that detects signals but cannot measure incidence, because neither the number of exposed people nor the completeness of reporting is known. Vaccine events go to VAERS, run jointly by CDC and FDA. The FDA can require post-marketing studies, add warnings or withdraw approval.

For drugs with serious risks, the FDA can require a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS): a medication guide, a communication plan for clinicians and, for the highest risks, elements to assure safe use such as prescriber or pharmacy certification, patient enrolment in a registry or documented laboratory monitoring (for example, pregnancy tests before dispensing a teratogen).

Generics, biosimilars and orphan drugs

A generic drug is approved through an Abbreviated NDA without repeating efficacy trials. It must contain the same active ingredient, strength, dosage form and route as the reference drug and be bioequivalent: the rate and extent of absorption, measured by peak concentration and area under the curve, fall within narrow statistical limits of the reference product. Inactive ingredients and appearance may differ. Biologics have an analogous biosimilar pathway. Drugs for rare diseases (fewer than 200,000 people in the US) can receive orphan designation, which brings incentives including a period of market exclusivity.

Other rules you should know

  • Off-label use: physicians may legally prescribe an approved drug for an unapproved indication, dose or population when evidence and judgment support it. Manufacturers may not promote unapproved uses.
  • Trial registration: applicable clinical trials must be registered at ClinicalTrials.gov and their summary results posted; medical journals require registration before the first participant is enrolled as a condition of publication.
  • Dietary supplements do not need FDA approval for safety or efficacy before sale; the FDA acts mainly after problems arise.
  • Devices are classed by risk; higher-risk devices need premarket approval with clinical data, and significant-risk device studies need an investigational device exemption.

Match the phase to the question: I is "is it safe and what dose?", II is "does it work?", III is "does it work better than what we have, in many people?", IV is "what happens when everyone uses it?"

s23g-s0506.bodyHtml:
Research ethics rests on three principles set out in the Belmont Report after public scandals in which people were enrolled without consent or denied available treatment: respect for persons (informed consent, protection for people with diminished autonomy), beneficence (minimize risk, maximize benefit, justify what remains) and justice (fair distribution of the burdens and benefits of research). The Nuremberg Code before it put voluntary consent first, and the Declaration of Helsinki sets standards for physician-investigators worldwide. The lesson of these histories is simple: scientific value never justifies overriding a participant's rights.

Research misconduct

US federal policy defines research misconduct as fabrication, falsification or plagiarism in proposing, performing, reviewing or reporting research.

TypeDefinitionExample
FabricationMaking up data or results and recording or reporting themEntering follow-up blood pressures for visits that never happened
FalsificationManipulating materials, equipment or processes, or changing or omitting data, so the record misrepresents the researchDropping participants whose results "spoil" the effect; splicing gel images
PlagiarismTaking another person's ideas, processes, results or words without appropriate creditCopying paragraphs of a colleague's grant into one's own

Honest error and differences of scientific opinion are not misconduct. A finding requires a significant departure from accepted practice, committed intentionally, knowingly or recklessly. Concerns go to the institution's research integrity officer, who protects good-faith complainants from retaliation; for Public Health Service-funded research the Office of Research Integrity oversees the process. Other questionable practices (selective reporting of outcomes, undisclosed changes of the primary end point, salami publication) are not formal misconduct but still distort the literature, which is one reason trials are registered in advance.

Authorship

Under the widely used journal-editor criteria, each author must meet all four: a substantial contribution to the conception or design, or to acquisition, analysis or interpretation of data; drafting the work or revising it critically for important content; approval of the final version; and agreement to be accountable for the work. Getting funding, general supervision of a group or providing patients or space alone does not qualify; those people are acknowledged. Gift (honorary) authorship lists someone who did not meet the criteria; ghost authorship omits someone, often an industry writer, who did substantial work. Artificial intelligence tools cannot be authors; their use is disclosed.

Conflicts of interest

A conflict of interest exists when a secondary interest (money, career, relationships) could unduly influence judgment about a primary interest (participant welfare, the integrity of data). Investigators disclose significant financial interests to their institution, which manages them (disclosure to participants, independent monitoring, divestment or removal from the study). Journals require disclosure by authors. Industry payments to physicians are reported publicly through the federal Open Payments program. Disclosure is necessary but does not by itself remove bias.

Disclosing a conflict does not make it acceptable in every case. When the conflict is severe, for example an investigator holding equity in the company whose drug they are testing and also assessing outcomes, management may require that someone else conduct that part of the work.

Equipoise and placebo

Clinical equipoise is genuine uncertainty within the expert community about which of the compared treatments is better. It is what makes randomization ethical; if one arm is known to be better, assigning people to the other is not. A placebo control is ethical when there is no proven effective treatment, or when there are compelling methodological reasons and participants given placebo face no risk of serious or irreversible harm. When an effective treatment exists for a serious condition, the usual alternatives are an active-control trial or an add-on design in which everyone receives standard treatment plus the new drug or placebo.

The placebo question is about what participants lose: withholding a proven treatment for a few weeks of mild symptoms may be acceptable, but withholding it where the condition can kill or cause permanent damage is not.

Vulnerable participants and fair selection

Justice asks who carries research burdens and who gains. Recruiting mainly from groups that are easy to reach or easy to persuade (people in poverty, institutionalized people, a clinic's uninsured patients), while the benefits flow to others, is unfair selection. Excluding groups without scientific reason (older adults, women, children, people with limited English) is also unjust, because it leaves them without evidence for their own care. Protections for vulnerable groups include extra review, independent consent monitors and limits on payment.

Responsibilities to participants and to data

  • Confidentiality: for sensitive studies, a Certificate of Confidentiality protects identifiable research information from compelled disclosure, for example by subpoena; NIH-funded studies collecting identifiable sensitive information receive one automatically.
  • Incidental findings: protocols should say in advance which unexpected findings will be returned and how. A potentially serious finding is communicated to the participant with a route to clinical evaluation; results from a research laboratory are confirmed in a clinically certified laboratory before they guide treatment.
  • Data sharing and retention: funders such as NIH require a data management and sharing plan; records are kept for the periods required by the funder, the FDA and the institution, under the confidentiality protections promised in consent.
  • Dual roles: a physician who is also the investigator must keep the participant's clinical interests first and make sure care is not compromised by the protocol.

s23g-s0601.bodyHtml:
Patient-centred interviewing treats the patient as the expert on his or her own experience and the physician as the expert on disease. The goal is a shared understanding of the problem, the patient's ideas and fears about it, and a plan the patient can follow. On Step 1 these skills appear as questions that ask you to recognise a technique ("Which response is an example of…?") or to pick the best phrasing.

The building blocks

SkillWhat it doesExample wording
Open-ended questionLets the patient set the agenda and tell the story"What brings you in today?" "Tell me about the pain."
FacilitationKeeps the story going without steeringNodding, "Go on," "Mm-hm," a short pause
Closed questionFills specific gaps after the story"Does it wake you at night?"
ReflectionShows you heard content or feeling"It sounds as if the not knowing is the hardest part."
Empathic statementNames and validates emotion"Anyone would be shaken by news like this."
SummaryChecks accuracy and marks a transition"Let me make sure I have this right…"
Plain languageReplaces jargon"Your kidneys are not filtering well" instead of "reduced GFR"

The classic sequence is a funnel: open first, then facilitation, then focused closed questions. Leading questions ("You haven't been drinking, have you?"), "why" questions about failure, multiple questions at once and early interruption all reduce what the patient tells you.

Delivering bad news

A structured approach protects the patient and the physician. One way to remember it is the six R's:

  1. Room: private space, seated, no interruptions, the people the patient wants present.
  2. Read what the patient already knows or suspects: "What have you been told so far?"
  3. Request permission and preference: how much detail, and who else should hear it.
  4. Reveal the news after a brief warning ("I'm afraid the results are not what we hoped"), in plain words and small pieces, pausing often.
  5. React to emotion: silence, a tissue, an empathic statement. Do not rush to facts or reassurance.
  6. Roadmap: summarise, agree on next steps and when you will meet again.

Exam trap: the option that reassures ("Don't worry, treatments are excellent now") or that launches into treatment details while the patient is crying is almost always wrong. Emotion comes before information.

Difficult encounters

With an angry patient, acknowledge the emotion and apologise for what went wrong (a long wait, a lost result) before explaining; do not argue, blame colleagues or threaten. Limits are set only for threats or abuse. A patient who requests an unnecessary test, antibiotic or scan is usually voicing a worry: explore it ("What concerns you most?"), then explain, rather than ordering the test or refusing flatly. A patient who offers a small token of thanks can be thanked graciously; valuable gifts are declined kindly, and gifts never buy better care.

Health literacy and numeracy

Many adults have limited health literacy, and you cannot tell by looking. Use universal precautions: plain language, two or three key messages, pictures and teach-back, in which the patient explains in his or her own words what to do ("I want to be sure I explained this well; how will you take this at home?"). "Do you understand?" is not a check.

For numbers, give absolute risks as natural frequencies with the same denominator and time frame. Worked example: a treatment lowers 5-year risk from 20% to 15%. Say "Of 100 people like you, 20 would have the event without treatment and 15 with it." The absolute risk reduction is 5 per 100 (NNT 1/0.05 = 20); the relative risk reduction is 5/20 = 25%. Quoting only "25% lower" makes the benefit sound larger than it is.

Motivational interviewing

Motivational interviewing is a collaborative style for resolving ambivalence about change. The physician asks open questions, affirms effort and strengths, reflects (especially both sides of ambivalence: "Part of you enjoys it, and part of you worries"), and summarises the patient's own reasons for change. The physician avoids the urge to fix, argue or lecture, because pushing produces push-back. Resistance is a signal to change tack, not to argue harder. Readiness can be gauged by asking where the patient is: not considering change, weighing it, preparing, acting or maintaining.

Pearl: in motivational interviewing the patient, not the physician, should be the one voicing the reasons for change. The best answer is often a reflection.

Adolescents and families

From early adolescence, part of every visit is spent with the teen alone. Explain this to parent and teen together as routine, and explain confidentiality honestly with its limits (serious risk to self or others, suspected abuse). Move up a ladder from safe to sensitive topics: home and family, school or work, friends and activities, mood and sleep, substances, sexual health, and safety. In family meetings, start by asking what the family understands, keep the patient's values at the centre, and let a capacitated patient decide how much family is involved.

Bridge: the same communication skills carry the informed-consent conversation, the capacity assessment and the surrogate discussion in later sections.

s23g-s0602.bodyHtml:
Patients with limited English proficiency and Deaf patients have worse outcomes when communication fails: more adverse events, longer stays, poorer understanding of diagnoses and medicines, and consent that is not truly informed. The fix is well established: a qualified medical interpreter for any substantive clinical conversation.

Who should interpret

OptionUse?Why
Qualified medical interpreter (in person, telephone or video)Yes: first choiceTrained in terminology, accuracy, completeness, confidentiality and role
Clinician with assessed proficiency in the patient's languageYesLanguage-concordant care; partial "college" fluency does not count
Adult family member or friendOnly if the informed patient asks, or in an emergency until a qualified interpreter is availableOmits, softens and adds; may have conflicts; privacy concerns
Untrained bilingual staffAvoid for clinical contentErrors with medical terms; not bound by interpreter standards
A childNo (rare true emergency only)Unreliable for medical content; inappropriate burden and role reversal
Machine translation appNo for clinical conversationUnverified accuracy for medical content

Ad hoc interpreters make more errors that could have clinical consequences than professional interpreters, and omission is a frequent type of error. Remote interpretation by telephone or video is acceptable and often faster than waiting for someone in person.

The law in outline

  • Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964: programs receiving federal funds (including Medicare and Medicaid) may not discriminate by national origin, which includes failing to give people with limited English proficiency meaningful access. Language assistance must be free to the patient.
  • Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act applies these protections to health programs and restricts relying on minors or accompanying adults to interpret, except in emergencies or when the patient specifically requests an adult companion and that is appropriate.
  • Americans with Disabilities Act: providers must ensure effective communication with people who are Deaf or hard of hearing, at no cost to them. For complex discussions such as consent, that usually means a qualified sign-language interpreter, in person or by video remote interpreting that actually works (a clear, real-time, smooth picture). Lip-reading and written notes are not equivalent access for complex information, and English may be a second language for someone whose first language is American Sign Language.

Exam trap: the bilingual teenager in the room is never the right interpreter, even when the option says "fluent." Pick the professional telephone or video interpreter, which is usually available within minutes.

Technique

  • Brief the interpreter beforehand when the topic is difficult.
  • Face the patient and speak to the patient in the first person ("How is your breathing?"), not to the interpreter ("Ask him…").
  • Use plain language in short segments and pause.
  • Expect everything to be interpreted, including side comments; if the interpreter summarises a long exchange, ask for the full content.
  • Check understanding with teach-back through the interpreter.
  • The physician, not the interpreter, remains responsible for informed consent and for checking understanding.

The surrogate as the patient's voice

A surrogate (health-care agent, guardian or default family decision-maker) is, in a sense, an interpreter of the patient's values when the patient cannot speak for himself. Two standards guide the surrogate:

StandardQuestion askedWhen used
Substituted judgment"What would the patient choose if able to tell us?"First choice whenever the patient's wishes or values are known (prior statements, a living will, how the patient lived)
Best interests"Which option gives this patient the most benefit for the least burden?"When wishes are unknown, or the patient never had capacity (for example, profound lifelong intellectual disability, young children)

The surrogate's own preferences ("I'm not ready to lose her") are not the standard. Physicians help surrogates by asking about the patient ("What would he say if he could join us?") and by offering a recommendation that fits those values.

Pearl: if a surrogate quotes the patient, that is substituted judgment; if the surrogate weighs benefit and burden without knowing the patient's view, that is best interests.

s23g-s0603.bodyHtml:
Informed consent is a process in which a patient with decision-making capacity, free of coercion, authorises a treatment after receiving the information a reasonable patient would need. The signed form only documents that the conversation happened; it is not the consent itself. Treating a capacitated patient without consent can be battery, and treating with inadequate disclosure can be negligence.

What must be disclosed

  • The diagnosis or the problem being treated.
  • The nature and purpose of the proposed intervention.
  • Its material risks (common risks and serious ones, even if rare) and its expected benefits.
  • Reasonable alternatives, including no treatment, with their own risks and benefits.
  • Material conflicts of interest, such as a financial stake in a recommended product.

Most US jurisdictions judge disclosure by what a reasonable patient would want to know (the patient-centred standard); some still use what a reasonable physician would disclose. Either way, the elements above are expected. The physician who performs the procedure is responsible for the discussion (a qualified team member may assist); a nurse may witness a signature but does not replace the discussion.

Exceptions

ExceptionWho initiatesKey condition
Emergency (implied consent)PhysicianDelay threatens life or serious harm, the patient cannot consent, no surrogate or known refusal is available
WaiverPatientA capacitated patient knowingly declines detailed information; document it and offer the information again later
Therapeutic privilegePhysicianRare: disclosure itself would cause serious, immediate harm. Not for ordinary anxiety, and never to prevent a refusal
Lack of capacityAssessmentConsent comes from the surrogate or an advance directive, not from no one

Exam trap: "The patient might refuse if I tell her" is never a reason to withhold a risk. Waiver comes from the patient; privilege comes from the physician and is almost never the answer.

Honesty: placebos and alternative therapies

Deceptive placebo use (presenting an inert pill as an active drug) violates informed consent and trust. A placebo may be used only with the patient's knowledge and agreement, for example open-label. A response to placebo does not show that symptoms are "not real." When patients use or ask about complementary or alternative therapies, the physician asks nonjudgmentally, discusses the evidence and interactions, and supports safe combinations with standard care.

Minors

Parents or legal guardians generally consent for patients under 18, and the child's assent should be sought as development allows. Important exceptions:

SituationWho consents
Emergency with no parent availableTreat under implied consent
Diagnosis and treatment of sexually transmitted infectionsThe minor, in every state
Contraception, prenatal care, substance-use and outpatient mental health careThe minor in many states; details vary by state
Emancipated minor (for example, married or on active military duty; in many states living independently and self-supporting)The minor, for all care
Mature minor (some states, case by case)The adolescent, for a specific decision

Parents may make many choices for their children, but not refuse life-saving or clearly beneficial treatment where refusal exposes the child to serious harm. Decisions for young children are judged by the child's best interests. In an emergency (for example, a child in hemorrhagic shock or diabetic ketoacidosis), physicians treat immediately. When time allows (a planned operation, a chronic illness), they seek a court order, and planned withholding of essential treatment is reported to child protective services as medical neglect. By contrast, a capacitated adult, including a Jehovah's Witness refusing blood, may refuse even life-saving treatment.

Vulnerable patients

People who are incarcerated keep the right to consent and to refuse; corrections officers cannot consent for them, and extra care is needed to make sure choices are voluntary. Adults with intellectual or physical disability are presumed to have capacity for many decisions; speak to them directly, use plain language and visual aids, and support (rather than replace) their decision-making.

Pearl: alternatives, including doing nothing, are the most often forgotten element of consent, and the most often tested.

s23g-s0604.bodyHtml:
Every adult is presumed to have decision-making capacity. Capacity is a clinical judgement, made by any treating physician, about whether this patient can make this decision now. Competence is a legal status decided by a judge, for example in a guardianship hearing. A physician's assessment can be evidence for the court, but the physician does not declare anyone incompetent.

The four abilities

A practical memory aid is four C's:

AbilityThe patient can…How it fails
Choose (communicate a choice)State a clear, reasonably stable preferenceCannot decide, or flips repeatedly; coma, severe aphasia without alternative communication
Comprehend (understand)Explain the condition, options, risks and benefits in own wordsCannot retain or paraphrase the information
Connect (appreciate)Accept that the facts apply to his or her own situation"That's true for others, not me"; delusional denial
Compare (reason)Weigh options against own values and reach a choice that follows from themConclusions that do not follow from stated values or facts

Capacity is decision-specific (a person with dementia may not manage investments but may decline a vaccine), time-specific (delirium fluctuates), and judged on a sliding scale: the riskier the decision, especially refusing a high-benefit, low-risk treatment, the more rigorous and well documented the assessment should be. The content of a choice does not decide capacity: an unusual or unwise choice is a reason to assess carefully, not proof of incapacity. A psychiatric diagnosis does not remove capacity on its own.

Before you decide

  • Look for reversible causes: hypoglycemia, hypoxia, infection and delirium, intoxication or withdrawal, pain, sedating drugs, sleep deprivation, hearing loss or a missing interpreter.
  • If the decision can wait, treat the cause and reassess when the patient is at his or her best.
  • If it cannot wait and capacity is absent, turn to the advance directive and surrogate; in a true emergency with no one available, treat.
  • Psychiatry or geriatrics can help when the assessment is difficult, but the treating physician does not need a consultation for a straightforward assessment.

Exam trap: "Ask a court to determine competence" or "Obtain a psychiatry consult" before a bedside assessment is rarely the best first step. The treating physician assesses capacity.

Informed refusal

A capacitated adult may refuse any treatment, including life-sustaining treatment, for any reason. The physician should explore the reasons, correct misunderstandings, make a clear recommendation, offer acceptable alternatives (harm reduction), document the discussion (risks explained, patient's understanding, decision) and invite the patient to reconsider at any time. A patient leaving against medical advice still receives prescriptions, follow-up and return instructions; signing an AMA form is optional, and insurers generally do not refuse payment simply because a patient left against advice. A refusal is also decision-specific: declining one treatment on one day is not a refusal of all future care.

When the patient cannot decide

  • Advance directives: a living will gives instructions for specified circumstances (check its trigger conditions, such as terminal illness or permanent unconsciousness); a durable power of attorney for health care names an agent. The Patient Self-Determination Act requires hospitals to tell patients about their right to make advance directives.
  • Agent: the person the patient named outranks relatives who were not named.
  • Default surrogate order (state law; typical): spouse, adult children, parents, adult siblings, then others; some states include domestic partners or close friends.
  • Standards: substituted judgment first; best interests if wishes are unknown.
  • Conflict: family meetings, then an ethics consultation; court only when still unresolved.

How it appears on Step 1

Step 1 items usually describe a patient's words and ask which ability is impaired, which standard a surrogate is using, or who makes a legal determination. Read the quoted words closely: inability to paraphrase points to understanding; "it doesn't apply to me" points to appreciation; conclusions that contradict the patient's own stated values point to reasoning; and an inability to settle on any choice points to communicating a choice. Remember that the four abilities are judged against the patient's own values, not the physician's, and that a choice most people would not make can still be a capacitated one.

Pearl: capacity belongs to a decision, not to a person. Ask "capacity for what, and when?" before choosing an answer.

s23g-s0605.bodyHtml:
Civil commitment allows the state to hospitalise a person with mental illness against his or her will. Because it removes liberty, it is tightly limited by law, and the details (who may start a hold, how long it lasts, hearing timelines) vary by state. The principles below hold across states and are what the exam tests.

Criteria

Involuntary admission requires a mental illness that causes at least one of:

  • Danger to self: suicidal intent or plan, or a recent serious attempt with continuing risk.
  • Danger to others: threats or violence driven by the illness, often with a target and means.
  • Grave disability (most states): inability, because of the illness, to provide for basic needs such as food, clothing, shelter or essential medical care, so that serious harm is likely.
Grounds for commitmentNot grounds on their own
Psychosis with a plan to harm a named personA psychiatric diagnosis
Severe depression with intent to dieRefusing psychiatric medication
Psychotic refusal of food and shelter in freezing weatherHomelessness or an eccentric lifestyle when basic needs are met
Mania with reckless danger to lifeFamily or neighbours requesting it
Intoxication alone (keep safe until sober, then reassess)

Two state powers are invoked: police power (protecting others) and parens patriae (protecting people who cannot protect themselves).

Process and due process

  1. Emergency hold: started by a physician, police officer or other authorised person (depending on the state) for a short, time-limited evaluation, commonly a few days.
  2. Continued commitment: needs a court hearing with notice, the right to counsel and the right to present evidence. The US Supreme Court requires at least clear and convincing evidence, more than the ordinary civil standard but less than the criminal one, and has held that a state cannot confine a nondangerous person who can live safely in freedom.
  3. Periodic review and release when criteria are no longer met.

A voluntary patient who asks to leave and is imminently dangerous can be converted to involuntary status through the state's process. For minors, parents may admit a child over the child's objection, but due process requires review by a neutral fact-finder, such as an independent physician; some states add more protection.

Exam trap: commitment is not consent to treatment. A committed patient generally keeps the right to refuse medication; nonemergency treatment over objection needs a separate legal process (court or formal review). Emergency medication is allowed only for imminent danger.

Least restrictive alternative

Care should take place in the least restrictive setting that is safe: outpatient treatment with a safety plan before voluntary admission, voluntary before involuntary, de-escalation before medication, oral before intramuscular, and medication before physical restraint.

Restraint and seclusion

Federal Medicare hospital rules allow restraint or seclusion only to ensure immediate physical safety after less restrictive measures fail, never for punishment, convenience or staffing. Key safeguards:

  • An order from a physician or other authorised practitioner; no as-needed (PRN) or standing orders.
  • For violent or self-destructive behaviour, a face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour.
  • Time-limited orders (for adults, up to 4 hours at a time; shorter for children and adolescents), renewed only if still needed.
  • Continuous monitoring, and release at the earliest possible time, even before the order expires.

Public-health detention

A different legal power applies to communicable disease. A person with infectious tuberculosis who will not adhere to treatment or isolation can, after less restrictive measures (education, incentives, directly observed therapy) fail, be subject to health-department orders for isolation, treatment or detention, with due process. The ground is risk to others from infection, not mental illness, so psychiatric holds are the wrong tool.

Pearl: for every "hold" question ask three things: Is there a mental illness? Is there a current danger (or grave disability) caused by it? Is there a less restrictive option that is safe?

s23g-s0701.bodyHtml:
Physicians meet abuse in every setting: the infant with an unexplained fracture, the older adult with pressure injuries, the woman whose partner answers for her. This section covers the legal framework (who must report, to whom and on what evidence) and the clinical patterns that should raise suspicion. The law differs from state to state in detail, but the principles below hold across the United States.

Child maltreatment: the reporting duty

Every state names physicians as mandated reporters of suspected child abuse and neglect. Three features recur in every statute:

  • Threshold: reasonable suspicion ("reasonable cause to believe"), not proof. The reporter does not investigate or decide whether abuse happened; child protective services (CPS) does.
  • Immunity: a report made in good faith is protected from civil and criminal liability even if no abuse is found. Failure to report can be a criminal offence and a licensing matter.
  • No consent needed: parents are not asked for permission, and confidentiality rules (including HIPAA) explicitly yield to the reporting law.

Neglect (failure to provide food, shelter, supervision, medical care or education) is by far the most common form of maltreatment in national data; physical abuse, sexual abuse and psychological maltreatment follow. Parents are the perpetrators in most cases, and infants under 1 year have the highest victimisation rate.

Recognising physical abuse

The single most useful question is whether the injury fits the child's developmental stage and the history. Red flags: no history or a changing history, delay in seeking care, injuries of different ages, and an injury in a child who cannot yet move independently.

FindingUsually accidentalRaises concern for abuse
BruisesShins, knees, forehead, elbows in a walking childAny bruise in a non-mobile infant; ears, neck, torso, buttocks, genitals; patterned marks (loops, hand, belt)
BurnsSplash pattern with irregular edges, drip marksImmersion (stocking or glove) pattern with sharp, symmetrical edges; cigarette-sized round burns
FracturesToddler's spiral tibial fracture, buckle fracture of the radius, supracondylar fracture after a fallPosterior rib fractures, classic metaphyseal lesions, multiple fractures of different ages, long-bone fractures in non-walking infants
HeadSimple linear skull fracture after a significant fallSubdural hemorrhage with extensive retinal hemorrhages; injury with no history

In abusive head trauma, rotational acceleration and deceleration tear the bridging veins that cross the subdural space, producing subdural hemorrhage, often without any external bruise. Rib fractures arise from squeezing of the chest. Classic metaphyseal lesions (corner or bucket-handle fractures) come from shearing forces as a limb is pulled or the infant is shaken.

A minor injury in a baby who cannot yet roll or crawl, such as a small facial bruise or a torn frenulum, is a sentinel injury. It is often the first visible sign of abuse and precedes severe injury in a large share of cases.

Sexual abuse and medical child abuse

Outside the newborn period, gonorrhea, syphilis or HIV (once perinatal or transfusion transmission is excluded) in a prepubertal child indicates sexual contact and therefore abuse. Chlamydia and trichomonas are also strongly suggestive. Factitious disorder imposed on another (illness fabricated or induced by a caregiver) is reportable child abuse; clues are symptoms seen only by one caregiver, normal extensive workups and resolution when the child is separated from that caregiver.

Mimics

Congenital dermal melanocytosis, bleeding disorders, osteogenesis imperfecta, phytophotodermatitis and some traditional remedies such as coining or cupping can look like abuse. A careful history, examination and selected tests separate them; documenting a birthmark at the newborn examination prevents later confusion.

Elder mistreatment

Elder mistreatment includes physical, sexual and psychological abuse, neglect by a caregiver, financial exploitation and abandonment. Most perpetrators are family members, often adult children or spouses. Risk rises with dementia, functional dependence and social isolation, and with a caregiver who is stressed, financially dependent or misusing substances. Signs include unexplained bruises (especially grip marks on the inner arms), pressure injuries, dehydration, poor hygiene, missed appointments, unpaid bills and a caregiver who refuses to leave the room. Reports go to adult protective services (APS); physicians are mandated reporters in most states. Self-neglect, in which an older adult without a responsible caregiver fails to meet her own needs, is also handled by APS.

Intimate partner violence

Intimate partner violence (IPV) is physical, sexual or psychological harm or stalking by a current or former partner. Pregnancy is a time of increased risk. For a competent adult the guiding principle is autonomy: in most states there is no general duty to report IPV, although many states require reporting of injuries caused by firearms or other weapons and a few require reporting of other assault injuries. Reporting against the patient's wishes can increase danger, so the physician screens privately, validates, assesses lethality (escalation, weapons, strangulation, threats to kill), makes a safety plan and documents.

Human trafficking

Trafficking is the use of force, fraud or coercion to obtain labour or commercial sex; for minors, any commercial sex act is trafficking regardless of force. Indicators include a companion who speaks for the patient or holds her documents, scripted answers, living at the workplace and signs of untreated injury. The patient is interviewed alone with a professional interpreter. Minors are reported as victims of child abuse; adults are offered resources and choose what to do.

Do not wait for certainty, a disclosure or an imaging result before reporting suspected child abuse, and do not ask the parents for permission. Conversely, do not call the police about a competent adult's IPV disclosure against her wishes unless a specific legal duty applies.

content.text: Physicians meet abuse in every setting: the infant with an unexplained fracture, the older adult with pressure injuries, the woman whose partner answers for her. This section covers the legal framework (who must report, to whom and on what evidence) and the clinical patterns that should raise suspicion. The law differs from state to state in detail, but the principles below hold across the United States.
of suspected child abuse and neglect. Three features recur in every statute:
reasonable suspicion ("reasonable cause to believe"), not proof. The reporter does not investigate or decide whether abuse happened; child protective services (CPS) does.
a report made in good faith is protected from civil and criminal liability even if no abuse is found. Failure to report can be a criminal offence and a licensing matter.
parents are not asked for permission, and confidentiality rules (including HIPAA) explicitly yield to the reporting law.

Neglect (failure to provide food, shelter, supervision, medical care or education) is by far the most common form of maltreatment in national data; physical abuse, sexual abuse and psychological maltreatment follow. Parents are the perpetrators in most cases, and infants under 1 year have the highest victimisation rate.

The single most useful question is whether the injury fits the child's developmental stage and the history. Red flags: no history or a changing history, delay in seeking care, injuries of different ages, and an injury in a child who cannot yet move independently.
Shins, knees, forehead, elbows in a walking child
Any bruise in a non-mobile infant; ears, neck, torso, buttocks, genitals; patterned marks (loops, hand, belt)
Splash pattern with irregular edges, drip marks
Immersion (stocking or glove) pattern with sharp, symmetrical edges; cigarette-sized round burns
Toddler's spiral tibial fracture, buckle fracture of the radius, supracondylar fracture after a fall
Posterior rib fractures, classic metaphyseal lesions, multiple fractures of different ages, long-bone fractures in non-walking infants
Simple linear skull fracture after a significant fall
Subdural hemorrhage with extensive retinal hemorrhages; injury with no history
In abusive head trauma, rotational acceleration and deceleration tear the

that cross the subdural space, producing subdural hemorrhage, often without any external bruise. Rib fractures arise from squeezing of the chest. Classic metaphyseal lesions (corner or bucket-handle fractures) come from shearing forces as a limb is pulled or the infant is shaken.
A minor injury in a baby who cannot yet roll or crawl, such as a small facial bruise or a torn frenulum, is a
. It is often the first visible sign of abuse and precedes severe injury in a large share of cases.
Sexual abuse and medical child abuse

Outside the newborn period, gonorrhea, syphilis or HIV (once perinatal or transfusion transmission is excluded) in a prepubertal child indicates sexual contact and therefore abuse. Chlamydia and trichomonas are also strongly suggestive. Factitious disorder imposed on another (illness fabricated or induced by a caregiver) is reportable child abuse; clues are symptoms seen only by one caregiver, normal extensive workups and resolution when the child is separated from that caregiver.

Congenital dermal melanocytosis, bleeding disorders, osteogenesis imperfecta, phytophotodermatitis and some traditional remedies such as coining or cupping can look like abuse. A careful history, examination and selected tests separate them; documenting a birthmark at the newborn examination prevents later confusion.
Elder mistreatment includes physical, sexual and psychological abuse,

by a caregiver, financial exploitation and abandonment. Most perpetrators are family members, often adult children or spouses. Risk rises with dementia, functional dependence and social isolation, and with a caregiver who is stressed, financially dependent or misusing substances. Signs include unexplained bruises (especially grip marks on the inner arms), pressure injuries, dehydration, poor hygiene, missed appointments, unpaid bills and a caregiver who refuses to leave the room. Reports go to
(APS); physicians are mandated reporters in most states. Self-neglect, in which an older adult without a responsible caregiver fails to meet her own needs, is also handled by APS.

Intimate partner violence (IPV) is physical, sexual or psychological harm or stalking by a current or former partner. Pregnancy is a time of increased risk. For a competent adult the guiding principle is

: in most states there is no general duty to report IPV, although many states require reporting of injuries caused by firearms or other weapons and a few require reporting of other assault injuries. s23g-s0702.bodyHtml:
Pregnancy and birth raise questions about whose decisions count, what the state may require and how professional conscience fits with patients' rights. On the exam the answer almost always rests on a few stable principles: the capacitated pregnant woman decides about her own body, counselling is non-directive, public health programmes have specific rules, and the physician never abandons a patient.

Autonomy in pregnancy and maternal-fetal conflict

A pregnant woman with decision-making capacity has the same right as any adult to accept or refuse treatment, including a cesarean delivery, fetal monitoring, transfusion or hospital admission recommended for the fetus. Obstetric professional bodies and the leading appellate decisions reject court-ordered obstetric interventions. When a recommendation is refused, the physician explores the reasons (fear, past trauma, misinformation, cost, childcare), corrects misunderstandings, offers alternatives, documents the informed refusal and continues the best care the patient accepts. A husband or other relative cannot consent on her behalf.

The fetus is a focus of beneficence, but it does not have a separate surrogate who can override the woman. Once born, the newborn is a separate patient: parents decide in the child's best interest, and they cannot refuse emergency, life-saving treatment for the child.

Substance use in pregnancy

Substance use disorders in pregnancy are treated as health conditions. All pregnant patients are screened with validated questions; urine drug testing, when used, requires informed consent. A hospital policy of testing pregnant women without consent and giving results to police was found unconstitutional by the US Supreme Court, and punitive approaches drive women away from prenatal care. Opioid use disorder is treated with agonist therapy (buprenorphine or methadone), which improves maternal and neonatal outcomes. Federal child-welfare law requires states to have procedures for notifying child protective services when an infant is affected by prenatal substance exposure and for a plan of safe care; such notification is not, by itself, an allegation of abuse, and the details vary by state.

Newborn screening and safe-haven laws

Newborn blood-spot screening is mandated by each state for a panel of conditions (for example phenylketonuria, congenital hypothyroidism, sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis) in which early treatment prevents death or disability. Because it is a mandated public health programme, it is the default and written consent is usually not sought; most states allow parents to decline, commonly for religious reasons, after counselling, and the refusal is documented.

Every state has a safe-haven law allowing a parent to leave an unharmed newborn at a designated site (always hospitals; often fire, police or EMS stations) anonymously and without prosecution for abandonment. Age limits range from a few days to about a month or more. Staff accept the infant, provide care and notify child welfare; they may offer, but not require, a medical-history form.

Periviable birth

Periviable birth is delivery between 20 0/7 and 25 6/7 weeks. Survival and the risk of severe impairment change week by week and with individual factors (antenatal corticosteroids, estimated weight, sex, singleton or multiple). Decisions between resuscitation and comfort care are shared: obstetric and neonatal teams give consistent information, explore the parents' values and document a plan that can be revisited.

Sterilization

Requirement for federally funded sterilizationRule
AgeAt least 21 years at the time of consent
CapacityMentally competent; not institutionalised
Waiting periodConsent signed at least 30 days and no more than 180 days before the procedure
ExceptionsPremature delivery or emergency abdominal surgery: at least 72 hours after consent, and for premature delivery the consent must have been signed at least 30 days before the expected delivery date
Invalid settingsConsent not obtained during labor, while seeking an abortion or under the influence of alcohol or drugs
SpouseNo spousal consent is required

These rules apply to procedures paid for with federal funds such as Medicaid; they grew out of a history of coerced sterilization. For any competent adult, spousal consent is not required, and parity or age above the legal minimum is not a reason to refuse; counselling covers permanence, regret and reversible alternatives.

Assisted reproduction

Fertility programmes obtain written decisions before embryos are frozen about their disposition after divorce, death, incapacity or disagreement. Courts generally enforce such agreements. Gamete donors and recipients receive counselling about genetic testing, anonymity and future contact.

Counselling, conscience and abortion

Counselling after prenatal screening is non-directive: accurate information, all options, and support for the patient's own choice. Abortion law has varied widely between states since 2022, so exam keys rest on duties that apply everywhere: honest options counselling, confidentiality, emergency care and no abandonment. A physician with a conscientious objection may decline to provide a service personally but must tell the patient, give accurate information and refer in a timely way, and must provide care in an emergency.

"Obtain a court order" or "ask the husband to consent" is almost never the right answer when a capacitated pregnant woman refuses an intervention. The right answer explores her reasons, then respects and documents an informed refusal.

Count the days on sterilization items: from the date the consent form was signed to the date of surgery must be at least 30. A scheduled term cesarean is not one of the exceptions.

s23g-s0703.bodyHtml:
Care at the end of life asks physicians to combine clear medical judgement with honest communication and respect for the patient's values. The exam tests the distinctions between palliative care and hospice, the ethics of withholding and withdrawing treatment and of symptom control, the determination of death, organ donation and the legal status of aid in dying.

Palliative care and hospice

Palliative care is interdisciplinary care that relieves symptoms and stress and supports quality of life for patients with serious illness at any stage, alongside disease-directed treatment. Hospice is palliative care for patients near the end of life who choose comfort as the primary goal.

FeaturePalliative careHospice (Medicare benefit)
WhenFrom diagnosis of serious illness onwardPrognosis of 6 months or less if the illness runs its usual course, certified by two physicians
Curative or life-prolonging treatmentContinuesForgone for the terminal illness (adults); children on Medicaid or CHIP may receive both
SettingHospital, clinic, homeMostly home; also nursing homes and inpatient hospice units
LeavingNot applicableThe patient may revoke at any time and re-elect later

Ethics of limiting treatment

A capacitated patient may refuse any treatment, including artificial nutrition and ventilation. Withholding and withdrawing are ethically and legally equivalent; if the reverse were true, clinicians would hesitate to start time-limited trials. When a patient lacks capacity, a surrogate (a named health care agent, or the default relative under state law) decides by substituted judgment, what the patient would choose, and uses the best-interest standard only when the patient's wishes are unknown.

A do-not-resuscitate order means no cardiopulmonary resuscitation in arrest; it does not mean "do not treat." Before surgery, DNR orders are reconsidered with the patient rather than automatically suspended. A POLST form converts a seriously ill person's goals into portable medical orders (resuscitation, scope of treatment, artificial nutrition) that EMS and hospitals follow.

Symptom control and double effect

Opioids relieve both pain and dyspnea at the end of life. The principle of double effect permits an action with a good intended effect and a foreseen but unintended bad effect if the act is not wrong in itself, the bad effect is not the means to the good, and the good is proportionate. Symptom-titrated opioids rarely shorten life. Palliative sedation, proportionate sedation for refractory symptoms in the last days of life, is likewise accepted. Neuromuscular blockers are never used to make a dying patient look comfortable.

Aid in dying and euthanasia

PracticeWho actsUS legal status
Withdrawing or withholding treatmentTeam, at the patient's or surrogate's requestLegal everywhere
Medical aid in dyingPhysician prescribes; patient takes the drug himselfLegal only in some states, for capacitated adults with a terminal illness and a prognosis of 6 months or less, with waiting periods and repeated requests
EuthanasiaPhysician administers a lethal drugIllegal in every state

Any request to hasten death should prompt exploration: uncontrolled symptoms, depression, fear of being a burden or losing control, and existential suffering are often treatable.

Death by neurologic criteria and organ donation

Death by neurologic criteria is the irreversible loss of all functions of the entire brain, including the brainstem, and it is legal death in every state. Before the examination, confounders are excluded: hypothermia (current guidance asks for a core temperature of at least 36 °C), sedative or paralytic drugs, severe metabolic or endocrine disturbance and hypotension. The examination shows coma, absent brainstem reflexes and apnea despite a sufficient rise in carbon dioxide; an ancillary test is used when the examination or apnea test cannot be completed. Spinal reflexes may persist.

Hospitals must refer every death and imminent death to the organ procurement organization (OPO). The OPO checks suitability and the donor registry and makes the request to the family; first-person authorization registered by the patient is legally valid. The treating team declares death independently of the transplant team (the dead donor rule).

Grief

Normal grief comes in waves triggered by reminders, allows functioning to return and may include brief experiences of seeing or hearing the deceased. Prolonged grief disorder is diagnosed when intense yearning or preoccupation persists at least 12 months after the death in adults (6 months in children), with impairment. Major depression may coexist and is suggested by pervasive worthlessness, loss of pleasure in everything and suicidal thinking unrelated to reunion with the deceased.

Hospice is not the answer for a patient who is starting treatment expected to control the disease; palliative care is. And a patient in hospice is never "locked in": the election can be revoked.

After death by neurologic criteria, say "died." Avoid "life support" and avoid asking the family for consent to stop the ventilator, which implies the patient is still alive.

s23g-s0704.bodyHtml:
Trust depends on confidentiality, honesty and clear boundaries. This section covers the four principles of medical ethics, the duty of confidentiality and its exceptions, HIPAA rules used in daily practice, truth-telling and professional boundaries.

The four principles

PrincipleMeaningTypical exam trigger
Respect for autonomyCapacitated patients make their own informed decisionsInformed consent or refusal, truth-telling
BeneficenceAct in the patient's best interestRecommending effective treatment, emergency care
NonmaleficenceAvoid causing harmDeclining a harmful or futile intervention
JusticeFair distribution and equal treatmentAllocating scarce resources, avoiding discrimination

Confidentiality and its exceptions

The default is to keep information confidential. Disclosure without consent is justified only when a recognised exception applies, and then only the information needed is shared with the person who needs it.

  • Serious risk to an identifiable person: a credible threat of violence against an identifiable victim creates a duty to protect (warn the person, notify police or hospitalise), following the line of cases that began with Tarasoff. Whether the duty is mandatory or permissive varies by state.
  • Risk to the patient: imminent suicide risk permits disclosure needed to keep the patient safe.
  • Reportable conditions: specified infectious diseases are reported to the health department in every state; health departments carry out partner notification.
  • Abuse: suspected child abuse, and elder abuse in most states, must be reported.
  • Other legal duties: for example gunshot wounds in most states, and in some states medical conditions that impair driving.
  • Consent and incapacity: the patient may authorise disclosure; if the patient is incapacitated, clinicians may share relevant information with family involved in care when that is in the patient's interest.

HIPAA in practice

HIPAA applies to health plans, clearinghouses and providers who bill electronically. Protected health information may be used and disclosed without authorization for treatment, payment and health care operations, when required by law, for public health activities, to report abuse, for certain judicial and law-enforcement processes and to avert a serious threat. The minimum necessary standard applies to most disclosures but not to those for treatment, to the patient or under an authorization. Psychotherapy notes, kept separately from the record, need a specific authorization for almost any disclosure. Patients have a right to see and obtain copies of their records. Protection continues for 50 years after death.

Family and friends: if the patient is present and capacitated, ask (or give the chance to object) before discussing information in front of them. Employers and life insurers need written authorization.

Minors

Parents usually consent for minors, but every state lets minors consent to care for sexually transmitted infections, and most allow consent for contraception, prenatal care and some substance use and mental health services; that care is confidential. Encouraging the adolescent to involve a trusted adult is good practice. Confidentiality is limited when the minor is at serious risk (abuse, suicidality).

Truth-telling

Capacitated patients have a right to know their diagnosis. When family members ask the physician to withhold bad news, the physician asks the patient how much she wants to know and who should be involved; a patient may waive information or delegate decisions. Therapeutic privilege, withholding information because disclosure itself would cause serious, immediate harm, is narrowly defined and rarely justified.

Boundaries

Romantic or sexual relationships with current patients are never acceptable. For physicians generally, a relationship with a former patient is unethical if it exploits trust or knowledge gained in care; for psychiatrists it is unethical with any former patient. Small gifts may be accepted; large gifts and bequests are declined. Physicians should not treat themselves or immediate family except in emergencies or for minor short-term problems, and should not prescribe controlled substances to them. On social media, physicians keep personal and professional accounts separate and never post identifiable patient information.

Paying for a family's insurance does not entitle a parent to an adolescent's confidential results, and a spouse is not entitled to a capacitated patient's information without permission.

When a disclosure without consent is justified, share the minimum needed with the person or agency that needs it, and tell the patient what you are doing and why.

s23g-s0705.bodyHtml:
Physicians are vulnerable to the same illnesses as their patients, and their work adds fatigue, access to drugs and a culture that discourages admitting difficulty. The profession's duties are to protect patients, to help impaired colleagues reach treatment and to seek help oneself.

What impairment means

Impairment is the inability to practise with reasonable skill and safety because of a condition such as a substance use disorder, mental illness, physical illness, cognitive decline or fatigue. A diagnosis is not impairment: a physician with well-treated depression, bipolar disorder or diabetes who practises safely is not impaired. Equating the two increases stigma and discourages treatment.

Substance use and drug diversion

Alcohol is the substance most often involved overall. Opioid misuse is relatively more common in specialties with easy access to potent drugs, notably anesthesiology. Signs of diversion include unusual dispensing, missing or unwitnessed waste, refusing breaks or relief, volunteering for extra cases, frequent bathroom breaks, coming in on days off and patients whose pain seems poorly controlled. Behavioural changes at work tend to appear late, after problems at home and in health.

Burnout and fatigue

Burnout dimensionWhat it looks like
Emotional exhaustionFeeling drained and depleted by work
DepersonalizationCynicism, detachment, treating patients as cases or objects
Reduced personal accomplishmentFeeling ineffective, that the work makes no difference

Burnout is common in residents and is associated with self-reported errors, depression and leaving medicine. Physicians die by suicide at higher rates than the general population. Fatigue from prolonged wakefulness impairs attention and judgement much as alcohol does, and fatigued people underestimate their impairment.

Accreditation standards for residency limit clinical and educational work to 80 hours per week averaged over 4 weeks (including in-house call and clinical work from home), continuous duty to 24 hours plus up to 4 hours for transitions, at least 1 day in 7 free (averaged), and in-house call to no more than every third night (averaged). Programs must provide sleep facilities, safe transport home and access to confidential mental health care.

Worked example: weekly hours of 82, 76, 85 and 73 total 316, an average of 79 hours, which complies even though two weeks exceeded 80.

The duty to act

  1. Protect patients now. A colleague who appears impaired at work is stopped from patient care immediately, through the supervisor or person in charge, and his or her patients are covered.
  2. Report through the proper channel. Usually the department chief, chief medical officer or the hospital's physician wellness committee; a medical student goes to the attending or clerkship director.
  3. Refer for evaluation and treatment. State physician health programs (PHPs) provide confidential assessment, referral to treatment and multi-year monitoring; physicians who comply often avoid public discipline and usually return to practice.

is the inability to practise with reasonable skill and safety because of a condition such as a substance use disorder, mental illness, physical illness, cognitive decline or fatigue. A diagnosis is not impairment: a physician with well-treated depression, bipolar disorder or diabetes who practises safely is not impaired. Equating the two increases stigma and discourages treatment.

Alcohol is the substance most often involved overall. Opioid misuse is relatively more common in specialties with easy access to potent drugs, notably anesthesiology. Signs of diversion include unusual dispensing, missing or unwitnessed waste, refusing breaks or relief, volunteering for extra cases, frequent bathroom breaks, coming in on days off and patients whose pain seems poorly controlled. Behavioural changes at work tend to appear late, after problems at home and in health.
Feeling drained and depleted by work
Cynicism, detachment, treating patients as cases or objects
Feeling ineffective, that the work makes no difference

Negligence is a civil wrong: a person who owes another a duty of care fails to meet it, and harm follows. Medical malpractice is negligence by a health professional acting in that role. It is a tort (a civil claim for money damages), not a crime, although grossly reckless conduct can also be prosecuted separately. To win, the plaintiff (the patient, or the family or estate after a death) must prove four linked elements. If any one link is missing, the claim fails, however bad the outcome.

The four elements

ElementQuestion the court asksTypical way it fails
DutyDid a physician–patient relationship (or another legal duty) exist?A casual opinion to a stranger at a party; no relationship formed
Breach (dereliction)Did the care fall below the standard of care?The care was reasonable even though the outcome was poor
CausationDid the breach more likely than not cause the harm?The harm came from the disease or an unrelated event
DamagesDid the patient suffer a real, compensable loss?An error that was caught or corrected with no lasting injury

A duty usually begins when a physician agrees, explicitly or by conduct, to evaluate or treat someone: seeing a patient in clinic, accepting a consult, or examining a patient in the emergency department. Breach is measured against the standard of care: what a reasonably careful and prudent physician in the same specialty would do in similar circumstances. It is not the best possible care, not what a famous centre would do, and not whatever the outcome turned out to be. Because jurors are not physicians, the standard of care and its breach are normally established by expert testimony. Specialists are generally held to the standard of their specialty.

Causation has two parts: the harm would not have happened but for the breach, and the harm was a foreseeable result of it (proximate cause). Damages may be economic (medical bills, lost income), noneconomic (pain and suffering) and, rarely, punitive when conduct is malicious or reckless. Many states cap noneconomic damages; the amounts vary and are not tested.

Burden of proof and special doctrines

Civil cases are decided on the preponderance of the evidence: the jury must find each element more likely than not (just over 50%). That is a lower bar than the criminal standard, beyond a reasonable doubt.

  • Res ipsa loquitur ("the thing speaks for itself"): when an injury would not ordinarily happen without negligence and the instrument was under the defendant's control (a sponge left in the abdomen), negligence may be inferred without an expert explaining the standard of care.
  • Respondeat superior (vicarious liability): an employer, such as a hospital, can be liable for negligent acts of its employees within the scope of their work. The employee remains personally responsible as well.
  • Lack of informed consent is a negligence theory: the physician failed to disclose a material risk or alternative, and a reasonable patient who had been told would have declined. Treating with no consent at all, or doing a different procedure, is battery.

A bad outcome is not proof of malpractice, and good care is not proof that no claim will be filed. On the exam, separate the elements: an obvious error with no lasting harm fails on damages; a careless omission followed by an unrelated death fails on causation.

Reporting and the National Practitioner Data Bank

Under federal law, any payment made on behalf of a physician to settle or satisfy a malpractice claim is reported to the National Practitioner Data Bank, which hospitals query when granting privileges. Licensing actions and certain restrictions on clinical privileges are also reported there. Settling a claim therefore has professional consequences, not just financial ones.

Why patients sue and what lowers claims

Claims track the relationship as much as the error. Patients who feel ignored, rushed, or misled are more likely to sue than patients with the same injury who felt heard. Clear explanations, time to ask questions, honest disclosure of errors, and an apology lower the risk. Many states have apology laws that keep expressions of sympathy (and in some states, admissions of fault) out of evidence; the details vary, but disclosure is required ethically everywhere.

Two federal and state protections you must know

RuleWhat it requires or protectsKey limits
EMTALA (federal)Any hospital that takes Medicare and has an emergency department must give anyone who comes requesting care a medical screening examination and, if an emergency condition exists, stabilise it or arrange an appropriate transferApplies regardless of insurance, ability to pay or immigration status; screening may not be delayed to ask about payment
Good Samaritan laws (state)Protect a person who gives emergency help in good faith, outside a normal care setting and without payment, from liability for ordinary negligenceDo not cover gross negligence or wilful misconduct; do not apply to care given in one's own job

EMTALA transfers are allowed for an unstable patient only when the patient asks in writing after being told the risks, or when a physician certifies that the expected benefits of care elsewhere outweigh the risks; the receiving hospital must agree and records and suitable transport go with the patient. A woman in active labour is considered stabilised only after delivery, unless such a transfer is made.

Duty, breach, causation, damages: picture four links of a chain. The plaintiff must show every link by a preponderance of the evidence. When an item asks which element is weakest, check each link against the vignette one by one.

Disclosure of errors, documentation and risk management in practice are applied in the Step 2 CK chapter on malpractice and culturally responsive care.
