s23g-s0802.bodyHtml:
Physician misconduct is conduct that betrays the trust society gives physicians: dishonesty, exploitation of patients, fraud against payers, practice without a licence or beyond competence, and mistreatment of colleagues or learners. It is handled by employers, by the state medical board (which licenses physicians and can reprimand, restrict, suspend or revoke), by federal agencies for fraud, and sometimes by criminal courts. Misconduct differs from negligence: negligence is a failure of care, misconduct is a failure of integrity or professional boundaries, and the two can coexist.

Boundaries and sexual misconduct

A sexual or romantic relationship with a current patient is always unethical, whoever initiates it and whatever the patient says they want. The power imbalance, the patient's dependence and the intimacy of clinical care make genuine consent impossible to separate from the relationship. A relationship with a former patient is unethical if the physician uses trust, knowledge or influence gained in the professional relationship; in psychiatry it is considered unacceptable essentially always. Sexual comments, unnecessary intimate examinations and examinations without clinical purpose are misconduct. Offering a chaperone for intimate examinations protects both the patient and the physician.

Fraud and the federal payment laws

LawCore prohibitionIntent needed?Who it covers
Anti-Kickback StatuteKnowingly and wilfully offering, paying, asking for or receiving anything of value to induce or reward referrals of business paid by federal health care programsYes: knowing and wilful; criminalAnyone: physicians, companies, hospitals, labs
Stark Law (physician self-referral)A physician may not refer Medicare (and Medicaid) patients for designated health services (such as imaging, clinical laboratory, physical therapy, home health) to an entity in which the physician or an immediate family member has a financial relationship, unless an exception appliesNo: strict liability; civil penalties and repaymentPhysicians and the entities that bill
False Claims ActKnowingly submitting false or fraudulent claims for federal payment (billing for services not done, upcoding)Knowing, including reckless disregardAnyone; whistle-blowers can bring suits

Upcoding is billing a more complex or expensive service than was provided or documented. Unbundling is billing the parts of a package separately to raise payment. Billing for services not rendered is the bluntest form of fraud. A practice that finds it has been overpaid by Medicare or Medicaid must report and return the money promptly once the overpayment is identified; keeping it becomes a false claim.

Industry relationships and Open Payments

Gifts from drug and device companies are judged by whether they serve patients and education or buy influence. Cash, gift cards, paid leisure travel, payments for attending a talk, and "consulting" fees for no real work should be declined. Modest items that primarily benefit patients or education are the most anyone should accept, and many institutions ban all gifts. The Physician Payments Sunshine Act created Open Payments: manufacturers of drugs, devices and biologics covered by federal programs must report payments and other transfers of value to physicians and teaching hospitals to CMS, which publishes them. The law requires disclosure; it does not forbid the payments. Physicians should disclose relevant financial interests to patients and follow institutional conflict-of-interest rules.

Stark versus anti-kickback: if the stem stresses that the physician did not intend to steer patients for money, Stark can still be violated (strict liability, physician self-referral, designated health services). Anti-kickback needs knowing and wilful intent but covers anyone and any federally paid item.

Honesty in records, research and training

  • Falsifying records: documenting an examination not performed, back-dating a note, or changing an entry after a bad outcome. Corrections are made as dated, signed addenda; the original stays visible.
  • Research misconduct has a specific federal definition: fabrication (making up data), falsification (manipulating data, methods or images) and plagiarism (using others' words or ideas without credit) in proposing, doing, reviewing or reporting research. Honest error and differences of opinion are not misconduct.
  • Academic dishonesty: cheating on examinations, copying a classmate's write-up, or signing in for someone absent. These predict later unprofessional behaviour and are reported through the school's honour or professionalism process.
  • Misrepresenting credentials: a student who lets a patient believe he is a physician is deceiving the patient; introduce yourself accurately.

Licence and scope

Practising medicine requires a licence from the state where the patient is located at the time of care, which matters for telehealth across state lines (interstate compacts make extra licences easier to get but do not remove the requirement). Practising with a lapsed or suspended licence, or performing procedures far outside one's training, is misconduct even if no patient is harmed.

Harassment, discrimination and the duty to report

Sexual harassment, demeaning learners, and discrimination by race, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation or gender identity are professionalism violations and, in employment and education, are covered by civil rights law. Institutions must provide reporting routes and must not retaliate against people who report. Physicians have an ethical duty to report a colleague's misconduct: usually first to the supervisor or the institution's leadership or compliance office, and to the state medical board when conduct threatens patients and the institution cannot or will not act (or when there is no institution, as in solo practice).

Three words sort most misconduct items: boundaries (never with a current patient), billing (bill what was done and documented; no payment for referrals), honesty (records, research and credentials are never falsified). The usual next step is to act directly and report through the proper channel, not to ignore it or go to the media.

s23g-s0803.bodyHtml:
A referral transfers part or all of a patient's care to another clinician. Done well it brings expertise, honours the patient's wishes and keeps care continuous. Done badly it becomes a way to abandon a patient, to discriminate, or to profit. The exam tests when a referral is required, when it is not enough, and how to end or transfer a relationship without harming the patient.

When to refer

SituationWhat the physician should do
The problem is beyond the physician's training or the setting's capabilityRefer or consult; keep coordinating care and communicate the question clearly
The patient asks for a specialist or a second opinionSupport it, share records, and explore any worry behind the request; a second opinion is not an insult
The physician has a conscientious objection to a legal, requested serviceTell the patient early, do not obstruct, refer in time for the service to remain an option, and give emergency care regardless
A family or personal history suggests a hereditary conditionRefer for genetic counselling before or alongside testing
The physician has a financial interest in the place being referred toAvoid prohibited self-referral (Stark); disclose interests; choose on clinical grounds

Conscientious objection and its limits

Physicians may decline to provide a specific legal service that conflicts with deeply held moral or religious beliefs. The patient's access, not the physician's comfort, sets the limits. The physician should tell prospective patients in advance which services they do not offer, give accurate information about all options, refer or transfer care promptly so the delay does not close an option, never use the objection to lecture or shame, and still give care in an emergency when no one else can. Objection is to a service, never to a class of patients.

"Refer to a colleague" is the correct move for a service the physician objects to; it is the wrong move when a physician tries to avoid a patient because of who the patient is (HIV status, disability, race, religion, sexual orientation or gender identity). Declining a patient on those grounds is discrimination, and refusing a person with HIV is unlawful under the Americans with Disabilities Act.

Ending a physician–patient relationship

Either party may end the relationship, but the physician must not leave a patient who still needs care without a way to get it. Abandonment is the unilateral end of the relationship, without reasonable notice and an opportunity to find another physician, while care is still needed; it can be a basis for liability and discipline. Acceptable reasons to end a relationship include threats or violence, repeated non-adherence that makes safe care impossible after it has been discussed, fraud such as altered prescriptions, and repeated unpaid bills when payment plans have been offered. Proper termination:

  • Written notice to the patient stating that the relationship will end on a set date, with a reasonable interval (many practices use about 30 days).
  • Continued care, including urgent and emergency care, during that interval.
  • Help finding a new physician (a list, the insurer's directory, a community clinic).
  • Transfer of records once the patient authorises it.
  • Not ending care in the middle of an acute episode, or when no other physician is available.

Sharing information with the next clinician

HIPAA permits a physician to disclose protected health information to another provider for treatment without the patient's written authorisation, and the minimum-necessary standard does not apply to disclosures to a provider for treatment. Patients also have a right to get copies of their own records, generally within 30 days of the request, for a reasonable cost-based fee. A good referral states the question, includes relevant results, and makes clear who is responsible for follow-up.

Genetic counselling and GINA

Genetic counsellors take a pedigree, explain what a result would and would not mean for the patient and relatives, and help choose the right test. Patients often fear discrimination. The federal Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act forbids health insurers from using genetic information for eligibility or premiums and forbids employers (with 15 or more employees) from using it in hiring, firing or promotion. It does not cover life, disability or long-term-care insurance.

Referral ethics: fees and self-referral

Paying or accepting money for a referral (fee splitting) is unethical and, when federal programs pay, can violate the Anti-Kickback Statute. Referring Medicare patients for designated health services to an entity the physician owns can violate the Stark Law. A referral should be justified by the patient's needs alone.

Referral answers on the exam have three tests: Is it in the patient's interest? Is it timely enough to keep the patient's options open? Does someone remain responsible for the patient until the new clinician takes over? An answer that leaves a gap in care is wrong even if it sounds polite.

Safety when a patient is dangerous

A patient who threatens or assaults staff can be discharged from a practice with proper notice. In the moment, safety comes first: leave the room, keep a clear exit, and call security. Emergency care is still provided, with security present, and EMTALA still applies in the emergency department.

s23g-s0804.bodyHtml:
Culture shapes how people describe symptoms, explain illness, make decisions, use traditional remedies, and judge whether a physician is trustworthy. The goal is not to memorise traits of groups, which breeds stereotypes, but to ask each patient and adapt. Cultural humility is the stance the exam rewards: lifelong self-reflection about one's own assumptions, curiosity about the patient's perspective, and active work to reduce the power imbalance between physician and patient. It differs from the older idea of cultural competence, which can imply that a finite body of knowledge about a group is enough.

Explanatory models

Every patient has an explanatory model: their own account of what the illness is, what caused it, why it started now, how serious it is, what treatment they expect, and what they fear. Eliciting it with open questions ("What do you think is causing this?" "What worries you most?" "What have you tried so far?") exposes mismatches early and lets the physician negotiate a plan both sides accept. Traditional healing practices that are not harmful should be respected and can run alongside medical care; practices with real risks (a remedy that interacts with a drug, delaying treatment for a time-sensitive condition) are discussed openly and a compromise is sought without ridicule.

Decision-making styles

Some patients want every detail; others want information shared with family, or want a relative to decide. Autonomy includes the right to delegate. The physician asks the patient, ideally alone and early, how they want to receive information and who should be involved, then follows that choice and revisits it. A family's request to withhold a diagnosis is answered by asking the patient, not by complying or refusing outright.

Religious requests

RequestUsual response
A clinician of the same gender for intimate examinationsAccommodate when possible; in an emergency explain and proceed with a chaperone
Fasting during a religious periodAsk about plans, adjust medication timing, discuss when fasting is unsafe
Refusal of blood products by an adult with capacityRespect it; ask which products and blood-sparing techniques are acceptable; plan ahead
Rituals at the end of lifeAccommodate within safety; involve chaplaincy and nursing

Language, literacy and disability

Patients with limited English proficiency should have a trained medical interpreter (in person, video or phone), not a family member, and never a child. Low health literacy crosses all languages; plain words and teach-back ("To make sure I explained it well, can you tell me how you'll take this?") check understanding. Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, practices must provide auxiliary aids for effective communication, such as a qualified sign language interpreter for a Deaf patient, and may not charge the patient for them. Speak to the patient directly, not to the companion, and ask what accommodations help.

Implicit bias and structural racism

Implicit bias is an automatic, unconscious association that shapes judgment without intent; it can coexist with sincere egalitarian beliefs. Studies have repeatedly found that Black and Hispanic patients receive analgesia for painful conditions less often than White patients with similar pain, a gap not explained by insurance or pain scores. Structural racism works through policies, systems and tools rather than individual attitudes. Clinical examples:

  • Older kidney-function equations added a race coefficient that raised the estimated GFR of Black patients at the same creatinine, which could delay diagnosis of chronic kidney disease, referral and transplant listing. Race-free equations replaced it in 2021.
  • Pulse oximeters can overestimate arterial oxygen saturation in people with darker skin pigmentation, so dangerous hypoxemia can be missed (occult hypoxemia).

A disparity that persists after adjustment for insurance, pain score and diagnosis is not explained by those variables; on the exam, implicit bias and structural factors are the answer, and the fix is a system one (standard protocols, audit and feedback), not telling patients to "report pain better".

Sexual orientation and gender identity

Use the name and pronouns the patient gives, and ask rather than assume. Collect gender identity with a two-step question: current gender identity and sex assigned at birth. Take a sexual history that does not presume partners' genders ("What are the genders of your partners?"). Screening follows the organs a person has: a transgender man with a cervix needs cervical cancer screening; a transgender woman may need prostate counselling.

Immigrants, refugees and people without stable housing

Fear of authorities, past trauma and unfamiliar systems keep some immigrants and refugees from care. Explain confidentiality and that emergency care does not depend on immigration status or ability to pay. For people experiencing homelessness, ask about where they sleep, food, storage of medicines and phone access, then build a plan they can actually follow, with social work. The question is never "will this patient comply?" but "what would make this plan possible?"

The best answer in a cultural item almost always asks the patient (about beliefs, preferences, barriers) before acting, uses a professional interpreter when language is a barrier, and accommodates any request that does not cause harm.

s23g-s0901.bodyHtml:
A health system is a set of interacting parts: patients and families, clinicians of many professions, equipment, software, policies, payment rules, buildings and the community outside the hospital. Outcomes come from how these parts work together, not from any one person. Systems thinking asks how the design of the whole made a good or bad outcome likely. It is the basis of modern patient safety: most harm comes from ordinary people working inside poorly designed systems, so blaming the last person to touch the patient rarely prevents the next event.

Active failures and latent conditions

An active failure is an unsafe act at the "sharp end", by the person in direct contact with the patient: picking the wrong vial, mis-keying a dose, skipping a check. Its effect is immediate and usually visible. A latent condition sits at the "blunt end": staffing decisions, confusing software screens, similar-looking packaging, a policy that conflicts with how work is really done, a culture that discourages questions. Latent conditions can lie dormant for years and are found in nearly every serious event. They are also where the most durable fixes are.

In the Swiss-cheese model, each layer of defence (design, policy, supervision, the front-line check) has holes. The holes move and change size. Harm reaches the patient only when the holes in every layer happen to line up.

The model explains two exam favourites: why an analysis that stops at "the nurse made an error" is incomplete, and why adding layers (independent checks, alerts, forcing functions) lowers the chance that a single slip becomes harm.

Human factors

Human factors engineering designs tasks and tools around how people actually think and behave. Performance falls with fatigue (sleep loss impairs attention and judgment in ways the tired person underestimates), interruptions (an interrupted medication preparation is a classic source of omitted or repeated steps), high cognitive load (many patients, many alarms, alarm fatigue) and poor design (look-alike controls, unclear displays). Effective responses change the environment rather than ask people to try harder:

StrengthExamplesWhy
StrongestForcing functions (connectors that physically cannot join the wrong line), removing a hazard (taking concentrated electrolytes off wards), automationMake the error impossible or very hard
IntermediateStandardised order sets, checklists, barcode scanning, simplified processes, redundancy, reduced interruptionsMake the right action the easy default
WeakestEducation, new policy, warnings, "be more careful" memos, disciplinary threatsDepend on memory and vigilance

When asked for the intervention most likely to prevent recurrence, choose the one that changes the system so the error cannot easily happen again (a forcing function or standardisation), not retraining or punishment of the individual.

High-reliability organisations

Some industries (aviation, nuclear power) run hazardous operations with very few accidents. Hospitals copy five habits of these high-reliability organisations: preoccupation with failure (near misses are studied, not ignored), reluctance to simplify explanations, sensitivity to front-line operations, commitment to resilience (recovering quickly when things go wrong) and deference to expertise (the person with the most relevant knowledge leads, whatever their rank). A culture of safety lets anyone stop a process when they see danger.

Just culture

Just culture balances learning with accountability by judging the behaviour, not the outcome:

BehaviourDescriptionResponse
Human errorInadvertent slip or lapse while trying to do the right thingConsole the person; fix the system
At-risk behaviourA choice whose risk is not recognised or is believed justified, often a common workaroundCoach; remove incentives for the shortcut
Reckless behaviourConscious disregard of a substantial, unjustifiable riskDisciplinary action is appropriate

A bad outcome does not make behaviour reckless, and a good outcome does not make a shortcut acceptable. Two nurses who take the same shortcut deserve the same response whether or not their patient was harmed.

Teamwork and communication

Communication failures contribute to a large share of serious events. Proven tools include structured handoffs (a standard format, a verbal exchange in a quiet place, a written summary and a chance for questions), closed-loop communication (the sender gives a clear message to a named person, the receiver repeats it back, the sender confirms, and the receiver reports when done), read-back of verbal and telephone orders and critical results, and a structured way to raise a concern: state the problem, the background, your assessment and a specific request. Any team member who sees a risk should speak up, and escalate up the chain of command if the concern is not addressed. Interprofessional teams work best when roles are clear and every member (nurse, pharmacist, therapist) is expected to contribute.

Care transitions and the wider system

Transitions (admission, transfer between units, discharge, handoffs between shifts) are high-risk because information is lost. Medication reconciliation compares the medicines the patient actually takes with those ordered at each transition and resolves every unintended difference. Good discharge includes a clear medication list, follow-up arranged, a summary sent to the next clinician, and teach-back (the patient explains the plan in their own words).

Health also depends on social determinants: income, housing, food security, education, transport, safety and social support. They shape access, adherence and outcomes as much as clinical care does. Clinicians screen for unmet social needs and link patients with community resources (food programmes, transport, housing support, social work). Schools and public health agencies are part of the system too: school nurses manage medicines and action plans during the day, and health departments do surveillance, outbreak control and environmental investigation (for example, finding the source of lead exposure).

The same systems lens underlies quality improvement (next section): measure the process, find the latent causes, and test changes to the system.

Quality improvement (QI) is the systematic, data-driven effort to make care safer, more effective, more patient-centred, timelier, more efficient and more equitable. Unlike research, which seeks generalisable knowledge and needs a fixed protocol, QI aims to improve a local process and changes its approach as it learns. (Projects that are designed to produce generalisable knowledge may still need research review.)

The Donabedian triad and types of measure

MeasureWhat it capturesExample (central lines)
StructureThe setting and resources: staff, equipment, policies, buildingsInsertion kits with all supplies stocked on every unit
ProcessWhat is done for patients and whether it is done rightPercentage of insertions with a completed insertion checklist
OutcomeThe effect on healthCentral line–associated bloodstream infections per 1,000 line-days
BalancingUnintended effects elsewhere in the systemRate of peripheral IV failures after a push to remove lines early

Process measures change quickly and are under the team's control; outcome measures matter most but need more time and more cases. Every project should track at least one balancing measure so that improvement in one place is not bought with harm in another.

The Model for Improvement and PDSA

The Model for Improvement asks three questions: What are we trying to accomplish (a specific, measurable, time-bound aim)? How will we know that a change is an improvement (measures)? What change can we make that will result in improvement? Changes are then tested in Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles: plan a test and predict its result, do it on a small scale, study the data against the prediction, and act (adopt, adapt or abandon). Small, rapid cycles are cheaper and safer than a big launch, and they build on each other until the change is reliable enough to spread.

Variation, run charts and control charts

Every process varies. Common-cause variation is the random noise built into a stable process; the response is to redesign the process if its average performance is not good enough, not to react to each high or low point. Special-cause variation arises from something outside the usual process (a new staff group, a broken device, an intervention) and should be investigated.

A run chart plots data over time with the median. Commonly used rules for a non-random signal: a shift of six or more consecutive points all above or all below the median (points on the median are skipped), a trend of five or more consecutive points all rising or all falling, too few or too many runs, or an obviously extreme point. A control chart adds a centre line (the mean) and upper and lower control limits, usually three standard deviations from the mean; a point outside a limit is a special cause.

A single month that is the "best ever" is not evidence of improvement if it lies within the usual range. Equally, a QI team does not need a randomised trial or a P value to recognise a shift on a run chart.

Analysing problems

Root-cause analysis (RCA) is a retrospective, structured review of an event (often a sentinel event) by an interdisciplinary team. It asks what happened, why, and what will prevent recurrence, focusing on systems rather than blame. Two common tools are the cause-and-effect (fishbone or Ishikawa) diagram, which sorts possible causes into categories, and the "5 whys", asking "why?" repeatedly until a fixable system cause appears. "The nurse forgot" is a starting point, not a root cause.

Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) is prospective: before a new process or device goes live, the team maps each step, lists how it could fail, and scores each failure mode for severity, likelihood of occurrence and difficulty of detection (often 1–10 each). Their product is the risk priority number (RPN = S × O × D). For example, a failure scored 8 for severity, 3 for occurrence and 5 for detection has an RPN of 120, and modes with the highest RPN (and any with catastrophic severity) are addressed first.

Pareto analysis ranks categories of a problem by frequency in a bar chart with a cumulative line; usually a few categories ("the vital few", roughly 80% of events from 20% of causes) account for most of the problem and are targeted first.

Other approaches

  • Checklists and bundles: a bundle is a small set of evidence-based practices that work best when all are done every time; compliance is often scored all-or-none. The central line insertion bundle (hand hygiene, full sterile barrier precautions, chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, careful site choice, and daily review of whether the line is still needed) is the classic example.
  • Lean: map the value stream and remove waste (waiting, unnecessary steps, motion, rework). Six Sigma: reduce variation and defects with a define-measure-analyse-improve-control sequence.
  • Benchmarking compares performance with peers or best performers; audit and feedback gives clinicians their own performance data, ideally with a comparison and a target, and reliably produces modest improvement.

Retrospective, after an event → root-cause analysis. Prospective, before a new process → FMEA. Most events in the fewest categories → Pareto. Is the process changing over time → run chart or control chart.

s23g-s0903.bodyHtml:
Patient safety is the prevention of harm caused by health care itself. Exam questions test precise vocabulary, so learn the definitions as a set.

Key definitions

TermMeaning
Medical errorFailure of a planned action to be completed as intended, or use of a wrong plan; defined by the process, whether or not harm follows
Adverse eventHarm caused by medical care rather than by the underlying disease; may or may not involve an error
Preventable adverse eventHarm that resulted from an error or from failure to follow accepted practice
Near missAn error that is caught before it reaches the patient
No-harm eventAn error that reaches the patient but causes no harm
Sentinel eventA patient safety event that results in death, permanent harm or severe temporary harm; triggers a root-cause analysis
Never eventA serious, largely preventable event that should never occur, such as surgery on the wrong site or patient, a retained foreign object, or a patient given to the wrong person on discharge

An adverse drug reaction to a correctly prescribed drug in a patient with no known risk (a first-ever allergic reaction) is an adverse event without error. A wrong dose that the pharmacist intercepts is an error and a near miss, but not an adverse event.

Types of error

  • Slip: the right plan, carried out wrongly through a failure of attention (choosing the adjacent drug on a pull-down menu).
  • Lapse: the right plan, with a step forgotten through a failure of memory (forgetting to restart a held anticoagulant).
  • Mistake: the wrong plan, from a gap in knowledge or a wrong rule (choosing a drug that is contraindicated because the contraindication was not known).
  • Omission (a needed action was not done, such as missed thromboprophylaxis) versus commission (a wrong action was done, such as giving the wrong drug).

Slips and lapses are prevented by design (reminders, forcing functions, fewer interruptions); mistakes are addressed with decision support, training and supervision.

Diagnostic error and cognitive bias

Diagnostic errors (missed, wrong or delayed diagnoses) are common and often harmful. Most involve both system factors (results not followed up, poor handoffs) and thinking errors:

BiasWhat happens
AnchoringSticking with an early impression despite new contradictory information
Premature closureStopping the search once a plausible diagnosis is found
AvailabilityJudging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind (a recent memorable case)
Confirmation biasSeeking or weighting only data that support a favoured diagnosis
Diagnostic momentumAccepting a label passed on by others without re-examining it
Framing effectBeing swayed by how information is presented ("frequent flyer", "anxious")

Remedies include deliberately asking "what else could this be?", diagnostic time-outs, checklists for high-risk complaints, and closed-loop systems for test results.

Medication safety

High-alert medications carry a high risk of serious harm when used in error: insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, concentrated electrolytes such as potassium chloride, neuromuscular blockers and chemotherapy. Defences include computerised provider order entry (CPOE) with dose-range and interaction checks (which also removes handwriting problems), barcode medication administration (scanning the patient's wristband and the drug at the bedside), smart pumps with drug libraries, independent double checks, and tall-man lettering for look-alike/sound-alike names (for example hydrOXYzine and hydrALAZINE). Avoid error-prone abbreviations: write "units" rather than "U", never use a trailing zero ("5 mg", not "5.0 mg") and always use a leading zero ("0.5 mg", not ".5 mg").

A trailing zero turns 1.0 mg into a possible 10 mg; a missing leading zero turns .5 mg into a possible 5 mg. Both are tenfold errors.

Procedures and hospital hazards

  • Universal protocol for invasive procedures: a pre-procedure verification of patient, procedure and site; site marking by the person who will do the procedure, with the patient involved where possible; and a time-out immediately before the incision in which the whole team confirms the details and anyone can stop the procedure.
  • Falls: assess risk (delirium, sedatives, orthostasis, urgency), review medicines, schedule toileting, keep the bed low; physical restraints do not prevent falls and can cause injury.
  • Pressure injuries: regular repositioning, pressure-redistributing surfaces, skin inspection, moisture control and nutrition.
  • Health care–associated infections: hand hygiene for all; central line bundles and prompt removal of unneeded lines (CLABSI); avoiding unnecessary urinary catheters and removing them early (CAUTI); and for surgical-site infection, appropriate prophylactic antibiotic timing before incision, clipping rather than shaving hair, and glucose and temperature control.

Reporting, duty hours and second victims

Incident-reporting systems work only if they are non-punitive and easy to use; near misses are reported too, because they reveal the same holes as harmful events without the harm. Resident duty hours (ACGME) are limited to 80 hours a week averaged over 4 weeks, with one day in seven free of clinical work averaged over 4 weeks and a cap on continuous scheduled work (24 hours, with up to 4 more for transitions of care). Clinicians involved in an error often suffer guilt, anxiety and loss of confidence; these second victims need timely peer support.

If an error was caught before reaching the patient, it is a near miss; if it reached the patient without harm, it is a no-harm event; if it caused harm, it is a preventable adverse event. All three should be reported.

Harm caused by medical care rather than by the underlying disease; may or may not involve an error
Harm that resulted from an error or from failure to follow accepted practice
An error that is caught before it reaches the patient
An error that reaches the patient but causes no harm
A patient safety event that results in death, permanent harm or severe temporary harm; triggers a root-cause analysis
A serious, largely preventable event that should never occur, such as surgery on the wrong site or patient, a retained foreign object, or a patient given to the wrong person on discharge

An adverse drug reaction to a correctly prescribed drug in a patient with no known risk (a first-ever allergic reaction) is an adverse event without error. A wrong dose that the pharmacist intercepts is an error and a near miss, but not an adverse event.
: the right plan, carried out wrongly through a failure of attention (choosing the adjacent drug on a pull-down menu).
: the right plan, with a step forgotten through a failure of memory (forgetting to restart a held anticoagulant).
: the wrong plan, from a gap in knowledge or a wrong rule (choosing a drug that is contraindicated because the contraindication was not known).
(a needed action was not done, such as missed thromboprophylaxis) versus
(a wrong action was done, such as giving the wrong drug).
Slips and lapses are prevented by design (reminders, forcing functions, fewer interruptions); mistakes are addressed with decision support, training and supervision.
Diagnostic errors (missed, wrong or delayed diagnoses) are common and often harmful. Most involve both system factors (results not followed up, poor handoffs) and thinking errors:
Sticking with an early impression despite new contradictory information
Stopping the search once a plausible diagnosis is found
Judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind (a recent memorable case)
Seeking or weighting only data that support a favoured diagnosis
Accepting a label passed on by others without re-examining it
Being swayed by how information is presented ("frequent flyer", "anxious")
Remedies include deliberately asking "what else could this be?", diagnostic time-outs, checklists for high-risk complaints, and closed-loop systems for test results.
carry a high risk of serious harm when used in error: insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, concentrated electrolytes such as potassium chloride, neuromuscular blockers and chemotherapy. Defences include
with dose-range and interaction checks (which also removes handwriting problems),
(scanning the patient's wristband and the drug at the bedside), smart pumps with drug libraries, independent double checks, and

for look-alike/sound-alike names (for example hydrOXYzine and hydrALAZINE). Avoid error-prone abbreviations: write "units" rather than "U", never use a trailing zero ("5 mg", not "5.0 mg") and always use a leading zero ("0.5 mg", not ".5 mg").
A trailing zero turns 1.0 mg into a possible 10 mg; a missing leading zero turns .5 mg into a possible 5 mg. Both are tenfold errors.

immediately before the incision in which the whole team confirms the details and anyone can stop the procedure.

: regular repositioning, pressure-redistributing surfaces, skin inspection, moisture control and nutrition.

: hand hygiene for all; central line bundles and prompt removal of unneeded lines (CLABSI); avoiding unnecessary urinary catheters and removing them early (CAUTI); and for surgical-site infection, appropriate prophylactic antibiotic timing before incision, clipping rather than shaving hair, and glucose and temperature control.
Reporting, duty hours and second victims
Incident-reporting systems work only if they are

and easy to use; near misses are reported too, because they reveal the same holes as harmful events without the harm. Resident duty hours (ACGME) are limited to 80 hours a week averaged over 4 weeks, with one day in seven free of clinical work averaged over 4 weeks and a cap on continuous scheduled work (24 hours, with up to 4 more for transitions of care). Clinicians involved in an error often suffer guilt, anxiety and loss of confidence; these

If an error was caught before reaching the patient, it is a near miss; if it reached the patient without harm, it is a no-harm event; if it caused harm, it is a preventable adverse event. All three should be reported.

s23g-s0904.bodyHtml:
The US has no single health system. Coverage is a patchwork of private and public programmes, and the source of a person's coverage usually depends on age, employment, income, disability and state of residence. Exam questions test who qualifies for what and what each programme pays for.

Main sources of coverage

ProgrammeWho it coversFunding and administration
Employer-sponsored insuranceWorkers and their families; the largest single source of coverage for people under 65Premiums shared by employer and employee; employer contributions are tax-advantaged
MedicarePeople aged 65 or older; younger people who have received Social Security disability benefits for 24 months; people with end-stage renal disease; people with ALS (no 24-month wait)Federal; run by CMS; funded by payroll taxes, premiums and general revenue
MedicaidLow-income people in eligible groups (children, pregnant people, parents, older and disabled people, and in expansion states most low-income adults)Joint federal–state; each state runs its own programme within federal rules
CHIPChildren in families whose income is too high for Medicaid but too low to afford private coverageJoint federal–state
ACA marketplacesPeople without affordable employer coverage who buy individual plansPrivate plans; income-based premium tax credits
Military and veterans' careService members, families, eligible veteransFederal (TRICARE, Veterans Health Administration)

The parts of Medicare

PartCovers
A (hospital insurance)Inpatient hospital care, limited skilled nursing facility care after a hospital stay, hospice, some home health
B (medical insurance)Physician services, outpatient care, preventive services, durable medical equipment
C (Medicare Advantage)Private plans that provide Part A and B benefits (often with drug coverage and networks)
DOutpatient prescription drugs, through private plans

Traditional Medicare does not cover long-term custodial care in a nursing home, routine dental care or most hearing aids. Medicaid is the largest payer for long-term nursing home care, often after older adults have spent down their savings. People who qualify for both programmes are "dual eligible".

Medicare is based mainly on age or disability, not income; Medicaid is based on income (and category). A 66-year-old executive has Medicare; a 30-year-old with low income may have Medicaid.

The Affordable Care Act

The ACA (2010) expanded coverage through three routes: Medicaid expansion, marketplaces with income-based subsidies, and insurance-market reforms. A 2012 Supreme Court decision made Medicaid expansion optional, so eligibility for low-income adults without children differs widely between states. Its lasting protections include: insurers may not deny coverage or charge more because of a pre-existing condition (individual premiums may vary only by age, tobacco use, location and family size); young adults may stay on a parent's plan until age 26; no lifetime dollar limits on essential benefits; and recommended preventive services covered without cost-sharing. Medicaid and CHIP enrolment is open all year, whereas marketplace enrolment happens during an annual open-enrolment period or after a qualifying life event (job loss, marriage, birth, a move).

Uninsured and underinsured

People remain uninsured because of cost, lack of an employer offer, living in a non-expansion state with income below the subsidy range, immigration status, or churning on and off Medicaid. Underinsured people have coverage but face out-of-pocket costs high relative to income, so they delay care. Both groups have worse outcomes and more preventable hospitalisations. The Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) guarantees that anyone who comes to the emergency department of a Medicare-participating hospital receives a medical screening examination and, if an emergency medical condition (including active labour) is found, stabilising treatment or an appropriate transfer, regardless of insurance or ability to pay. It is a safety net for emergencies, not a source of ongoing care.

Federal and state public-health roles

BodyMain roles
CMSRuns Medicare; oversees Medicaid, CHIP and the federal marketplace; sets conditions of participation for hospitals
FDAApproves and monitors drugs, biologics (including vaccines) and medical devices; recalls; most food safety; tobacco
CDCNational surveillance, outbreak investigation, guidelines, immunisation recommendations, interstate and international quarantine
State and local health departmentsNotifiable-disease reporting, contact tracing, isolation and quarantine orders, school vaccine rules, environmental health
State medical boardsLicense and discipline physicians

Public-health law rests on the states' police power to protect the population. The Supreme Court upheld compulsory vaccination in Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905). Every state requires certain vaccines for school entry and allows medical exemptions; some also allow religious or personal-belief exemptions. States can order isolation (of the sick) and quarantine (of the exposed) and, for a person with infectious tuberculosis who refuses treatment, court-backed isolation; the federal government controls spread between states and from abroad.

National goals such as the Healthy People objectives, set by HHS each decade, track measurable targets (vaccination rates, tobacco use, health equity). Telehealth has widened access, but the physician generally must be licensed in the state where the patient is located during the visit; interstate compacts speed up multi-state licensing without creating a national licence.

Medicaid enrolment is year-round; marketplace enrolment needs open enrolment or a qualifying event. EMTALA requires screening and stabilisation, never a payment check first.

s23g-s0905.bodyHtml:
How clinicians and hospitals are paid shapes what they do. Each payment model rewards some behaviours and risks others; the exam asks you to predict the incentive.

Payment models

ModelHow payment worksIncentiveMain risk
Fee-for-serviceA fee for each visit, test or procedureMore servicesOveruse; fragmented care
SalaryFixed pay regardless of volumeNeutral to volumeLower productivity
CapitationFixed amount per enrolled person per month, whatever care they useKeep patients healthy; use fewer servicesUnderuse; avoiding sick patients; provider bears financial risk
Prospective payment per admission (DRG)Medicare pays a hospital a set amount per inpatient stay based on the diagnosis-related groupShorter stays, efficient careEarly discharge; "upcoding"
Bundled (episode) paymentOne payment for all care in an episode (e.g., joint replacement plus 90 days)Coordinate care, cut waste within the episodeSelecting low-risk patients; more episodes
Pay-for-performance / value-based purchasingBonuses or penalties tied to quality and cost measuresMeet the measured targetsNeglecting what is not measured

Medicare pays physicians from a fee schedule built on relative value units (physician work, practice expense and malpractice cost) multiplied by a conversion factor. The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program lowers Medicare payments, up to a capped percentage, for hospitals whose 30-day readmissions for selected conditions (such as heart failure, myocardial infarction and pneumonia) exceed the expected rate. An accountable care organisation (ACO) is a network of clinicians and hospitals that accepts responsibility for the total cost and quality of care for a defined population; if spending falls below a benchmark while quality targets are met, the ACO shares the savings.

Managed care plan types

PlanPrimary care gatekeeper/referralsOut-of-network coverage
HMOYesNone except emergencies
EPOUsually noNone except emergencies
POSYesYes, at higher cost
PPONoYes, at higher cost

Cost-sharing terms

  • Premium: what is paid to have coverage, whether or not care is used.
  • Deductible: what the patient pays each year before the plan starts sharing costs.
  • Copayment: a fixed amount per service. Coinsurance: a percentage of the allowed cost.
  • Out-of-pocket maximum: the yearly cap on the patient's in-network cost-sharing; after it is reached the plan pays 100%. Premiums do not count toward it.

Worked example (hypothetical plan): deductible 1,000, then 20% coinsurance, out-of-pocket maximum 3,000. For a 6,000 allowed bill early in the year, the patient pays 1,000 + 0.20 × 5,000 = 2,000. For a 20,000 bill, 1,000 + 0.20 × 19,000 = 4,800, which the cap reduces to 3,000. High-deductible plans have lower premiums and are often paired with a tax-advantaged health savings account.

Market failures

Moral hazard: once insured, people use more care (and may take fewer precautions) because they no longer pay the full price; cost-sharing is the usual counter. Adverse selection: people who expect to need care are more likely to buy insurance, so the pool becomes sicker, premiums rise, healthier people leave, and the market can spiral; mandates, subsidies, employer group coverage and open-enrolment windows counter it.

Moral hazard is about behaviour after getting insurance; adverse selection is about who chooses to buy it.

Economic evaluation

TypeOutcome unitUse
Cost-minimisationOutcomes shown to be equalPick the cheaper option
Cost-effectivenessNatural units (cases found, life-years)Cost per unit of effect
Cost-utilityQuality-adjusted life-years (QALYs)Compare across diseases
Cost-benefitMoney (benefits valued in currency)Net benefit; is it worth doing at all

The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio is ICER = (costnew − costold) ÷ (effectnew − effectold). If a new treatment costs 12,000 more and adds 0.4 QALY, ICER = 30,000 per QALY. An option that costs more and does less is dominated; one that costs less and does more dominates. One QALY is one year in perfect health; two years at a utility of 0.5 also equal one QALY.

Why US spending is high and price transparency

The US spends far more per person than other high-income countries without using more physician visits or hospital days; most of the gap reflects higher prices (for hospital care, physician services and drugs), plus high administrative costs and rapid uptake of costly technology. Policy responses include rules requiring hospitals to publish their prices, the No Surprises Act (which protects patients from surprise out-of-network bills for emergency care and for out-of-network clinicians at in-network facilities, and gives uninsured or self-pay patients a right to a good-faith cost estimate), and the shift from volume to value-based payment.

Predict the incentive from the payment: paid per service → more services; paid per person → fewer services; paid per stay → shorter stays; paid per episode → leaner episodes.

s23g-s1101.bodyHtml:
Step 2 CK rarely asks for a definition on its own. It hands you a quality report, a county health profile or a patient's question and asks what to conclude or do. The skill is choosing the right measure, spotting the wrong denominator and recognising when a change in numbers reflects something other than a change in health.

Choosing the right frequency measure

SituationMeasure to useWhy
Comparing central line infections between ICUs with different lengths of stayInfections per 1,000 catheter-daysExposure time differs; a rate per patient would penalise units with long stays
Planning clinic capacity for people living with a chronic diseasePrevalence (and the absolute count)Existing cases drive visits and drug use
Deciding whether a prevention programme is workingIncidencePrevention changes the arrival of new cases
Comparing death rates between a retirement county and a college townAge-adjusted ratesCrude rates mostly reflect the age structure
Describing how lethal an outbreak strain isCase-fatality proportionDeaths among those who have the disease
Household spread of an infectionSecondary attack rateNew cases among susceptible contacts only

Why numbers change without a change in health

  • Diagnostic or definitional change: a lower threshold, a new more sensitive test or a broader reporting definition raises recorded incidence and prevalence overnight.
  • Treatment effects: longer survival without cure raises prevalence; a cure lowers prevalence; neither changes incidence directly.
  • Population change: ageing raises crude rates of chronic disease; in-migration of affected people raises prevalence.
  • Small numbers: with a few hundred births a year, one or two extra infant deaths change the rate dramatically. Pool several years or report a confidence interval before acting.

A county infant mortality rate that "doubled" from 3 to 6 deaths among about 1,000 births is well within chance variation. The expected next step is to aggregate several years and review individual deaths, not to declare a crisis or attribute the change to one cause.

Standardisation in practice

When a hospital, region or occupational group is compared with a benchmark, the report usually gives an observed-to-expected ratio (the SMR or its hospital equivalent). Expected events come from applying reference rates to the group's own case mix, so a ratio above 1 means more events than expected for that mix. A small hospital's ratio has a wide confidence interval; a ratio of 1.3 with an interval of 0.8–2.1 does not show excess mortality.

Vital statistics and what they point to

Infant mortality splits into neonatal (under 28 days) and postneonatal (28 days to under 1 year) components with different causes and different fixes.

Rising componentLeading causes to suspectInterventions that address it
NeonatalPreterm birth, low birthweight, congenital anomalies, intrapartum complicationsAccess to prenatal care, antenatal corticosteroids for threatened preterm birth, delivery of high-risk pregnancies at hospitals with appropriate neonatal care
PostneonatalSudden unexpected infant death (often unsafe sleep), infections, injuriesSafe-sleep education (back to sleep, own firm flat surface, no soft bedding), immunisation, injury prevention, home visiting

Health status at the bedside

Functional status determines what support a patient needs. Loss of instrumental activities (managing medications, finances, shopping, cooking) with intact basic ADLs usually calls for targeted support such as medication packaging, a home health nurse, help with finances or meals and an evaluation for cognitive impairment, rather than a move to a nursing facility. Loss of basic ADLs (bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring) means hands-on care is needed.

When a patient rates their health as fair or poor despite reassuring examination findings, take it seriously: self-rated health independently predicts mortality and functional decline. Ask what lies behind the rating; it often uncovers depression, pain, unrecognised functional loss, financial stress or a symptom the patient has not mentioned.

When judging whether a treatment helps patients live better, choose a patient-reported outcome measure (a validated function or quality-of-life scale) over laboratory or imaging surrogates. When setting public health priorities around premature death, rank causes by YPLL, which puts injuries, overdose and suicide near the top, rather than by death counts, which favour diseases of old age.

For any table in a stem, check three things before answering: the denominator (people, person-time, live births), the time frame, and whether the groups being compared differ in age. Most wrong conclusions in these items come from one of the three.

s23g-s1102.bodyHtml:
At Step 2 CK depth, survival curves and impact measures are tools for counselling a patient and for judging a trial report. Questions ask what a result means for the person in front of you, which conclusion an abstract supports and how to express a benefit in absolute terms.

Explaining survival figures to patients

  • Median survival is the time by which half the people in the study had died; half lived longer, often much longer. It is not a prediction of the individual patient's lifespan.
  • Survival at a time point (for example, "about 6 in 10 people were alive at 2 years") is usually easier for patients to understand than a hazard ratio.
  • Conditional survival: once a patient has survived for some time, the chance of surviving a further period is S(later) ÷ S(now). If 2-year survival is 0.50 and 4-year survival is 0.40, a patient alive at 2 years has a 0.40 ÷ 0.50 = 80% chance of reaching 4 years, much better than the 40% quoted at diagnosis.
  • The tail of a curve that rests on a handful of patients at risk is unreliable; a plateau there may not be real.

Judging a survival comparison in an abstract

Look forWhat it tells you
Hazard ratio and its 95% CIDirection and precision of the relative effect; a CI that crosses 1.0 is not significant
Shape of the curvesWhen benefit or harm happens; crossing curves mean the effect changes over time and a single HR is a poor summary
Numbers at riskHow much data supports each time point
Absolute survival at clinically meaningful timesThe basis for the NNT and for patient counselling
Censoring patternHeavy or uneven drop-out (especially if sicker patients leave) can bias the curves

A hazard ratio of 0.75 does not mean "25% of patients are cured" or "25% fewer patients die by the end of the trial". It means that, at any moment during follow-up, patients still at risk in the treatment group had about a 25% lower event rate. Translate it into absolute numbers at a stated time before counselling.

Early harm, later benefit

Operations and other up-front treatments often have early procedural mortality followed by long-term benefit. Their survival curves start below the comparison arm and cross it later. An overall hazard ratio near 1.0 in such a trial does not mean "no effect"; it averages an early harm and a late benefit. The right conclusion is time-specific: higher risk of death in the first months, more people alive at the end. Patients weigh these differently, which is why shared decision-making matters most here.

Absolute effects: NNT, NNH and impact

Worked example: 5-year survival is 64% with treatment and 54% without. Absolute risk reduction (in deaths) = 46% − 36% = 10 percentage points, NNT = 10 over 5 years. If 3% of treated patients have a serious bleed compared with 1% of untreated patients, NNH = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50. "Treat 10 people for 5 years to keep one more alive; one in 50 treated has an extra serious bleed" is the sentence a patient can use.

For a community, the population attributable fraction answers which exposure to target. A common exposure with a modest RR often causes more cases than a rare exposure with a large RR. For a health system, cost-effectiveness analysis lists strategies by cost and QALYs: drop any dominated strategy (costs more, gains fewer QALYs), then compute incremental ratios between the remaining strategies in order of cost. Ranking conditions for a disease-control budget uses DALYs, which bring disabling, rarely fatal conditions such as depression and chronic pain into view.

Every number you give a patient should be absolute, time-bound and framed both ways ("about 90 in 100 are alive at 5 years with treatment and 80 in 100 without"). Relative figures alone overstate benefit and should not be the only figures given.

content.text: At Step 2 CK depth, survival curves and impact measures are tools for counselling a patient and for judging a trial report. Questions ask what a result means for the person in front of you, which conclusion an abstract supports and how to express a benefit in absolute terms.
is the time by which half the people in the study had died; half lived longer, often much longer. It is not a prediction of the individual patient's lifespan.
(for example, "about 6 in 10 people were alive at 2 years") is usually easier for patients to understand than a hazard ratio.

: once a patient has survived for some time, the chance of surviving a further period is S(later) ÷ S(now). If 2-year survival is 0.50 and 4-year survival is 0.40, a patient alive at 2 years has a 0.40 ÷ 0.50 = 80% chance of reaching 4 years, much better than the 40% quoted at diagnosis.
The tail of a curve that rests on a handful of patients at risk is unreliable; a plateau there may not be real.
Judging a survival comparison in an abstract
Direction and precision of the relative effect; a CI that crosses 1.0 is not significant
When benefit or harm happens; crossing curves mean the effect changes over time and a single HR is a poor summary
How much data supports each time point
Absolute survival at clinically meaningful times
The basis for the NNT and for patient counselling
Heavy or uneven drop-out (especially if sicker patients leave) can bias the curves

A hazard ratio of 0.75 does not mean "25% of patients are cured" or "25% fewer patients die by the end of the trial". It means that, at any moment during follow-up, patients still at risk in the treatment group had about a 25% lower event rate. Translate it into absolute numbers at a stated time before counselling.

Operations and other up-front treatments often have early procedural mortality followed by long-term benefit. Their survival curves start below the comparison arm and cross it later. An overall hazard ratio near 1.0 in such a trial does not mean "no effect"; it averages an early harm and a late benefit. The right conclusion is time-specific: higher risk of death in the first months, more people alive at the end. Patients weigh these differently, which is why shared decision-making matters most here.
Absolute effects: NNT, NNH and impact

Worked example: 5-year survival is 64% with treatment and 54% without. Absolute risk reduction (in deaths) = 46% − 36% = 10 percentage points, NNT = 10 over 5 years. If 3% of treated patients have a serious bleed compared with 1% of untreated patients, NNH = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50. "Treat 10 people for 5 years to keep one more alive; one in 50 treated has an extra serious bleed" is the sentence a patient can use.

s23g-s1103.bodyHtml:
Clinicians are the front end of surveillance. Step 2 CK items test whether you report what must be reported, recognise a real signal, and support the health department's investigation without overreacting or delaying control measures.

Reporting

  • Reporting a notifiable disease to the local or state health department is a legal duty of the clinician (and the laboratory). It does not need the patient's consent, and the HIPAA Privacy Rule expressly permits disclosure to public health authorities for this purpose.
  • Tell the patient that the report will be made and why; reassure them that health departments keep reports confidential and use them to protect others, including through contact tracing.
  • Some conditions must be reported immediately by phone on suspicion, before laboratory confirmation (for example, suspected measles). The list and timelines are set by each state, so check the local list; the principle that reportable conditions are reported does not vary.
  • An unusual cluster (several patients with the same unusual illness) should be reported even if the condition is not on the list.

Is this an outbreak?

Before mobilising, confirm that the excess is real.

Apparent rise caused byClue
A new or more sensitive laboratory test (for example, a multiplex PCR panel replacing culture)Rise begins when the test was introduced, spread across unrelated patients, often with organisms not linked by typing
A change in case definition or reporting rulesStep change in counts at the date of the change
A larger catchment population (a new clinic, a seasonal influx)Rates per population are stable even though counts rise
Laboratory contamination (pseudo-outbreak)Positive cultures without clinical illness; one batch, instrument or technician
Syndromic system artefactChanges in triage coding or software; no matching rise in confirmed diagnoses

A syndromic surveillance alarm (for example, a jump in emergency department visits for vomiting in one postcode) is a prompt to verify: review the records, contact the clinicians and look for confirmed diagnoses. Public announcements or closures are not the first step.

Working an outbreak

  1. Case definition: clinical features plus time, place and person. Start broad to find cases (sensitive); tighten (confirmed, probable, possible) for analysis. Never build the suspected exposure into it.
  2. Line list and epidemic curve: the curve's shape suggests the mode; the timing from exposure to the peak suggests the agent.
  3. Analytic study: retrospective cohort for a closed group (a wedding, a ward, a cruise); case-control for open community outbreaks.
  4. Control measures as soon as a probable source is identified: remove the food, close the pool, issue a boil-water advisory, exclude ill food handlers. Waiting for a completed analytic study while exposure continues is wrong.
  5. Communication with clinicians, the public and the facility.

Food-specific attack rate tables

Calculate, for each item, attack rate among eaters and among non-eaters, then the ratio. The vehicle combines a high attack rate among eaters, a low attack rate among non-eaters and an explanation for most cases. Check the arithmetic carefully: each row's ill eaters plus ill non-eaters must equal the total ill.

Worked example: 50 of 60 people who ate the custard became ill (83%) versus 5 of 40 who did not (12.5%), a ratio of about 6.7. Of 90 people who drank the punch, 52 became ill (58%), compared with 3 of 10 who did not (30%), a ratio under 2; most of the ill drank punch only because almost everyone did.

Two common errors: choosing the food with the most ill eaters, and treating a point-source outbreak's secondary cases (household members who fell ill days later and did not attend the event) as evidence against the source. Secondary cases are expected after enteric point-source outbreaks such as norovirus.

Step 2 CK default sequence for any suspected outbreak in your practice: confirm the diagnosis, report to the health department, protect people from continuing exposure, then support the investigation. Ethics consults, legal advice and media statements are not part of the first steps.

s23g-s1104.bodyHtml:
Transmission questions on Step 2 CK ask what to do now: which room and which mask for this patient, who needs prophylaxis, what to tell a family, and what a change in the reproduction number means for a community.

Choosing precautions on admission

Precautions are started on suspicion, before confirmation, and are layered on standard precautions for every patient.

PresentationPrecautionsNotes
Cough, weight loss, upper-lobe cavity; suspected pulmonary tuberculosisAirborne: negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room, N95 respirator for staffContinue until tuberculosis is excluded or the patient is no longer infectious on effective treatment
Fever, cough, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash; suspected measlesAirborneReport immediately; check the immunity of exposed staff and patients
Vesicular rash in several dermatomes or generalised (varicella or disseminated zoster)Airborne plus contactLocalised zoster in an immunocompetent patient: standard precautions with the lesions covered
Suspected bacterial meningitisDropletUntil 24 hours of effective antibiotics
Influenza, pertussisDropletSurgical mask within close range
Diarrhoea from Clostridioides difficileContactHand washing with soap and water; sporicidal cleaning of the room
MRSA or VRE colonisation or infection (per facility policy)ContactDedicated equipment

Post-exposure measures

  • Close contacts of meningococcal disease (household members, roommates, people directly exposed to oral secretions) receive chemoprophylaxis as soon as possible: rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone. Casual contacts (classmates in a large lecture hall) do not.
  • Measles exposure in a susceptible person: MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure can prevent or modify disease; immune globulin within 6 days is used for people who cannot receive the vaccine (infants under 6 months, pregnant women without evidence of immunity, severely immunocompromised people) or who present after 72 hours.
  • Newborn of a mother positive for hepatitis B surface antigen: hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin within 12 hours of birth, then completion of the vaccine series and post-vaccination testing.
  • Isolation and quarantine: the sick or infected are isolated; exposed but well contacts may be quarantined (restricted) for about one incubation period. Home quarantine is usually advised by the health department, which can enforce it when needed.

Chemoprophylaxis or vaccination after exposure is for defined close contacts, not everyone who shared a building. Mass prophylaxis of a whole campus or school is a public health department decision for unusual situations, not the default next step.

Reading Rt and herd immunity for a community

Health departments report the effective reproduction number. Rt above 1 means each case is generating more than one new case and the epidemic is growing; below 1, it is shrinking, though cases continue until it fades out. Relaxing measures can push Rt back above 1 because R0 has not changed. For a vaccine-preventable disease, the coverage needed to stop sustained spread is (1 − 1/R0) ÷ vaccine effectiveness. Local clusters of unvaccinated people (a school or a religious community) can sustain outbreaks even when national coverage exceeds the threshold, so outbreak response focuses on catch-up vaccination of the susceptible group.

Vertical transmission

Prenatal screening for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B in every pregnancy exists because effective interventions in pregnancy, at delivery and in the newborn prevent most mother-to-child transmission: antiretroviral therapy for the mother and prophylaxis for the infant (HIV), penicillin (syphilis) and the newborn vaccine plus immune globulin (hepatitis B).

Hand hygiene and carriers in daily practice

Alcohol-based hand rub is the default before and after every patient contact because it is faster and better tolerated than washing; washing with soap and water is needed when hands are visibly soiled and when caring for patients with C. difficile or norovirus, whose spores or particles resist alcohol. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Healthy carriers matter in the workplace: a food handler who still sheds Salmonella Typhi months after recovery, or a health care worker colonised with an outbreak strain, can sustain spread without ever looking ill, so exclusion and clearance rules for these workers are set by the health department and the employer's occupational health service.

If you are unsure which precaution applies, start the stricter one while the diagnosis is confirmed. Removing a precaution is easy; undoing an exposure of a ward is not.

s23g-s1105.bodyHtml:
Step 2 CK turns demography and prevention into decisions: which services a clinic should build for the population it serves, how to read a rise in case counts, which preventive measure fits a patient's stage of disease, and when to say no to a test that does not help.

From population structure to services

Population featureImplication for care
Wide base (many infants and young children, many women of reproductive age), e.g. a recently resettled refugee communityPrenatal care, well-child visits, catch-up immunisation, nutrition, contraception
Bulge at 18–24 years, e.g. a university townSexual and reproductive health (contraception, chlamydia and gonorrhoea screening of sexually active young women), mental health, alcohol and injury prevention
Narrow base, large 65+ and 85+ groupsChronic disease management, falls prevention, dementia care, medication review, home and long-term care, advance care planning
Excess of women at the oldest agesMore widowed older women living alone; osteoporosis and functional support needs

An ageing population raises the number of people with chronic disease even when age-specific risk is unchanged. Projecting future caseload means applying current age-specific rates to the projected age structure, not scaling today's total by population growth. Worked example: dementia prevalence of 2% at 65–74 years, 8% at 75–84 and 25% at 85+ applied to 20,000, 10,000 and 4,000 people gives 400 + 800 + 1,000 = 2,200 cases; if the older groups grow to 24,000, 15,000 and 8,000, the same rates give 480 + 1,200 + 2,000 = 3,680, a rise of about 67%, although the 65+ population grew by only about 38%.

If crude incidence of a cancer rises but the age-adjusted incidence is flat, the right conclusion is population ageing, and the right action is to plan capacity, not to launch an environmental cluster investigation.

Matching the intervention to the stage

  • Susceptible, unexposed: vaccination due for age (for example, recombinant zoster vaccine from age 50; HPV vaccination routinely at 11–12 years), counselling, pre-exposure prophylaxis where indicated.
  • Exposed, not yet ill: post-exposure prophylaxis, still primary prevention; for example, rabies immune globulin plus vaccine after a bat exposure that cannot be ruled out (including a bat found in the room of a person who was asleep) when the bat is not available for testing.
  • Asymptomatic, disease possible: screening recommended for the patient's age and risk (USPSTF grade A or B services).
  • Established disease: rehabilitation and measures to prevent complications and recurrence (tertiary in epidemiologic terms).
  • Any stage: quaternary prevention, avoiding tests and treatments whose harms outweigh benefits.

When the answer is "not this test"

Quaternary prevention and good screening practice often require declining a request kindly. Examples where evidence shows harm or no benefit for average-risk, asymptomatic adults include screening for ovarian cancer and routine imaging for acute low back pain without red flags. The best response explains the reasoning, addresses the worry behind the request, offers what does help and keeps the door open; it neither orders the test to keep the patient happy nor dismisses the concern.

Population strategy decisions

When a health department with limited money must choose, the prevention paradox applies: most cardiovascular events, strokes and many injuries arise from the large group at moderate risk. Policies that shift the whole distribution (lower sodium in processed foods, smoke-free laws, safer road design) usually prevent more events than programmes confined to the highest-risk few, though both strategies complement each other. Screening programmes should be judged by disease-specific mortality in the population, not by survival measured from diagnosis, which lead time and overdiagnosis inflate.

For a "most appropriate preventive measure" question, first place the patient on the natural history (healthy, exposed, preclinical, clinical), then choose the evidence-based measure for that point; a measure aimed at a different stage is the distractor.

s23g-s1201.bodyHtml:
Step 2 CK rarely asks you to name a design in the abstract. It asks which study would answer a clinician's or health department's question, what a published report allows you to tell a patient, or what to do when you see something unexpected. Start from the question, not the design.

Clinical questionBest-fitting designWhy
Is this unusual presentation or reaction new?Case report or case seriesFast description; raises a hypothesis
How many of my patients have this now?Cross-sectional surveyGives prevalence at one time
What causes this rare disease?Case-control studyEfficient for rare outcomes and many exposures
What does this uncommon exposure do?Cohort studyEfficient for rare exposures and several outcomes
What triggers this acute event?Case-crossover studyEach case is his or her own control
Does a population-level factor matter?Ecological study (to raise the question)Uses routine group data
Does this treatment work?Randomized trial (or a systematic review of trials)Randomization controls confounding

When you see something new

A clinician who suspects a new adverse drug reaction should report it to the regulator's adverse-event reporting program (in the United States, the FDA's voluntary program for health professionals and the public). Proof of causation is not required; a plausible time relation and improvement when the drug is stopped are reasons enough. Reports from many clinicians form the signal that prompts analytical studies and label changes. Writing up a case for a journal is a separate step that needs the patient's written consent for publication and the removal of every identifying detail that is not essential.

What descriptive evidence lets you say to a patient

When a patient brings a case report or a striking anecdote, acknowledge the interest, explain in plain words that one person's improvement can have many explanations (natural fluctuation, regression to the mean, other changes, placebo response), and move to the controlled evidence. From a case series you can usefully tell patients what a reaction looks like and when it tends to occur; you cannot tell them how likely it is, because a series has no denominator. If the authors reported only selected cases, even the description may mislead.

Ecological and cross-sectional claims in the news

Patients often meet ecological findings ("countries that eat more X have less Y"). The honest answer is that group-level correlations do not show that the individuals with the exposure are the ones with the better outcome, and that such data justify a study, not a change in treatment. Cross-sectional surveys are similar in one respect: because exposure and outcome are measured together, they cannot show which came first.

Reading the variables

In any design, identify the independent variable (exposure, predictor or intervention), the dependent variable (outcome) and the covariates adjusted for as potential confounders. In observational studies the adjustment is only as good as the confounders that were measured; unmeasured ones remain.

Interpreting a cohort result for a patient

Translate ratios into absolute terms. If a cohort shows 6% of exposed and 4% of unexposed people develop an outcome, the relative risk is 1.5, but the absolute difference is 2 percentage points: about 2 extra cases per 100 exposed people. Patients understand natural frequencies ("6 in 100 versus 4 in 100") better than ratios, and absolute differences make small relative effects look appropriately small. Add the caveat that observational associations can reflect confounding.

Trap: "The study showed an association, so I should advise everyone to change" skips the step of asking which design produced the association. Ecological, cross-sectional and case-control findings carry more risk of bias than cohort findings, and all of them carry more than randomized trials.

Trap: "do a randomized trial" is wrong whenever the exposure is harmful or cannot be assigned (smoking, occupational toxins, pregnancy exposures). Observational designs are then the appropriate, not the inferior, choice.

Pearl: for "most appropriate study design" questions, first ask what is rare. Rare outcome → case-control. Rare exposure → cohort. Neither rare and you want current burden → cross-sectional. A treatment question → randomized trial.
