s23g-s1802.bodyHtml:
Step 2 CK misconduct items put you in the room when something improper happens: a resident asks you to bill a higher level, a representative offers a trip, a classmate cheats, a patient asks you out, an attending makes sexual comments. The best answer is direct, honest and proportionate: decline or correct what is wrong, protect patients and learners, and report through the proper channel when the problem is serious or repeated.

A step ladder for responding

SeriousnessExamplesUsual first action
Minor, one-off, correctableA note copied forward with an outdated findingRaise it directly with the person; ask that it be corrected
Serious or repeatedBilling for visits that did not happen; falsified research data; cheating on an examinationReport to the supervisor, course director, compliance or research-integrity office
Threat to patients; institution will not actSexual contact with patients; repeated harmState medical board (and the institution)

Students and residents are protected from retaliation when they report in good faith, and most institutions have anonymous routes. "Ignore it", "post it online" and "confront the person in front of patients" are wrong answers.

Billing integrity

Bill only for what was done and documented, at the level the documentation supports. Upcoding, billing for services not rendered, and billing a supervising physician's service that did not occur are fraud. If you find that your practice has submitted improper claims, stop the practice, involve the compliance officer, and correct and repay the claims; an identified overpayment from a federal program must be returned promptly. Chart items may show an audit table: compare what was documented with what was billed, line by line.

"It's what everyone does" and "the documentation template generated that level" are not defences. Neither is "the patient benefited". The physician who signs a claim is responsible for it.

Industry, gifts and conflicts of interest

Decline cash, gift cards, paid leisure travel, honoraria for simply attending, and payments tied to prescribing or device use. Payments made to induce use of federally reimbursed products can violate the Anti-Kickback Statute. Legitimate consulting for real work at fair market value is allowed but is disclosed: manufacturers report such payments to the federal Open Payments database, which anyone can search. If a patient asks whether you have ties to a company, answer honestly, explain how you choose treatments, and offer alternatives. A surgeon with a financial relationship with a device maker discloses it to the patient and the institution and picks devices on clinical evidence.

Boundaries with patients

When a patient expresses romantic interest, decline kindly and clearly, keep the clinical relationship professional, and continue caring for the patient if that remains workable. Avoid shame: the boundary is the physician's responsibility, not the patient's fault. If the physician has developed feelings that may affect judgment, the right step is to transfer care, not to start a relationship. Use chaperones for intimate examinations and explain each step. When a patient discloses sexual misconduct by another physician, listen, believe and support them, tell them it was wrong and not their fault, and offer to help them report it to the state medical board.

Honesty in records, training and research

  • Never document findings you did not obtain; never write a note, form or excuse that is false (a fake sick note for a friend, a disability form for someone you have not examined).
  • Introduce yourself with your real role. A student says "I'm a medical student" even if a patient calls them doctor.
  • Cheating and plagiarism are reported through the school's honour or professionalism system.
  • Fabricated or falsified research data are reported to the principal investigator or the institution's research-integrity office; the data must not be published.

Harassment and discrimination

Sexual harassment of students or staff (comments, unwanted touching, quid pro quo pressure) is misconduct and is covered by federal civil rights law in education and employment. A resident who hears about it from a student should listen, respect the student's wishes as far as safety allows, explain the confidential and formal reporting routes (the school's mistreatment office or Title IX coordinator), and help them use them. The resident should not promise total secrecy if patients or others are at risk.

In misconduct items the key is often the most specific honest action: "I can't bill that level because the note doesn't support it" beats both silent compliance and a vague threat to report.

Licence and scope in a mobile practice

For telehealth, the physician generally must be licensed in the state where the patient is during the visit. A physician whose licence has lapsed must stop practising until it is renewed. Doing procedures beyond one's training, even to help a patient, is beyond scope; refer or seek supervision.

s23g-s1803.bodyHtml:
Referral items on Step 2 CK ask what to do when a patient needs something you cannot or will not provide, when you want to end a relationship, or when care moves between clinicians. The answer must keep the patient safe and keep their options open: no gap in care, no delay that closes an option, no discrimination, and no profit from the referral.

Conscientious objection in practice

A physician may decline to provide a legal service that conflicts with sincere moral beliefs. Ethical guidance attaches duties to that freedom:

  • Tell in advance. Let patients know when they establish care (or when a request is likely) which services are not offered, so they are not surprised at the moment of need.
  • Inform fully. Give accurate, unbiased information about all options, including the one you will not provide.
  • Refer in time. Arrange or facilitate a timely referral to a clinician who provides the service, with records.
  • Do not obstruct or shame. No lectures, no delays, no withholding of information.
  • Emergencies come first. Give urgent care when no one else can.

Objection applies to actions, not to a category of patient. A clinician may step away from a lawful act such as deactivating a cardiac device at a capacitated patient's request, provided a colleague does it promptly; they may not refuse to care for the patient at all.

"Refer the patient" is not always the answer. If the request is for usual care that the physician can provide and the physician wants to avoid the patient because of HIV status, disability, race, religion, sexual orientation or gender identity, the answer is to provide the care. Standard precautions protect clinicians; refusing a patient with HIV violates the ADA.

Ending the relationship

Reasons that can justify ending a relationship include threats or violence toward staff, persistent abusive behaviour after a warning, fraud, and sustained non-adherence that makes safe care impossible after it has been addressed. The steps: discuss the problem first where safe, send written notice with an end date that gives a reasonable time to find a new physician, continue to provide urgent care and refills until then, offer help finding a new physician, and transfer records with the patient's authorisation. Ending care during an acute illness, or in a place where no other physician is available, is abandonment.

Safety in the moment

If a patient becomes threatening in clinic, leave the room, keep the exit clear, and call security; de-escalate only if it is safe. Do not try to restrain alone or argue. Emergency care is still provided with security present.

Second opinions and patient-requested referrals

RequestBest response
Second opinion before major surgery or cancer treatmentSupport it warmly, send records and imaging, offer names
A referral that does not seem indicatedExplore the worry behind it first; then explain your reasoning, and refer if the patient still wishes and it is reasonable
Something beyond your trainingRefer, and stay involved for coordination

Genetic counselling

A personal or family history that suggests a hereditary cancer syndrome (for example several relatives with breast or ovarian cancer, cancers at young ages, or a known familial mutation) prompts a risk assessment and referral for genetic counselling, which then guides testing. Counselling covers what a result means for the patient and relatives, the possibility of uncertain results, and the limits of GINA (health insurance and employment are protected; life, disability and long-term-care insurance are not).

Self-referral and money

A physician who owns part of an imaging centre, laboratory or physical-therapy practice may not refer Medicare patients there for those designated health services unless a Stark exception applies; telling the patient about the ownership does not fix the problem. The usual answer is to refer to a facility without a financial relationship. Payments for referrals (fee splitting, kickbacks) are never acceptable.

Transitions and continuity

Care breaks down at handoffs. At discharge or transfer, communicate directly with the receiving clinician, send a clear summary with pending results and who will follow them up, reconcile medications, and book the follow-up appointment before the patient leaves. HIPAA allows sharing records with another clinician for treatment without the patient's written authorisation.

When a referral answer looks right, check for the gap: does someone own the patient's care until the next clinician takes over? An option that is correct in principle but leaves the patient on their own (a list of names and no interim care) is usually the trap.

Culturally responsive care on Step 2 CK is about the next sentence you say. The keyed answer asks the patient about their beliefs and preferences, uses a professional interpreter, accommodates requests that do not cause harm, negotiates when a practice carries risk, and fixes systems when data show unequal care. Vignettes describe individual people; no group membership predicts what a particular patient believes.

Asking before assuming

Open questions elicit the patient's explanatory model: "What do you call this problem?" "What do you think caused it?" "What have you been using to treat it?" "What are you most worried about?" "What would you like from today's visit?" The answers show where the patient's plan and the medical plan already agree and where they need negotiation.

Family-centred decisions and truth-telling

When a family asks that a patient not be told a diagnosis, do not simply comply and do not override them by going straight to the patient with the news. Acknowledge the family's protective wish, then ask the patient, privately, how much they want to know and who they want involved. If the patient wishes to delegate, that is an exercise of autonomy: share information with the chosen person, document the preference, suggest naming them as a health care agent, and check from time to time whether the patient still wants it that way.

A capacitated patient's own wishes outrank a relative's request. But "tell the patient everything immediately, whatever the family says" is also wrong; first ask the patient what they want to know.

Religious practices in clinical decisions

ScenarioBest approach
An adult with capacity refuses transfusion before elective surgeryRespect the refusal; ask which products and techniques are acceptable (cell salvage, volume expanders, some fractions vary by person); optimise hemoglobin before surgery; document
A child needs a transfusion urgently and the parents refuseGive the life-saving transfusion; seek a court order when time allows in non-emergency cases
A patient plans to fast during daylight hoursAsk about the plan, adjust medication timing and doses together, explain warning signs that should end the fast
A request for a clinician of the same genderAccommodate when possible; in an emergency explain why you must proceed, with a chaperone
End-of-life rituals at the bedsideAccommodate within safety and infection control; involve the chaplain

Language and communication access

Use a trained medical interpreter for any important discussion with a patient who has limited English proficiency: consent, new diagnoses, discharge instructions. Family members filter and soften; children should never interpret. Under the ADA, a Deaf patient who uses sign language is entitled to a qualified interpreter at no cost to the patient. For a patient with an intellectual disability, speak directly to the patient in plain language, allow time, and involve the support person as the patient wishes.

LGBTQ+ inclusive care

Ask names and pronouns and use them. Ask about sexual partners without presuming their genders, and about practices relevant to testing (which sites to swab). Screening follows anatomy: a transgender man with a cervix is offered cervical cancer screening on the usual schedule, with an explanation of each step and attention to comfort. Keep questions relevant to the clinical problem; curiosity is not a reason to ask about surgeries.

Immigrants and refugees

Patients may avoid care for fear that information will be shared with immigration authorities. Explain that medical information is confidential and that emergency care does not depend on immigration status or insurance. Ask about trauma gently, offer interpreters, and connect patients with social work and community resources for coverage and follow-up.

Homelessness and social needs

Screen for housing, food, transport and phone access, then design the plan around them: simpler regimens, medicines that do not need refrigeration where possible, walk-in follow-up, and social work referral. Ask "What would make this plan hard to follow?" rather than labelling the patient non-adherent.

Implicit bias and disparities

When audit data show that a group receives less analgesia, fewer referrals, or slower care at the same severity, the effective fixes are system-level: standardised protocols and order sets, prompt pain reassessment, stratified audit and feedback, and accountability. Individual bias training alone has limited effect. Equally, tools with built-in racial adjustments should be replaced when race-free tools exist, as happened with the kidney-function equation.

Four moves solve most cultural items: ask (beliefs and preferences), interpret (professional interpreter), accommodate (any harmless request), adapt the system (protocols and audit for disparities).

content.text: Culturally responsive care on Step 2 CK is about the next sentence you say. The keyed answer asks the patient about their beliefs and preferences, uses a professional interpreter, accommodates requests that do not cause harm, negotiates when a practice carries risk, and fixes systems when data show unequal care. Vignettes describe individual people; no group membership predicts what a particular patient believes.

Open questions elicit the patient's explanatory model: "What do you call this problem?" "What do you think caused it?" "What have you been using to treat it?" "What are you most worried about?" "What would you like from today's visit?" The answers show where the patient's plan and the medical plan already agree and where they need negotiation.

When a family asks that a patient not be told a diagnosis, do not simply comply and do not override them by going straight to the patient with the news. Acknowledge the family's protective wish, then ask the patient, privately, how much they want to know and who they want involved. If the patient wishes to delegate, that is an exercise of autonomy: share information with the chosen person, document the preference, suggest naming them as a health care agent, and check from time to time whether the patient still wants it that way.
A capacitated patient's own wishes outrank a relative's request. But "tell the patient everything immediately, whatever the family says" is also wrong; first ask the patient what they want to know.
An adult with capacity refuses transfusion before elective surgery
Respect the refusal; ask which products and techniques are acceptable (cell salvage, volume expanders, some fractions vary by person); optimise hemoglobin before surgery; document
A child needs a transfusion urgently and the parents refuse
Give the life-saving transfusion; seek a court order when time allows in non-emergency cases
A patient plans to fast during daylight hours
Ask about the plan, adjust medication timing and doses together, explain warning signs that should end the fast
A request for a clinician of the same gender
Accommodate when possible; in an emergency explain why you must proceed, with a chaperone
Accommodate within safety and infection control; involve the chaplain

Use a trained medical interpreter for any important discussion with a patient who has limited English proficiency: consent, new diagnoses, discharge instructions. Family members filter and soften; children should never interpret. Under the ADA, a Deaf patient who uses sign language is entitled to a qualified interpreter at no cost to the patient. For a patient with an intellectual disability, speak directly to the patient in plain language, allow time, and involve the support person as the patient wishes.

Ask names and pronouns and use them. Ask about sexual partners without presuming their genders, and about practices relevant to testing (which sites to swab). Screening follows anatomy: a transgender man with a cervix is offered cervical cancer screening on the usual schedule, with an explanation of each step and attention to comfort. Keep questions relevant to the clinical problem; curiosity is not a reason to ask about surgeries.

Patients may avoid care for fear that information will be shared with immigration authorities. Explain that medical information is confidential and that emergency care does not depend on immigration status or insurance. Ask about trauma gently, offer interpreters, and connect patients with social work and community resources for coverage and follow-up.

Screen for housing, food, transport and phone access, then design the plan around them: simpler regimens, medicines that do not need refrigeration where possible, walk-in follow-up, and social work referral. Ask "What would make this plan hard to follow?" rather than labelling the patient non-adherent.

When audit data show that a group receives less analgesia, fewer referrals, or slower care at the same severity, the effective fixes are system-level: standardised protocols and order sets, prompt pain reassessment, stratified audit and feedback, and accountability. Individual bias training alone has limited effect. Equally, tools with built-in racial adjustments should be replaced when race-free tools exist, as happened with the kidney-function equation.
Four moves solve most cultural items: ask (beliefs and preferences), interpret (professional interpreter), accommodate (any harmless request), adapt the system (protocols and audit for disparities).

s23g-s1901.bodyHtml:
Step 2 CK turns systems thinking into ward decisions: what you say at a handoff, how you raise a concern with a senior colleague, what you check before discharge, and how you respond when a patient's real barrier is money, food or transport. The keyed answer is almost always the one that protects the patient now, uses a structured and verifiable form of communication, and fixes the gap at its source rather than working around it.

Handoffs that work

A good handoff is verbal and face-to-face (or by phone if unavoidable), happens in a quiet place, follows a standard structure and is backed by a written summary. A widely studied structure covers the illness severity (stable, watcher, unstable), a brief patient summary, a to-do list with owners and times, situational awareness with contingency plans ("if the potassium is below 3.5, give…"), and a synthesis by the receiver, who restates the key points and asks questions. The sickest patients go first and get the most time. An email, a text or a written list alone is not a handoff for an unstable patient.

Closed-loop communication and read-back

In a resuscitation, orders go to a named person ("Ana, give 1 mg of epinephrine IV"), who repeats the order, carries it out and announces when it is done. For telephone and verbal orders and for critical lab results, the receiver writes the information down and reads it back; the sender confirms. Ask for spelling of look-alike drug names and say numbers as digits ("one-five", not "fifteen" versus "fifty").

Speaking up and escalation

When any team member thinks a patient is at risk, the expected behaviour is to state the concern directly, with the facts, and to propose an action: "I'm concerned that his blood pressure has fallen to 82/50 since the last dose; I'd like to hold the next dose and have you see him now." If the concern is dismissed and the risk remains, repeat it and then escalate through the chain of command (senior resident, attending, charge nurse, rapid response team). Silence because of hierarchy, and going around the team to complain later, are both wrong answers. Questions involving interprofessional colleagues reward respect: take a pharmacist's or nurse's safety concern seriously, check it, and thank them.

Do not pick the option that quietly "documents the disagreement" or "waits until rounds" while a patient is at risk now. Address the risk first; documentation and reporting follow.

Fatigue and cognitive load

A clinician who recognises that fatigue is impairing safe work should tell the supervising physician and arrange for a colleague to take over or double-check critical tasks; residency programmes must provide back-up and a safe way home (rest or transport) after long shifts. Treat fatigue as a system hazard, not a personal failing to be hidden.

Transitions of care and medication reconciliation

Before discharge or transfer, reconcile three lists: what the patient took at home, what was given in hospital, and what is planned afterwards. Every difference must be either intentional and documented (a drug stopped for a reason, with the reason told to the patient and the next clinician) or corrected. Common traps are a home anticoagulant held for a procedure and never restarted, duplicate drugs in the same class (a hospital formulary substitute plus the home brand), and new drugs started for a temporary indication with no stop date.

Discharge elementWhy it matters
Reconciled medication list given to the patientPrevents omissions and duplications at home
Teach-back of the planChecks understanding in the patient's own words, whatever their literacy
Follow-up appointment made before leavingEarly follow-up lowers readmission
Discharge summary sent to the next clinicianPending results and changes are not lost
Direct clinician-to-clinician handoff for a facility transferThe receiving team knows what to watch for

Teach-back is not "Do you have any questions?" or "Do you understand?". It asks the patient to explain the plan, for example "To be sure I explained it well, tell me how you will take your water pill and what you'll do if your weight goes up."

Social needs and community resources

Uncontrolled chronic disease often reflects a social barrier rather than "non-compliance": unaffordable drugs, food insecurity, unstable housing, no transport, caregiving strain. Ask non-judgementally, then act: simplify and lower the cost of the regimen (generics, fewer doses), adjust treatment to food access (for example, less hypoglycaemia risk), and refer to social work, community health workers, food programmes, transport services, adult day programmes or caregiver respite. Screening without a referral pathway helps no one.

Public-health partners matter too. For a child, the school nurse needs a written medication authorisation and an asthma or seizure action plan to give treatment during the day. A child with an elevated blood lead level is reported to the health department, which investigates the home environment for the source; clinicians alone cannot remove lead paint.

Best answers in systems questions are concrete and closed-loop: a named person, a read-back, a reconciled list, a teach-back, an appointment made, a referral placed.

s23g-s1902.bodyHtml:
Step 2 CK asks you to act as a member of a quality team: pick the right measure, design the next test of change, read a run or control chart, choose the right analysis after an event, and decide what to do with data. The logic is always the same: define the aim, measure the process, test changes small, learn and spread.

Writing the aim and choosing measures

A good aim is specific, measurable and time-bound: "Reduce the median time from ED triage to first antibiotic dose for patients with suspected sepsis from 180 to under 120 minutes within 6 months." Then choose a family of measures:

MeasureSepsis project example
OutcomeIn-hospital mortality from sepsis
ProcessDoor-to-antibiotic time; percentage of patients screened at triage
StructureAntibiotics stocked in the ED dispensing cabinet
BalancingBroad-spectrum antibiotic use in patients who turn out not to have infection; C. difficile infection

Rates need the right denominator. Device-associated infections are expressed per 1,000 device-days (for example, 3 central line infections over 1,500 line-days = 2.0 per 1,000 line-days), because the risk accrues with each day a device is in place; dividing by patient-days or admissions mixes exposure with population.

Testing changes with PDSA

Start with the smallest useful test: one nurse, one shift, a few patients. Predict what will happen, collect a few data points, compare with the prediction, then adopt, adapt or abandon. Once a change works reliably in one setting, test it under other conditions (nights, another unit) before spreading it, and keep watching balancing measures. A hospital-wide launch of an untested change is the classic wrong answer; so is waiting for a randomised trial before trying anything.

"Educate staff" and "send a reminder email" are weak changes. Prefer changes built into the work: a default order set, a standing nurse-driven protocol, a stocked kit, a hard stop in the electronic record.

Reading a run chart

Plot the measure over time with the median of the baseline. Look for:

  • a shift: six or more consecutive points on one side of the median;
  • a trend: five or more consecutive points all going up or all going down;
  • an obviously extreme ("astronomical") point;
  • too few or too many runs (crossings of the median) for the number of points.

If none of these is present, the variation is consistent with chance and no conclusion about the change should be drawn yet. A point that is merely the highest so far, or two good months in a row, is not a signal.

Reading a control chart

A control chart shows the mean and control limits (about three standard deviations from it), calculated from a stable baseline. Points inside the limits without a pattern reflect common-cause variation: if overall performance is unacceptable, change the process for everyone rather than chasing individual points. A point outside a limit signals special-cause variation: investigate what was different at that time (a staffing gap, a broken device, a new drug, a data error) and respond to that cause. Reacting to common-cause noise as if it were special ("tampering") makes a process worse.

Choosing the right analysis

SituationTool
A sentinel event has happenedRoot-cause analysis by an interdisciplinary team, focused on systems, with an action plan
A new device, drug or workflow is about to startFailure mode and effects analysis
Many incident reports in many categoriesPareto chart to find the vital few
Long waits and wasted steps in a clinicLean value-stream mapping
Physicians vary in following a guidelineAudit and feedback with peer comparison

In a root-cause analysis, keep asking "why?" past the human act. "The resident ordered the wrong dose" leads to "the order set defaulted to the adult dose", which leads to "paediatric weight-based dosing is not built into the order entry system". The action plan targets the deepest fixable cause and assigns an owner, a deadline and a measure.

The answer to "what should the team do next?" after a successful small test is to test the change on a larger scale or under new conditions while continuing to measure, not to stop measuring or to roll it out everywhere at once.

s23g-s1903.bodyHtml:
When an error happens, Step 2 CK expects a fixed sequence: care for the patient first, then tell the supervising physician, then disclose to the patient, then report, then help the system learn. Each step has a typical wrong answer.

1. Treat the patient

Assess and treat the effects of the error immediately: check vital signs and examine the patient, give an antidote or reverse the effect where one exists (naloxone for opioid excess, glucose for insulin-induced hypoglycaemia), increase monitoring and get help. Disclosure, paperwork and analysis wait until the patient is safe.

2. Disclose honestly

Patients (or their surrogates, if the patient lacks capacity) should be told promptly about errors that reach them, especially those that cause or could cause harm. Good disclosure is planned with the attending and often with risk management, but the responsible physician does not hand it off to someone else or delay it until the investigation ends. It includes:

  • a plain statement of what happened, using the word "error" or "mistake" where true;
  • the known and possible effects on the patient and what is being done about them;
  • an apology and an expression of regret;
  • what will be done to prevent recurrence, and a promise to share what the review finds;
  • a contact person and time for questions.

Avoid speculation, blaming colleagues ("the nurse gave it wrong"), vague euphemisms ("an unexpected reaction") and false reassurance. Many states have apology laws that limit the use of expressions of sympathy as evidence, but honest disclosure is an ethical duty everywhere, and it is associated with more trust and fewer lawsuits, not more. A request by a senior colleague to conceal an error does not change the duty; the right response is to discuss it with that colleague and, if needed, involve the department or risk management, while ensuring the patient is told.

"Waiting until the root-cause analysis is complete" before telling the patient is wrong. Disclose what is known now and promise follow-up as more is learned.

3. Report

Enter an incident report for errors, no-harm events and near misses. Reporting is non-punitive and confidential; its purpose is to find system weaknesses, and it does not replace disclosure or documentation of the facts in the medical record (write what happened and what was done, not blame or the fact that an incident report was filed). Sentinel events are reviewed with a root-cause analysis.

Diagnostic reasoning at the bedside

When a patient's course does not fit the working diagnosis, stop and ask what else could explain it. A patient labelled "intoxicated" who stays confused must have glucose checked and be examined for head injury; a "known panic attack" with new hypoxaemia needs a work-up for pulmonary embolism. Accepting the label passed on at handoff (diagnostic momentum), anchoring on the first impression and closing the search too early are the classic biases.

Medication and procedural safety in practice

SituationSafe action
Writing a dose of insulin or heparinWrite "units" in full; use order entry with dose checks
A pharmacist flags a dose or interactionReview and change the order; thank them; report the near miss
The time-out reveals a discrepancy (side, consent, implant)Stop; resolve it with the chart, imaging and the patient before incision
Who marks the operative siteThe person doing the procedure, with the awake patient confirming
Confused older inpatient getting out of bedFind and treat the cause of delirium, frequent observation or a sitter, bed alarm, low bed; avoid restraints and sedatives where possible
Central line no longer neededRemove it; review line necessity daily
Bed-bound patientReposition regularly, pressure-redistributing mattress, inspect skin, manage moisture and nutrition
Hair at a surgical siteLeave it, or remove with clippers, not a razor

The clinicians involved

Clinicians involved in an error often feel shame, fear and self-doubt (the "second victim" response). The right answer for a colleague is to acknowledge the distress, offer peer support or the institution's support programme, and keep them involved in learning from the event, not to tell them to forget it or to keep quiet. Residents must report their duty hours accurately; being asked to under-report is itself a patient-safety and professionalism problem to raise with the programme.

Order of actions after an error: patient safety now → attending → disclosure with apology → incident report → system analysis → support for the staff involved.

s23g-s1904.bodyHtml:
Policy questions on Step 2 CK are framed as patients: an uninsured man in the emergency department, a retiree confused about drug coverage, a young adult losing student insurance, a parent asking for a vaccine exemption, a patient with tuberculosis who will not stay in isolation. Know the programme rules and the public-health powers well enough to give the patient correct advice.

EMTALA in the emergency department

Any person who comes to the emergency department of a hospital that participates in Medicare and requests care must receive a medical screening examination to determine whether an emergency medical condition exists. Registration may continue in parallel, but questions about insurance or payment must not delay the screening or treatment. If an emergency condition (including active labour) is present, the hospital must stabilise it within its capability or arrange an appropriate transfer: the patient is transferred because the hospital cannot provide the needed care (or the patient asks, after being told the risks), a physician certifies that the benefits outweigh the risks, the receiving hospital has accepted, and records go with the patient. Transfer because of lack of insurance is prohibited. Hospitals with specialised capabilities must accept appropriate transfers if they have capacity. A patient with decision-making capacity may refuse examination or treatment after being told the risks; the refusal is documented.

EMTALA does not require free ongoing care after stabilisation, and it applies only to emergencies. It also does not allow a "wallet biopsy" before screening.

Advising patients about coverage

Patient situationWhat to tell them
Turning 65, worried about outpatient drug costsParts A and B do not cover most outpatient prescriptions; add a Part D plan or choose a Medicare Advantage plan with drug coverage
Older adult who will need permanent nursing home careMedicare covers only limited skilled post-hospital stays, not long-term custodial care; Medicaid may pay once income and assets meet state limits
Young adult under 26 who lost student coverageMay join a parent's plan that offers dependent coverage, even if married, living independently or not a tax dependent
Chronic disease, afraid to change jobsIndividual and group plans may not exclude or surcharge pre-existing conditions
Low income after dischargeApply for Medicaid at any time of year (eligibility for adults depends on whether the state expanded); marketplace plans need open enrolment or a qualifying life event
Under 65 with ESRD or ALSMay qualify for Medicare without reaching 65

Choosing Medicare Advantage versus traditional Medicare is a trade-off: Advantage plans have a yearly out-of-pocket limit and often extra benefits, but use networks and prior authorisation; traditional Medicare allows any participating clinician nationwide but has no built-in out-of-pocket cap, so many beneficiaries add supplemental (Medigap) coverage.

Vaccination requirements and exemptions

School-entry vaccine requirements are set by each state. All states accept medical exemptions, for a true contraindication such as severe immunosuppression for live vaccines or anaphylaxis to a previous dose. Non-medical exemptions differ between states. When a parent is hesitant, the first step is to explore their concerns and give clear information; a physician should not sign a medical exemption without a medical reason. During an outbreak, unvaccinated children may be excluded from school by the health department.

Isolation, quarantine and reporting

Public-health authority belongs mainly to the states (their police power), carried out by state and local health departments; the federal government (CDC) handles interstate and international spread. Clinicians and laboratories must report notifiable diseases to the health department; this is a permitted disclosure that does not need the patient's consent. For a patient with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis who refuses treatment or isolation, the physician should counsel the patient and notify the health department, which can require directly observed therapy and, as a last resort, obtain a legal order for isolation.

Agencies in everyday practice

  • A suspected device malfunction or serious drug reaction: report to the FDA's adverse-event reporting system.
  • An adverse event after vaccination: report to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, run jointly by CDC and FDA.
  • An outbreak in a school or a restaurant: the local health department leads, with CDC support if needed.
  • Hospital rules that come with Medicare payment (conditions of participation): CMS.

Telehealth and licensure

For a video visit, the physician generally needs a licence in the state where the patient is physically located at the time of the visit. Interstate licensure compacts make it faster to obtain additional state licences but do not create a single national licence. The same standard of care, consent and privacy rules apply as in person.

In access questions, the best answer connects the patient to the programme they actually qualify for (Medicaid application, parent's plan, Part D, social work or a financial counsellor) rather than delaying needed care.

Any person who comes to the emergency department of a hospital that participates in Medicare and requests care must receive a

to determine whether an emergency medical condition exists. Registration may continue in parallel, but questions about insurance or payment must not delay the screening or treatment. If an emergency condition (including active labour) is present, the hospital must
it within its capability or arrange an

: the patient is transferred because the hospital cannot provide the needed care (or the patient asks, after being told the risks), a physician certifies that the benefits outweigh the risks, the receiving hospital has accepted, and records go with the patient. Transfer because of lack of insurance is prohibited. Hospitals with specialised capabilities must accept appropriate transfers if they have capacity. A patient with decision-making capacity may refuse examination or treatment after being told the risks; the refusal is documented.
EMTALA does not require free ongoing care after stabilisation, and it applies only to emergencies. It also does not allow a "wallet biopsy" before screening.
Turning 65, worried about outpatient drug costs
Parts A and B do not cover most outpatient prescriptions; add a Part D plan or choose a Medicare Advantage plan with drug coverage
Older adult who will need permanent nursing home care
Medicare covers only limited skilled post-hospital stays, not long-term custodial care; Medicaid may pay once income and assets meet state limits
Young adult under 26 who lost student coverage
May join a parent's plan that offers dependent coverage, even if married, living independently or not a tax dependent
Chronic disease, afraid to change jobs
Individual and group plans may not exclude or surcharge pre-existing conditions
Apply for Medicaid at any time of year (eligibility for adults depends on whether the state expanded); marketplace plans need open enrolment or a qualifying life event
May qualify for Medicare without reaching 65

Choosing Medicare Advantage versus traditional Medicare is a trade-off: Advantage plans have a yearly out-of-pocket limit and often extra benefits, but use networks and prior authorisation; traditional Medicare allows any participating clinician nationwide but has no built-in out-of-pocket cap, so many beneficiaries add supplemental (Medigap) coverage.
School-entry vaccine requirements are set by each state. All states accept

, for a true contraindication such as severe immunosuppression for live vaccines or anaphylaxis to a previous dose. Non-medical exemptions differ between states. When a parent is hesitant, the first step is to explore their concerns and give clear information; a physician should not sign a medical exemption without a medical reason. During an outbreak, unvaccinated children may be excluded from school by the health department.

Public-health authority belongs mainly to the states (their police power), carried out by state and local health departments; the federal government (CDC) handles interstate and international spread. Clinicians and laboratories must report notifiable diseases to the health department; this is a permitted disclosure that does not need the patient's consent. For a patient with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis who refuses treatment or isolation, the physician should counsel the patient and notify the health department, which can require directly observed therapy and, as a last resort, obtain a legal order for isolation.
A suspected device malfunction or serious drug reaction: report to the FDA's adverse-event reporting system.
An adverse event after vaccination: report to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, run jointly by CDC and FDA.
An outbreak in a school or a restaurant: the local health department leads, with CDC support if needed.
Hospital rules that come with Medicare payment (conditions of participation): CMS.
For a video visit, the physician generally needs a licence in the state where the

is physically located at the time of the visit. Interstate licensure compacts make it faster to obtain additional state licences but do not create a single national licence. The same standard of care, consent and privacy rules apply as in person.

In access questions, the best answer connects the patient to the programme they actually qualify for (Medicaid application, parent's plan, Part D, social work or a financial counsellor) rather than delaying needed care.

s23g-s1905.bodyHtml:
On Step 2 CK, health economics appears as a patient comparing plans, a bill that seems wrong, a hospital reacting to a payment rule, or an abstract reporting an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio. Work it through with arithmetic and with the incentive each payment creates.

Comparing plans for a patient

Expected yearly cost = premiums + expected out-of-pocket spending (deductible, copayments and coinsurance, up to the out-of-pocket maximum). Three steps:

  1. Estimate the allowed cost of the care the patient expects (a planned operation, regular visits, drugs).
  2. Apply each plan's rules in order: copays for services not subject to the deductible, then the deductible, then coinsurance, then cap the total at the out-of-pocket maximum.
  3. Add the premium, which never counts toward the cap.

Worked example (hypothetical): a plan with a yearly premium of 2,400, deductible 2,000, 20% coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximum 5,000. For a 15,000 operation the patient pays 2,000 + 0.20 × 13,000 = 4,600 (below the cap), so the year costs 2,400 + 4,600 = 7,000. A healthy person who expects little care usually does best with the lowest premium; a person expecting a large expense often does best with the lowest out-of-pocket maximum or the best balance of the two.

Do not choose the plan with the lowest deductible or lowest premium by reflex. Do the sum, and remember the out-of-pocket maximum.

Networks and referrals

An HMO member needs a referral from the primary care physician to see most specialists and has no coverage out of network except emergencies. A PPO member may self-refer and go out of network at higher cost. An EPO has a network like an HMO, usually without referrals, and pays nothing out of network except emergencies. A POS plan uses a primary care gatekeeper but pays something out of network. Before a planned out-of-network visit, the patient should check network status and referral rules.

Surprise bills and estimates

Under the No Surprises Act, patients in plans covered by the law owe only in-network cost-sharing for emergency services (even at an out-of-network hospital) and for out-of-network clinicians who treat them at an in-network facility; for clinicians the patient does not choose, such as anaesthesia, radiology, pathology and assistant surgeons, this protection cannot be waived. Uninsured or self-pay patients scheduling care are entitled to a good-faith estimate of the expected charges. Hospitals must also publish their prices for common services.

Value-based payment in hospitals and practices

ProgrammeWhat it rewardsLikely response
Inpatient DRG paymentEfficient staysShorter length of stay, earlier discharge planning
Readmissions penaltyFewer excess 30-day readmissionsDischarge follow-up calls, early clinic visits, medication reconciliation
Bundled episode paymentLow total cost of the episode with good qualityFewer complications, discharge home rather than to a facility when safe, coordination with post-acute care
ACO shared savingsLower total cost of care for an attributed population with quality targets metCare management for high-risk patients, preventive care, avoiding duplicated tests
CapitationKeeping enrolled people healthy within a fixed budgetPrevention, phone and telehealth care, careful referral

Reading a cost-effectiveness abstract

  1. Identify the comparator (usual care, or the next best strategy).
  2. Compute differences: ΔCost and ΔEffect (QALYs or natural units).
  3. ICER = ΔCost ÷ ΔEffect. Example: 4,000 more and 0.08 QALY more gives 50,000 per QALY.
  4. Check dominance: cheaper and better dominates; dearer and worse is dominated and is removed before ICERs are calculated between the remaining strategies, which are compared in order of effectiveness.
  5. Compare the ICER with the decision-maker's willingness-to-pay threshold, and look at the sensitivity analyses: if a plausible change in one input moves the conclusion, the result is uncertain.
  6. Note the perspective (health system, payer, societal) and time horizon, which change which costs are counted.

A cost-effectiveness ratio is meaningful only relative to a comparator. "Cost per QALY" of one strategy on its own (average ratio) is not an ICER.

Why the bill is so high

Compared with peer countries, the US has similar or lower use of many services (doctor visits, hospital days) but much higher prices per service and higher administrative costs. When an exam table shows similar utilisation and higher price indices, the conclusion is that prices drive the spending gap.
